## 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 (id: eng-2ch-p22-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous stories, we heard how the people of Israel who wanted to obey Yahweh moved from the northern kingdom of Israel to the southern kingdom of Judah. This made King Rehoboam and Judah strong, because the people followed Yahweh. Now, in this story, we will hear what happened after Rehoboam became strong.

Stop here and listen: If you have already translated 1 Kings 14:21–31, which contains the same information as this story, listen to your translation of that passage as a group. Pause this audio here.

As the story begins, we hear that after Rehoboam became strong, Rehoboam and all the people of Judah stopped obeying Yahweh's law. So, in the fifth year that Rehoboam was king, Shishak, the king of Egypt, came and attacked Jerusalem.

People called the kings of Egypt "pharaohs." Most people believe that Shishak was the pharaoh from 931 B.C. to 910 B.C. or from 945 B.C. to 924 B.C.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How does a person become the most important leader in your culture? If that leader dies, how do people decide who will be the next leader? Pause this audio here.

So Shishak and all of the soldiers with Shishak came to fight against the people in Jerusalem. You will remember that Jerusalem was not only where Rehoboam lived, but Jerusalem was also the city where King David had built the royal palace and where King Solomon had built the temple, the place where the Israelites worshiped Yahweh. The storyteller says that Shishak came with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen, or men to help drive the chariots and fight from the chariots. Shishak also brought a countless number of soldiers from Egypt, including Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites or Nubians. These were all people who had come from other countries to live in Egypt. Libyans were people who came from the coast of North Africa, west of Egypt. We are not sure who the Sukkites were, but the Sukkites may have come from the desert west of Egypt. Some translations call the Cushites or Nubians "Ethiopians," but these people did not come from the land we call Ethiopia today. These people came from Cush or Nubia, which was the land south and east of Egypt. With all of these soldiers, Shishak fought against and took control of all of the strong, protected cities in Judah until Shishak came to Jerusalem, toward the northern end of Judah.

Stop here as a group and look at a map that shows Egypt, the lands west of Egypt where these people groups might have come from, and Israel to the north. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of Israel that shows the kingdom of Judah. Find the city of Jerusalem in Judah. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about people who live in one place but who come from different places and cultures. Tell how these people live and work together, even though these people may look and act differently from one another. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that at this time, the prophet Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah in Jerusalem. Shemaiah told these men that Shemaiah had a message from Yahweh. This message was that because the people of Judah had turned away from Yahweh, Yahweh would now turn away from Judah, so that Shishak's army would beat Judah in battle. However, when the leaders of Judah heard this message, the leaders acted humbly and said that Yahweh was right to punish the leaders. So Yahweh spoke to Shemaiah again. This time, Yahweh said that because the leaders were sorry for the bad things they had done, Yahweh would keep the leaders alive. However, Yahweh would still allow King Shishak to defeat Judah and make the people serve Shishak. Yahweh wants the people of Judah to see how difficult it is to serve foreign kings. Then the people will understand that it is always better to serve Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about a parent who instructs a child to keep the child safe. Tell how the child disobeys those instructions and does something dangerous. Then tell how the parent disciplines the child because the parent loves the child and wants the child to learn to be safe. Pause this audio here.

Because Yahweh promised to protect the leaders, we know that Shishak's army did not destroy Jerusalem. However, the storyteller says that when Shishak came to Jerusalem, Shishak took away all of the valuable things from Yahweh's temple and from the king's palace. Shishak even took away the gold shields that King Solomon had made. So King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold shields. Bronze is a less expensive metal than gold. Rehoboam gave these bronze shields to the officers of the royal guard who stood at the door of the king's house to protect the king. Every time King Rehoboam went to the house of Yahweh to worship, the guards came and carried those shields. And when the king left the temple, the guards took the shields back to the guardroom, a special place in the temple where the guards kept the ceremonial equipment that the guards used to serve the king.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what ceremonial items do you use when you do a job for a king or important leader? Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a shield. Pause this audio here.

When Rehoboam acted humbly and admitted that Rehoboam had done wrong, Yahweh turned his anger away from Rehoboam so that Shishak did not completely destroy Judah. Instead, God caused good things to happen in Judah. And King Rehoboam became powerful as king once again in Jerusalem. The storyteller says that Rehoboam was 41 years old when Rehoboam first became king of Judah, and Rehoboam reigned in Jerusalem for a total of 17 years. The storyteller also reminds us that out of all the towns in Israel, Jerusalem was the town where Yahweh chose for people to come and worship Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, where do people go to worship God or the local spirits or gods? Who decides the correct place or places where people should worship? Pause this audio here.

Rehoboam's mother was Naamah, one of the many non\-Israelite women Solomon married and had children with. Naamah was from the Ammonite people who lived northeast of the Dead Sea. And Rehoboam did many bad things because Rehoboam did not choose to fully serve Yahweh.

The story says that many things happened while Rehoboam was king of Judah, and the prophet Shemaiah wrote about these things in a book, or scroll. The storyteller also says that the prophet Iddo wrote about Rehoboam in Iddo's book of family histories. However, we know that these writings no longer exist, so we cannot read these writings to learn more about Rehoboam. The storyteller does remind us that Rehoboam was always at war with Jeroboam, the king of the northern kingdom of Israel.

Finally, Rehoboam died, and people buried Rehoboam's body near Rehoboam's ancestors in the old part of Jerusalem that people called the City of David. In ancient Israel, people usually buried a king's body in a tomb, which is a special cave or room that people carved into a large rock. Then Reboboam's son Abijah became the next king of Judah.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define this passage's scenes, characters, and setting. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has five scenes.

**In the first scene:** King Rehoboam stops obeying Yahweh, so King Shishak of Egypt comes to attack Judah with so many soldiers that no one can count them all. Shishak takes control of Judah's cities all the way to Jerusalem.

**In the second scene:** Shemaiah the prophet tells Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah that Yahweh has abandoned Judah because the people of Judah have abandoned Yahweh. However, when Rehoboam and the leaders hear this, they humble themselves and agree that Yahweh is right. And so Yahweh says Yahweh will not destroy Judah completely.

**In the third scene:** King Shishak attacks Jerusalem and steals the expensive things from the temple and the royal palace. But because Rehoboam humbles himself, Yahweh does not destroy Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah.

**In the fourth scene:** King Rehoboam grows strong as king in Jerusalem, and Rehoboam reigns as king for 17 years. But Rehoboam does evil things as king because Rehoboam does not choose to follow Yahweh fully.

**In the fifth scene:** Rehoboam dies, and Rehoboam's son Abijah becomes the next king of Judah.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Rehoboam
* Yahweh
* All of the people of Judah, the southern kingdom of Israel
* King Shishak of Egypt
* King Shishak's army
* Soldiers from the countries of Libya, Suk, and Ethiopia
* Shemaiah, Yahweh's prophet
* The leaders of Judah
* The guards at Rehoboam's palace
* Rehoboam's mother, Naamah, who was an Ammonite
* The prophet Iddo
* Rehoboam's ancestors
* And Abijah, Rehoboam's son

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, the storyteller says that after Rehoboam had taken control of the kingdom and become a strong king, Rehoboam abandoned the law of Yahweh, and all of the people of Israel did too. Here, "all of Israel" means all of the people who lived in the southern kingdom of Judah. You will remember that the law was all of the commandments or instructions that Yahweh had given to the people of Israel through Moses.

So in the fifth year after Rehoboam became king, because the people had been unfaithful to Yahweh and stopped obeying Yahweh, King Shishak came up from Egypt to attack Jerusalem. You will remember that after Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, Yahweh told Moses that if the Israelites obeyed Yahweh, Yahweh would protect the people, but if the people stopped obeying Yahweh, Yahweh would allow the Israelites' enemies to defeat the Israelites. So here, Yahweh allows the Egyptians to attack the kingdom of Judah because the people have stopped obeying Yahweh.

King Shishak comes up from Egypt with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. You will remember that a chariot was a special cart with two wheels that horses would pull. Two special soldiers, called horsemen, would ride in a chariot into battle. One soldier would drive the chariot while the other soldier would fight. Chariots made an army very strong and difficult to defeat.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a chariot. Pause this audio here.

Shishak also brought with him a very large number of other soldiers who lived in Egypt. The storyteller says that no one could count the number of soldiers Shishak brought because there were so many soldiers. The storyteller says these people included Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites or Ethiopians. All of these people with Shishak captured the fortified cities of Judah, which probably means the larger cities or towns in Judah that people had built walls around to protect those cities. Finally, Shishak and his army came to Jerusalem, the city where Rehoboam lived.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about a very large number of people? Pause this audio here.

Next, the storyteller says that the prophet Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who had all come to Jerusalem when Shishak attacked the other cities. You will remember that the storyteller told us about Shemaiah in a previous story, where Yahweh sent Shemaiah to give Rehoboam a message. In this story, Shemaiah gives another message from Yahweh. This time, Shemaiah says that Yahweh tells Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah that because they have abandoned Yahweh, Yahweh will now abandon them. This means that Yahweh will no longer protect the people from their enemies, just as Yahweh had warned the Israelites through Moses many generations ago.

But when the leaders of Judah heard this message that Shemaiah spoke from Yahweh, the leaders humbled themselves. This means that the leaders agreed that the leaders had done wrong and that the leaders were now sorry. The leaders also said Yahweh was right to punish the leaders because the leaders had done wrong.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a child who disobeys that child's parent. Tell how the parent tells the child that they must discipline the child. Finally, tell how the child admits they had done wrong and that the child deserves punishment. Pay attention to the words you use to describe how the child acts when the child says this. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that when Yahweh saw how the leaders humbled themselves, the word of Yahweh again came to Shemaiah. This means that Yahweh told Shemaiah another message to tell the leaders. Yahweh said that because the leaders humbled themselves, Yahweh would not let Shishak destroy the leaders, and Yahweh would not pour out Yahweh's wrath on Jerusalem. To pour out is special language that shows that when Yahweh feels angry, Yahweh usually does something to show that Yahweh is angry. Although Yahweh would not pour out Yahweh's anger, the leaders of Judah would have to serve Shishak. This way, the leaders would learn that it is better to serve Yahweh than to serve a foreign king.

So when Shishak, the king of Egypt, came up against or attacked Jerusalem, Shishak carried off the treasures from Yahweh's temple and from the royal palace. This means that Shishak's army took the most valuable things that the people of Judah owned. The storyteller says that Shishak even took the gold shields that Solomon had made. You will remember from 2 Chronicles 9 how King Solomon had made 200 shields from gold. The storyteller says that King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold shields. The storyteller does not say when Rehoboam did this, but this probably means that sometime after Shishak took the shields, Rehoboam had craftsmen make new shields from bronze. Then Rehoboam assigned these shields to the commanders of the guard on duty at the entrance to the royal palace. Whenever King Rehoboam went to Yahweh's temple, the guards went with Rehoboam and carried the shields. And afterward, the guards took the shields back to the guardroom, or the place where the guards stored the shields.

The storyteller says that because Rehoboam humbled himself, Yahweh's wrath turned from Rehoboam so that Rehoboam was not killed. This means that Yahweh held back Yahweh's anger and did not punish Rehoboam like Yahweh had planned. The storyteller also says there were good things in Judah during this time. This may mean that people had all that they needed and lived safely and comfortably. But it is even more likely that the storyteller means that even though people sinned in Judah during this time, many people were basically faithful to God. So King Rehoboam regained his power as king in Jerusalem.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a parent who felt very angry because of how a child disobeyed the parent. Tell how the parent decided not to discipline the child even though the child deserved discipline. Pay attention to the words you use to describe how the parent felt angry, but how the parent did not take any angry actions. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that Rehoboam was 41 years old when Rehoboam first became king, and Rehoboam reigned as king of Judah for 17 years in Jerusalem. The storyteller also reminds us that Yahweh himself chose Jerusalem out of all the tribes of Israel to put Yahweh's name there. You will remember that in that culture, a person's name represented that person's character or their self. This means that Yahweh chose Jerusalem as the place where the people of Israel would come to worship Yahweh and where Yahweh's presence would stay in the temple.

Rehoboam's mother's name was Naamah, and Naamah was an Ammonitess, a woman from the country of Ammon. The storyteller also reminds us that Rehoboam did evil and sinned. Rehoboam did not set his heart to seek Yahweh. This means that Rehoboam did not want to obey Yahweh, and that Rehoboam did not serve Yahweh or ask what Yahweh wanted Rehoboam to do.

The storyteller asks a question that he does not expect anyone to answer: "All of the acts of Rehoboam, or the things that Rehoboam did as king, are they not written in the records of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer?" You will remember that a seer is like a prophet. These men wrote down the important things that Rehoboam did so that people would remember these things. These men probably wrote these things down on scrolls, or long pieces of animal skin or paper that people rolled around two long sticks. However, we know that these writings no longer exist today.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture keep important stories or information about the past? How do you talk about the way people keep this information? Pause this audio here.

King Rehoboam and King Jeroboam were constantly at war with each other. Then Rehoboam rested with his fathers, or ancestors, and people buried Rehoboam in the City of David. "Rested" is a nice way to say that Rehoboam died. To bury a dead body means to put that person's body into a place in the ground where no one can see the body. In ancient Israel, people usually buried the body of a king in a tomb, which is a special cave or room that people carved into a large rock. The City of David was the older part of the city of Jerusalem that existed when David was king. And then Rehoboam's son Abijah became the next king after Rehoboam.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about how someone died and what people did with that person's body. Pay attention to the words you use to talk about these things. Then talk as a group about how you will translate this part of the story so people will understand. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has five scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Rehoboam
* Yahweh
* All of the people of Judah, the southern kingdom of Israel
* King Shishak of Egypt
* King Shishak's army
* Soldiers from the countries of Libya, Suk, and Ethiopia
* Shemaiah, Yahweh's prophet
* The leaders of Judah
* The guards at Rehoboam's palace
* Rehoboam's mother, Naamah, who was an Ammonite
* The prophet Iddo
* Rehoboam's ancestors
* And Abijah, Rehoboam's son

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

After Rehoboam had taken control of Judah and become a strong king, Rehoboam and all the people of the kingdom rejected Yahweh and stopped obeying Yahweh's commands. So because the people disobeyed, Shishak, the king of Egypt, came and attacked Jerusalem. This happened during the fifth year after Rehoboam became king. Shishak came from Egypt with 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and a countless number of soldiers that included Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites. And Shishak captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far north as Jerusalem.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I told the Israelites long ago that if the people obeyed me, I would protect the people, but if the people did not obey me, I would allow their enemies to defeat them; or
* I love my people, the Israelites, and want them to obey me and worship only me, so it makes me angry when the Israelites worship idols; or
* If Rehoboam and the people are going to worship idols and do these evil things, I will do whatever it takes to stop them.

Continue the drama.

Then the prophet Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who had all gathered together in Jerusalem because they were afraid of Shishak. And Shemaiah said, "This is what Yahweh says, 'You have turned away from me. So now I will turn away from you, and I will let Shishak defeat you in battle.'" But when the leaders heard what Yahweh said, Rehoboam and the rest of the leaders humbled themselves and said, "What Yahweh does is fair." When Yahweh saw that the leaders humbled themselves, Yahweh gave another message to Shemaiah. Yahweh said, "Because the leaders have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them. Instead, I will rescue the leaders from their enemy. I will not let Shishak destroy Jerusalem because of my anger. But I will let Shishak defeat the leaders and make them serve Shishak. This way, the leaders will learn that it is better to serve Yahweh than to serve other kings."

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing Rehoboam and the other leaders of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We should not have disobeyed Yahweh. Yahweh always protected our ancestors when they obeyed Yahweh, and we need Yahweh's protection now; or
* We feel so relieved that Yahweh decided he would not kill us! or
* I hope Shishak does not treat us too badly or take too much of our wealth and power away from us.

> Continue the drama.
> 
> When King Shishak of Egypt and his army fought against Jerusalem and defeated them, Shishak took away all of the expensive things from Yahweh's temple and from Rehoboam's palace. Shishak even took all of the gold shields that Solomon had made. So Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold shields. Rehoboam gave the shields to the officers of the guards who protected the door of the king's palace. Whenever the king went to Yahweh's temple, the guards went with the king and carried the shields. And afterward, the guards brought the shields back to the storage room.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Rehoboam, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am very grateful that Shishak did not kill me, but I feel sad and ashamed that I lost all those beautiful things my father, Solomon, made; or
* These bronze shields are not nearly as beautiful and impressive as the gold ones Solomon made, but hopefully, people will still be impressed when they see the large number of men I have to guard me.

> Continue the drama.
> 
> Because Rehoboam humbled himself, Yahweh stopped being angry against Rehoboam. This is why Yahweh did not allow Shishak to destroy the kingdom of Judah. In fact, God caused some good things to happen in Judah. King Rehoboam made himself powerful in Jerusalem and continued to be king there. Rehoboam was 41 years old when he first became king, and Rehoboam reigned in Jerusalem for 17 years. Jerusalem was the town that Yahweh chose from all the clans in Israel to be the place where people would come to worship Yahweh. Rehoboam's mothers's name was Naamah, and Naamah was from the country of Ammon. Rehoboam did very bad things because Rehoboam did not choose to fully serve Yahweh. Shemaiah the prophet wrote about everything that Rehoboam did as king in Shemaiah's book, and Iddo the prophet also wrote these things in Iddo's book of family histories. The armies of Rehoboam, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel, were always fighting.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Shemaiah the prophet, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I wrote the stories about King Rehoboam so people would not forget these things; or
* These stories will help our people remember how Yahweh has been faithful to Israel even when Israel was not faithful to Yahweh; or
* Rehoboam did many evil things, but I hope these stories will remind people to obey Yahweh.

Continue the drama.

Rehoboam died, just like his ancestors died. And the people buried Rehoboam's body in the part of Jerusalem that people call the City of David. And Rehoboam's son Abijah became the new king of Judah.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Rehoboam, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am grateful that I was able to be king for so many years; or
* Shishak took a lot of wealth and power from me, but I am happy that Yahweh allowed me to live and that good things happened in Judah after that; or
* Although I was sorry when Yahweh said he would punish us, the truth is that I liked serving the idols and doing the things Yahweh said not to do.

Ask the person playing Abijah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* My father was king for a long time, and I hope I can be king for a long time too; or
* I know my father worshiped idols of the gods from other people groups, so I will worship those idols too; or
* My father always fought with King Jeroboam, so I will fight Jeroboam too.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 12:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

When Rehoboam's **kingdom** was established, Rehoboam and all of **Israel** abandoned Yahweh's **law**. A kingdom is the territory that a king rules. You will remember that at this time, Israel was divided into two kingdoms with two different kings. Although people called the southern kingdom "Judah" and the northern kingdom "Israel," all of the people were still part of the nation of Israel. But in this story, "Israel" specifically refers to the people living in the southern kingdom of Judah. The law means the set of instructions God gave the people of Israel. For more information about kingdom, Israel, and law, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for kingdom, Israel, and law as you used in previous passages.

Shishak came with 1,200 **chariots** and attacked Judah's "fortified," or strong, **cities**. These cities probably had walls around them for protection. Use the same words for chariots and for cities as you have used in previous passages.

When Shishak comes to attack Jerusalem, Shemaiah, the **prophet,** comes to Rehoboam and the princes of Judah to give a message, or "**word**," from **Yahweh**. A prophet is a person who gives messages from God to the people. A message, or word, might be an instruction from God about something that needs to be done, or it might tell about something that is going to happen in the future. But most of the time, these messages were warnings to the people to stop disobeying God. The name Yahweh is the personal name for God that showed the close relationship that God had with the people of Israel. When people hear this name of God, the people are reminded especially of the covenant, the special promise, that God had made with the Israelites at the time of Moses. Use the same words or phrases for prophet, word, and Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on prophet, word, and Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

When they heard this message from Yahweh, King Rehoboam and the princes, or leaders, of Judah **humbled** themselves and said that Yahweh was righteous. To humble themselves means that the princes, or leaders, admitted they were wrong. Use the same word or phrase for humbled as you used in previous passages.

In this story, a prince means a person who rules or holds authority over other people, like a chief or main leader. A righteous person is someone who does what is right, fair, or just.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for **princes** and **righteous**. Look up righteousness in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

When the leaders humble themselves, Yahweh says that Yahweh will not pour out Yahweh's wrath on Jerusalem **by the hand of** Shishak. The storytellers in the Bible often use the word hand as special language to mean a person's power or strength. Use the same word or phrase for "by the hand of" as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **pour out his wrath**. Look up wrath in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this phrase in another book of the Bible, use the same phrase that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

However, Yahweh says that Yahweh will make Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah to be Shishak's **servants** or **slaves** so that they will learn the difference between serving Yahweh and serving the kings of other **lands**. A servant is a person who does work for someone else. If a servant does not get paid for his work and does not have the freedom to leave his master when he wants, then people call the servant a slave. Here, the word lands means the territory or areas of land that other kings rule. Use the same words or phrases for servants or slaves, and lands, as you used in previous passages. Refer to servants in the Master Glossary for more information.

Shishak took treasures from the **temple** and the **palace**. Translate king's house, or "palace," and temple in the same way you have in previous passages. Temple is in the Master Glossary.

Shishak took the **shields** of **gold**, so Rehoboam made shields of **bronze** to replace those shields. A shield is something that soldiers use to protect themselves from an enemy's attack. People usually made shields with a wooden frame and covered that frame with animal hide or leather. Shields that people covered with metal were not common because, although this kind of shield provided better protection, it was also heavier and more difficult to carry. Gold is a very expensive metal that is yellow in color and does not tarnish. Bronze is also a yellow metal, but bronze is less expensive and does tarnish. Use the same words or phrases for shields, gold, and bronze as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a shield that is covered in metal, if needed. Pause this audio here.

Rehoboam did **evil** because Rehoboam did not set Rehoboam's **heart** to seek Yahweh. Evil is the opposite of good. A person who is evil willingly does bad things that hurt other people. When people stop obeying God, those people begin to do evil actions. In the Bible, people often use the heart as special language to mean the place where a person's thoughts, feelings, and decisions happen. Someone with a "wicked heart" thinks evil things and makes evil decisions. And someone with a "good heart" wants to do the right things and feels sad when they have sinned. Use the same word or phrase for "hearts" as you used in previous passages. For more information on heart, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **evil**. Look up evil in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that Shemaiah the **prophet** and Iddo the **seer** wrote down all of the important things that happened during Rehoboam's time as king in Iddo's book of genealogies. A genealogy is a list of people who have the same ancestor. A seer is another word for a prophet. For more information on prophet, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for prophet and seer as you used in previous passages.

The storyteller calls these books the "words" of Shemaiah and of Iddo. Remember that these are probably **scrolls** that people wrote on. If you use the word for scrolls in your translation, refer to the Master Glossary for more information about scrolls.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **genealogies**. For more information, refer to genealogy in the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

At the end of the story, the storyteller says that Rehoboam **slept with his fathers** and they buried Rehoboam in the **City of David**. "Slept with his fathers" is special language that is a nice way to say that Rehoboam died and that people buried Rehoboam near the same place people had buried Rehoboam's "fathers," which here means ancestors. You will remember that people usually buried kings in a cave or room that people had carved out of rock, but this word for buried is a general word for how someone puts a dead body in a cave or a grave in the ground. You will remember that people called this part of Jerusalem the "City of David" because it was the part of the city that existed when David was king. Use the same words or phrases for "slept with his fathers" and "City of David" as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **buried**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

## 2 Chronicles 13:13–14:1 (id: eng-2ch-p24-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 13:13–14:1 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 13:13–14:1 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 13:13–14:1 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, King Abijah of Judah and Abijah's army, and King Jeroboam of Israel and Jeroboam's army, came together in one place to fight a battle. But before the soldiers began to fight, King Abijah went up on a hill and spoke loudly so that King Jeroboam and everyone else could hear. King Abijah said that King Jeroboam had disobeyed Yahweh and made idols to worship instead of worshiping Yahweh. But the people of Judah continue to worship Yahweh. And so Yahweh is with Judah and will not let Jeroboam and the kingdom of Israel win this battle.

In this story, we will now learn what happens during the battle. First, the storyteller explains that while Abijah was still speaking, King Jeroboam set an ambush by secretly sending some of Jeroboam's soldiers to a place on the other side of Abijah's army, so those soldiers could attack the army of Judah by surprise from behind. So now Jeroboam had soldiers ready to fight both in front of Abijah's army and behind Abijah's army.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture fight battles? What are some common war strategies or decisions that leaders make in a battle to surprise the enemy and help win the battle? Pause this audio here.

This is a very dangerous situation for the soldiers of Judah. When soldiers fight an enemy, it is very important to see the enemy so the soldiers can block an attack and know how and when to fight back. But when a soldier is watching and fighting an enemy in front, that soldier cannot see what is happening behind the soldier or block an attack from behind. So when an enemy attacks from both in front and behind like this, that enemy can easily kill the soldiers.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time when soldiers made a decision in a battle to surprise their enemy. Pause this audio here.

When the army of Judah turns around and sees the soldiers Jeroboam has sent to attack them from behind, the soldiers of Judah realize they are in great danger. So the army of Judah cries out or shouts for Yahweh to help Judah. And the priests, who help the Israelites worship and obey Yahweh, blow their trumpets. You will remember from the book of Numbers that Yahweh had told the priests to blow their trumpets whenever the Israelites needed Yahweh's help in battle. Then the men of Judah shout very loudly. Soldiers often did this when they would attack an enemy to show the soldiers' strength and to make the enemy afraid. And when the men of Judah shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel. In the Bible, God often uses things like sickness, wild animals, or floods to punish people, but here God gives the army of Judah the power to punish Israel.

The soldiers of Israel ran away from the soldiers of Judah, and God caused the soldiers of Judah to win the battle. Abijah's soldiers killed 500,000 well\-trained soldiers of Israel. These were all of Israel's best soldiers. That day, the people of Israel lost the battle, and the people of Judah won, because they trusted Yahweh, the God their ancestors worshiped.

Abijah and his soldiers went after Jeroboam's soldiers and captured some of Jeroboam's cities. Abijah and his soldiers took control of Bethel and its surrounding villages, Jeshanah and its surrounding villages, and Ephron and its surrounding villages. All of these cities and their villages were in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Bethel was about 16 kilometers north of Jerusalem, Jeshanah was about 25 kilometers north of Jerusalem, and Ephron was about 6\.5 kilometers northeast of Bethel and 21 kilometers northeast of Jerusalem.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of Israel. Find the cities of Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron in the territory of Benjamin. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller explains that after this battle, Jeroboam never became powerful again during Abijah's reign. Finally, Yahweh punished Jeroboam so that Jeroboam became sick and died. But Abijah became more and more powerful. In those days, one way that a king showed he was powerful was to have many wives and children. Abijah married 14 wives and had 22 sons and 16 daughters.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a person who had a very large family with many children. What did people think about that person because the person had a large family? Pause this audio here.

King Abijah did many other things while Abijah was king of Judah. And the prophet Iddo wrote down the things that Abijah did and said in Iddo's book. Unfortunately, Iddo's book no longer exists today, so no one knows what that book said about Abijah.

Finally, Abijah died, and people buried Abijah just like people had buried Abijah's ancestors. The people buried Abijah in the part of Jerusalem that people called the City of David. Abijah's son Asa became the next king of Judah. And during Asa's reign, the country was at peace or without any war for 10 years.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 13:13–14:1 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

**In the first scene:** King Jeroboam of Israel secretly sends men to the other side of the army of Judah so that the army of Israel can fight Judah from both sides at the same time. But when Judah's army sees that they will have to fight the battle on both sides, Judah's army cries to Yahweh for help, and Yahweh helps the army.

**In the second scene:** Abijah's army defeats the army of Israel, and the Israelite soldiers run away. But Abijah's army runs after the Israelite army and kills 500,000 soldiers. Abijah's army is able to do this because the people rely on Yahweh. Abijah also takes cities and villages from Jeroboam.

**In the third scene:** We learn that Jeroboam never got his power back after Jeroboam lost this battle to Abijah. Yahweh caused Jeroboam to die, but Abijah grew very powerful. And Abijah had many wives and children. Then Abijah died, Abijah's son Asa became king, and the people lived in peace for 10 years.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Jeroboam
* The army of Israel
* King Abijah
* The army of Judah
* God, whose name is Yahweh
* The priests
* The people of the cities of Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron and their villages
* King Abijah's wives and children
* King Abijah's fathers, or ancestors
* King David
* And Asa, Abijah's son

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Jeroboam sets an ambush. This means that Jeroboam secretly sends some of Jeroboam's soldiers around to the back side of Judah's army so that Jeroboam's soldiers can fight Judah's army from both the front and the back.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about a surprise attack from behind, like Jeroboam uses to fight the army of Judah in this story? If needed, remember the discussion you had as a group in step two. How will you talk about this part of the story in your translation? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller makes it clear that when the army of Judah looks around, Judah's soldiers are surprised that Israel's soldiers have secretly come behind them. So the army of Judah cries out to Yahweh. This means that the soldiers pray loudly or shout for Yahweh to save them. Also, the priests blow the trumpets. Trumpets are instruments that people use to make a very loud musical sound. Craftsmen made the priests' trumpets from metal, and this kind of trumpet was long and straight. A priest would put the end of a trumpet against his lips and blow short blasts of air into the trumpet to make a loud noise.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a trumpet. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss how you will show in your translation that the army of Judah is surprised by the soldiers of Israel behind them. Pause this audio here.

Then the men of Judah raise the battle shout. This means that the men all shout together at one time to make a very loud noise. And when the men shout, God defeats or strikes Jeroboam and all the Israelites in front of Abijah and the soldiers of Judah. The Israelite soldiers run away from the soldiers of Judah, and God gives the Israelite soldiers into the "hand" of the army of Judah. In this special language, a person's hand represents power. So the storyteller is saying that God caused the soldiers of Judah to win the battle by giving the soldiers power to defeat Israel.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about how God gave someone power to defeat someone else. How do you talk about the way God gives that person power over someone or some other group? Pause this audio here.

Abijah and his soldiers strike the army of Israel with great force. This means that Judah's soldiers fight Israel's army with their weapons and kill many of Israel's soldiers. Abijah's army kills half a million, or 500,000, of Israel's best soldiers. All of these soldiers of Israel fall dead, which means that the soldiers of Judah wound these soldiers so badly in battle that the soldiers fall down on the ground and die. Thus, the men of Judah defeat the men of Israel. Israel's army no longer has the power to fight Judah's army and win. And Judah's army wins the battle, because the people of Judah rely on Yahweh, the God of their fathers. This does not mean that God is the God of the people of Judah's actual fathers, but of their ancestors or forefathers.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about your forefathers or the important ancestors who came long before you? How will you talk about this in your translation? Pause this audio here.

Then King Abijah's army chases King Jeroboam's army and captures three of Israel's cities and the villages around those cities. Those cities are Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron.

Now the storyteller explains what happens after the battle. The storyteller says that Jeroboam did not recover Jeroboam's power in the days of Abijah. This means that King Jeroboam was not able to grow Jeroboam's army big and powerful again during the time that Abijah was king of Judah. And Yahweh struck Jeroboam down, and Jeroboam died. This probably means that after some time had passed, Yahweh caused Jeroboam to become sick, so that Jeroboam died.

But, in contrast to Jeroboam, Abijah grew mighty. This means that Abijah continued to get more military and political power. The storyteller also says that Abijah married 14 wives and had 22 sons and 16 daughters.

Now, the storyteller says that Iddo the prophet wrote down all the important information about what Abijah did as king and the important things Abijah said in Iddo's book. You will remember that in this time, a book was different from the books we use today. Usually, a book was a scroll, a type of ancient book where people wrote everything on one very long piece of paper or animal skin and then rolled that paper or animal skin around a stick. You will remember that the storyteller mentioned Iddo's book earlier in 2 Chronicles. Unfortunately, Iddo's book no longer exists.

Finally, the storyteller says that Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried Abijah in the City of David. "Slept with his fathers" is special language that is a nice way to say that Abijah died, and that people buried Abijah's body near the bodies of Abijah's ancestors in the old part of Jerusalem that people called the City of David. You will remember that in those days, people usually buried a king's body in a tomb, which is a special cave or room that people carved into a large rock. Then Asa, Abijah's son, reigned in Abijah's place. This means that Asa became the next king of Judah. And in Asa's days, or the time Asa was king, the land had rest for 10 years, which means people experienced peace and did not have war.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about a time when no war, famine, or other bad things happened in your community. Pay attention to the words you use to describe that time. How will you describe the time of peace that people experienced in this story when Asa was king? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 13:13–14:1 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

As the story begins, the storyteller says that Jeroboam set an ambush. To ambush means to attack by surprise from a hidden place. So this means that Jeroboam secretly sent some of Israel's soldiers to a place where the army of Judah would not expect Israel to attack.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **ambush**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

When the army of Judah saw the soldiers behind them, the army cried out to **Yahweh** for help, and the **priests blew the trumpets**. You will remember that the priests were people who worked in the temple of God in Jerusalem. God had appointed priests to be between God and the people. Priests made it possible for people to come before God and to have a good relationship with God. In the book of Numbers, we hear how Yahweh gave instructions that when the people went to battle, the priests must blow the trumpets so that Yahweh would save the people from their enemies. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh, priests and for "blew the trumpets" as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and priests, see the Master Glossary.

When the army of **Judah** ran after the army of Israel, **God** gave Israel **into their hand**, and Judah **struck them with great force**. In the Bible, the phrase "into their hand" means to give someone power or control over someone else, and to strike with great force means to attack with great physical strength. Use the same words or phrases for Judah, God, and "into their hand" as you used in previous passages. See the Master Glossary for more information about Judah and God.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "**struck them with great force**." If you have already translated this phrase in another book of the Bible, use a similar phrase here. Pause this audio here.

When Abijah's men attacked Israel, the soldiers of Israel fell dead. This means that these soldiers of Israel were wounded so badly in the battle that the soldiers fell down on the ground and died.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **fell dead**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

All of these soldiers of Israel who died were **chosen men**. This means that the leaders of Jeroboam's army chose these men to be soldiers, so these men knew how to fight. Use the same word or phrase for chosen men as you used in previous passages.

The men of Judah prevailed and subdued the soldiers of Israel. To subdue means that you conquer or defeat someone. To prevail means that you have succeeded or won.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for **subdue** and **prevail**. If you have already translated these ideas in another book of the Bible, use similar words to those you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Abijah took three **cities** and those cities' surrounding **villages** from Jeroboam. Cities are usually larger settlements with walls around them, and villages are smaller settlements with no walls. Use the same words or phrases for cities and smaller villages as you used in previous passages.

After Abijah died, Abijah's son Asa reigned in Abijah's place. To **reign** means to be the king and to have the authority and power to rule the country. So when Asa "reigns in his place," it means that Asa becomes the new king of Judah just as Abijah had been king of Judah. Use the same word or phrase for reign as you used in previous passages.

Then Judah had rest or peace for 10 years. This means that people experienced calm, quiet, or an absence of war.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **rest** or **peace**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Speaking the Word
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
