## 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 (id: eng-2ch-p25-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the last story, King Jeroboam of Israel tried to trap King Abijah and the army of Judah by attacking from the front and back. The people of Judah cried out to God, the priests blew their trumpets, and the men shouted. God helped Judah's army win the battle, and Abijah became a strong king of Judah. Later, Abijah died, people buried Abijah, and Abijah's son Asa became the next king of Judah.

The storyteller says that King Asa does things that Yahweh, his God, thinks are good and right. Asa follows Yahweh's ways, and Yahweh is pleased with Asa. The phrase "Yahweh, his God" means that Yahweh is Asa's personal God—the one Asa worships, trusts, and obeys. Asa has a special relationship with Yahweh.

Now the storyteller starts to tell us the good and right things that King Asa does. The storyteller will keep talking about King Asa's good actions in the next story, too.

King Asa obeys what Yahweh has commanded. Asa removes the altars for foreign gods and takes away the high places. A "high place" was a place of worship, often on a hill or a raised platform with steps, where people made sacrifices to idols. Asa also breaks into pieces the sacred pillars, or stones people use to worship other gods. These were standing stones that people set up to honor different gods. Asa also cuts down the Asherah poles. These were wooden poles or trees that other people groups used to worship the goddess Asherah in Judah. People set these poles or trees up, made them holy, and treated them like they were the goddess.

Stop here and look at the images of a high place, sacred stones, and Asherah poles. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Where are the places where people in your community worship gods? What do people call these places? Pause this audio here.

King Asa tells the people of Judah to seek Yahweh. To seek Yahweh means to trust and obey Yahweh. Yahweh is the God that the ancestors of the people of Judah worshiped. Asa orders the people of Judah to follow Yahweh's laws and commandments. At the time of King Asa's reign, the Israelites had God's laws, which Moses had written down.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do your leaders say you must do to follow the gods in your land? What kind of things do you have to do to make these gods happy? What happens if you do not do what the gods want? Pause this audio here.

King Asa destroys the high places and the altars for burning incense to other gods in every city of Judah. Because of the good and right things that King Asa does, the people of Judah live in peace while Asa is king.

King Asa strengthens the defenses of the cities of Judah. Asa strengthens or rebuilds the walls, towers, gates, and bars around the cities. Asa can do all this because the land is peaceful. No army attacks King Asa during those years, because Yahweh gives Asa peace.

King Asa tells the people of Judah that they should make their cities strong and put walls around the cities. The people should build watchtowers and make gates with bars to lock the gates. These defenses will work together to make the cities of Judah hard to attack. These are probably the same cities that King Solomon and King Rehoboam had made strong before, but later an enemy named Shishak destroyed them. Asa's strong cities probably help protect the roads that lead to important places like Jerusalem. Asa says to the people of Judah that the land still belongs to them because the people of Judah have followed the commands of Yahweh their God. That is why Yahweh gave the people of Judah peace with all the countries around them. Yahweh gave King Asa and Judah peace because Yahweh was keeping his promise. Yahweh had promised to give Israel, including the land of Judah, peace and safety if the people obeyed Yahweh. And the people succeed in building well\-protected cities, and everything goes well for the people.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a city wall from the time of King Asa. Pause this audio here.

King Asa has an army of 300,000 men from the tribe of Judah. Each soldier carries a large shield and a spear. Asa also has 280,000 soldiers from the tribe of Benjamin. These soldiers carry small shields and bows. A bow was a wooden weapon that people used to shoot arrows at enemies from far away. It is possible that each tribe had its own special job in the army, and so the armies of Judah and Benjamin had different weapons. All the soldiers are strong and brave fighters. Having a strong and well\-equipped army shows that Asa is a good king. Asa trusted God and led Asa's people well.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the picture of the items the soldiers of Judah carried—a spear and a large shield. Now look at the items the soldiers of Benjamin carried—a bow and a small shield. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How does your people's army work? Do the soldiers all do the same job, or do the soldiers work in different groups that do different jobs and use different weapons? Pause this audio here.

A man named Zerah, who is a Cushite, comes to fight King Asa's army. Zerah leads a huge army with thousands of soldiers and 300 chariots. Zerah and his men march all the way to the city of Mareshah. We do not know much about Zerah or why Zerah started this war. In the Bible, people sometimes called the land of Cush "Ethiopia." That area is now part of Sudan, southern Egypt, and Ethiopia. Mareshah was a strong city in Judah. Cush was about 1,000 to 1,200 kilometers away from Mareshah.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the map and follow the journey Zerah and his army took to get from Cush to Mareshah in Judah. Pause this audio here.

So King Asa comes with his army to fight Zerah. The men of Asa and the men of Zerah take their places, ready for battle, in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

Then King Asa prays to Yahweh, Asa's God. Asa says to Yahweh that Yahweh is the only one who can help weak people fight against strong armies. Asa asks Yahweh to help the people of Judah because the people of Judah trust in Yahweh. Asa says the people of Judah have come to fight the huge army of Zerah to honor Yahweh. Asa says that Yahweh is the God of Judah and asks Yahweh not to let people win against Yahweh.

Yahweh defeats the army of the Cushites when King Asa and the soldiers from the tribe of Judah attack the Cushites. The Cushite people run away. King Asa and his soldiers chase the Cushites all the way to Gerar City, which is outside the land of Judah. The storyteller says that "the Cushites now fall until none remains alive." This may mean that so many people from Cush die that the Cushites are not able to go on fighting, or it could mean that all the people from Cush die. Yahweh and his army defeat the Cushites completely. The men of Judah carry away a large amount of plunder, or valuable things, from the Cushites.

Stop here and, as a group, follow on the map the journey King Asa's army takes when they chase the Cushite army from the Valley of Zephathah to Gerar City. Pause this audio here.

The soldiers from Judah attack and defeat all the cities near Gerar City, which, like Gerar, are outside the land of Judah. The soldiers from Judah kill many people and destroy the cities. The people in those cities are very scared of Yahweh, so the people in those cities do not fight back well. The soldiers from Judah take plunder from the cities because the people in the cities have many valuable things.

Asa's army also attacks the tents of the sheep and camel herdsmen and takes lots of sheep and camels. The herdsmen are not soldiers in Zerah's army. Then Asa and his army return to Jerusalem.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the map and follow the journey King Asa and his army took when they went from the city of Gerar back to Jerusalem.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has nine scenes.

**In the first scene:** The storyteller tells us that King Asa does things that Yahweh, Asa's God, thinks are good and right, and the storyteller explains what those things are. Asa destroys things that people use to worship idols. Asa removes the foreign altars, takes away the high places, breaks into pieces the sacred stones, and cuts down the Asherah poles.

**In the second scene:** King Asa tells the people of Judah to seek Yahweh, the God whom the ancestors of the people of Judah worshiped. Asa orders the people of Judah to obey Yahweh's laws and commandments.

**In the third scene:** King Asa destroys the high places and the altars for burning incense to other gods in every city of Judah. Because of the good and right things that King Asa does, the people of Judah live in peace while Asa is king.

**In the fourth scene:** King Asa strengthens the defenses of the cities of Judah. Asa can do all this because no army attacks King Asa during those years, because Yahweh gives Asa peace. King Asa tells the people of Judah that the people should make their cities strong and put walls around the cities, build watchtowers, and make gates with bars to lock the gates. Asa tells the people of Judah that they still have the land because the people follow Yahweh's commands. Yahweh gives the people peace with other nations. The people succeed in building well\-protected cities, and everything goes well for the people.

**In the fifth scene:** The storyteller tells us about the size of King Asa's army. King Asa has an army of 300,000 men from the tribe of Judah and 280,000 soldiers from the tribe of Benjamin. The armies of each tribe use different armor and have different weapons. All the soldiers are strong and brave fighters.

**In the sixth scene:** A Cushite named Zerah comes to fight King Asa's army with a huge army and 300 chariots. Zerah and his men march all the way to the city of Mareshah. King Asa comes with his army to fight Zerah. The soldiers on both sides line up ready to battle in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

**In the seventh scene:** King Asa prays to Yahweh and says only Yahweh can help weak people win against strong armies. Asa asks Yahweh to help Judah because the people trust Yahweh and have come to fight Zerah's big army to honor Yahweh.

**In the eighth scene:** Yahweh defeats the army of Cush when King Asa and his army attack the Cushites. The Cushite people run away. King Asa and his soldiers chase the Cushites all the way to Gerar City. Many or all people from Cush die, and the Cushites are not able to go on fighting. Yahweh and the army of Judah defeat the Cushites completely. The men of Judah carry away a large amount of plunder from the Cushites.

**In the ninth scene:** Asa and his army attack and defeat all the cities near Gerar City. Asa's soldiers take plunder from the cities because the people in the cities have many valuable things. Asa's army also attacks the tents of the herdsmen and takes lots of sheep and camels. Then Asa and his army return to Jerusalem.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Asa of Judah
* Yahweh
* People of the tribe of Judah
* The army of the tribe of Judah
* The army of the tribe of Benjamin
* Zerah the Cushite
* The Cushite army
* People in the cities near Gerar City
* And herdsmen in tents near Gerar City

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Asa has just become the new king of Judah. The storyteller tells us that Asa does what is good and right "in the eyes of Yahweh his God." This means that Asa follows Yahweh's ways, and Yahweh is pleased with Asa. By saying that Yahweh was "his" or "Asa's" God, the storyteller shows that Yahweh was Asa's personal God.

Now the storyteller begins to tell us what the good and right things were that King Asa did.

Asa removes the foreign altars, which were altars of foreign gods, and takes away the high places where people made sacrifices to idols. Asa also breaks into pieces the sacred stones people used to worship other gods. Asa also cuts down the Asherah poles, which people used to worship the goddess Asherah. Asa does not destroy any of those things himself, but Asa's workers do.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How will you translate "altars of foreign gods," "high places," "pillars or sacred stones," and "Asherah poles." Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you say it when a king tells his people to do something, and the people do it, but everyone says the king did it? Talk about a time when a ruler in your people group gave an order, the workers did the job, but people talked about it as if the ruler had done the job himself. Pause this audio here.

King Asa tells the people of Judah to seek Yahweh. To seek Yahweh meant to trust Yahweh and to obey Yahweh. Yahweh is "the God of their fathers," which means that Yahweh is the God whom the ancestors of the people of Judah worshiped. Asa orders the people of Judah to obey "the law and commandment," which refers to all of Yahweh's laws and commandments.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What words do you use in your language to talk about God's laws and commandments? What do your people call general rules or ways to act that everyone in your community must follow? Pause this audio here.

King Asa also destroys the high places and the altars for burning incense to other gods in every city of Judah. Remember that Asa does not destroy the high places himself, but Asa's workers do. Because of the good and right things that King Asa does, the people of Judah live in peace while Asa is king.

King Asa "builds up" strong cities. Asa does not build new cities, but Asa's workers repair the walls around the cities while the land of Judah is at peace. No army attacks King Asa during those years, because Yahweh gives Asa peace, or rest. Here, the word for peace is not the usual one. Instead, it comes from the same word as Sabbath, which means rest in the original language. King Asa tells the people of Judah that the people should make their cities strong and put walls around the cities. The people should build watchtowers and make gates with bars to lock the gates. Tall, strong stone walls all around the city will keep enemies out. High towers of stone or brick that people build into the walls will allow guards to watch for danger from far away. People will use the gates to go in and out of the city and use wooden or metal bars to close the gates at night and during attacks. These defenses will work together to make the cities of Judah hard to attack. Asa says to the people of Judah, "The land is still ours, because we have followed the commands of Yahweh our God. That is why Yahweh gave us peace with all the countries around us." When King Asa says, "we have followed the commands of Yahweh," King Asa refers to himself and to all the people of Judah. And the people succeed in building well\-protected cities, and everything goes well for the people.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a city wall from the time of king Asa. Pause this audio here.

Now the storyteller tells us about the size of King Asa's army. King Asa has an army of 300,000 men from the tribe of Judah. Each soldier carries a large shield and a spear. Asa also has 280,000 soldiers from the tribe of Benjamin. These soldiers carry small shields and bows. All the soldiers are strong and brave fighters.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the picture of the items the soldiers of Judah carried—a spear and a large shield. Now look at the items the soldiers of Benjamin carried—a bow and a small shield. Pause this audio here.

A man named Zerah, who is a Cushite, comes to fight King Asa's army. Zerah leads a huge army that the original language calls "a thousand times thousands" of soldiers, along with 300 chariots. This number is not exact, but it shows that the army was very large. Zerah and Zerah's men march all the way to the city of Mareshah. In the Bible, people sometimes called the land of Cush "Ethiopia." That area is now part of Sudan, southern Egypt, and Ethiopia. Mareshah was a strong city in Judah. Cush was about 1,000 to 1,200 kilometers away from Mareshah. It would take Zerah and Zerah's army around 45 to 60 days to walk from Cush to Mareshah.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the map and follow the journey Zerah and Zerah's army took to get from Cush to Mareshah in Judah. Pause this audio here.

King Asa comes with his army to fight Zerah. The soldiers on both sides line up, ready to battle, in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah. The valley is probably north of Mareshah, but no one knows for sure.

Then King Asa prays to Yahweh, Asa's God. Asa says, "Yahweh, you are the only one who can defend weak people against many people. Help your people, Yahweh our God, because we are trusting in you. It is because we trust in your name that we have come to fight this great army. Yahweh, you are our God, so do not let human beings defeat you."

Yahweh defeats the army of the Cushites when King Asa and the soldiers from the tribe of Judah attack the Cushites. The Cushite people run away. King Asa and his soldiers chase the Cushites all the way to Gerar City. Gerar was a Philistine city between Gaza and Beersheba, about 40 kilometers southwest of Mareshah. The storyteller says that "the Cushites now fall until none remain alive." This may mean that so many people from Cush die that the Cushites are not able to go on fighting, or it could mean that all the people from Cush die. Yahweh and his forces defeat the Cushites completely. "His forces" refers to Asa's army, which was also Yahweh's army. The storyteller clearly states that it is Yahweh who wins the victory, not Judah's army. The men of Judah carry away a large amount of plunder, or valuable items, from the Cushites.

Stop here and, as a group, follow on the map the journey King Asa's army takes when they chase the Cushite army from the Valley of Zephathah to Gerar City. Pause this audio here.

The soldiers from Judah attack and defeat all the cities near Gerar City. The word for "defeat" in the original language means both to kill the people and destroy the cities. The people in those cities are very scared of Yahweh, so the people in those cities do not fight back well. The soldiers from Judah take plunder from the cities because the people in the cities have many valuable things.

Stop here and, as a group, talk about the words you use in your language when you describe how people defeat a city, which involves killing people and destroying the buildings. What word or words will you use in this story? Pause this audio here.

Asa's army also attacks the tents of the herdsmen and takes lots of sheep and camels. Here, the word for "attack" in the original language means "to kill." Asa's army kills the herdsmen and takes the animals. Then Asa and his army return to Jerusalem. Jerusalem was 70 to 80 kilometers away from Gerar. It takes Asa's army between three and five days to return to Jerusalem.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the map and follow the journey King Asa and his army took when they went from the city of Gerar back to Jerusalem. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has nine scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Asa of Judah
* Yahweh
* People of the tribe of Judah
* The army of the tribe of Judah
* The army of the tribe of Benjamin
* Zerah the Cushite
* The Cushite army
* People in the cities near Gerar City
* And herdsmen in tents near Gerar City

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

King Asa does things that Yahweh, Asa's God, thinks are good and right. Asa gets rid of things people use to worship idols. Asa removes the foreign altars, takes away the high places, breaks into pieces the sacred stones, and cuts down the Asherah poles.

King Asa tells the people of Judah to seek Yahweh the God that the ancestors of the people of Judah worshiped. Asa orders the people of Judah to obey Yahweh's laws and commandments.

King Asa destroys the high places and the altars for burning incense to other gods in every city of Judah. Because of the good and right things that King Asa does, the people of Judah live in peace while Asa is king.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Asa, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am angry that the previous kings of Judah allowed people to worship foreign gods in Judah! It is sinful to worship other gods. We must worship Yahweh alone; or
* I am happy that from now on we will do what is right in the eyes of Yahweh my God; or
* We must remove and destroy the places and items of idol worship. Then Yahweh will forgive us and bless the tribe of Judah.

Continue the drama.

King Asa strengthens the defenses of the cities of Judah. Asa can do all this because no army attacks King Asa during those years, because Yahweh gives Asa peace. King Asa tells the people of Judah that the people should make their cities strong and put walls around the cities, build watchtowers, and make gates with bars to lock the gates. Asa tells the people of Judah that the people still have the land because the people follow Yahweh's commands. Yahweh gives the people peace with other nations. The people succeed in building well\-protected cities, and everything goes well for the people.

King Asa has an army of 300,000 men from the tribe of Judah. Each soldier carries a large shield and a spear. Asa also has 280,000 soldiers from the tribe of Benjamin. These soldiers carry small shields and bows. All the soldiers are strong and brave fighters.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing people of the tribe of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We thank Yahweh for giving us a good king. King Asa listens to Yahweh and does what Yahweh says; or
* We are happy that Yahweh has given our tribe peace, and we have had no war with other countries;
* We feel safe with King Asa. Asa ordered the workers to strengthen our cities, and our tribe has a large army.

Continue the drama.

A Cushite named Zerah comes to fight King Asa's army with a huge army and 300 chariots. Zerah and his men march all the way to the city of Mareshah. King Asa comes with Asa's army to fight Zerah. The soldiers on both sides line up ready to battle in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Zerah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel confident that we can win against the people of Judah because we have a huge army and the people of Judah are weak and easy to defeat; or
* I feel excited because we can take control of Judah's cities, and steal their treasures, land, and animals; or
* I feel proud of my huge army and chariots. My army will not let me down.

Continue the drama.

King Asa prays to Yahweh and says only Yahweh can help weak people win against strong armies. Asa asks Yahweh to help Judah because the people trust Yahweh and have come to fight Zerah's big army to honor Yahweh.

Yahweh defeats the army of Cush when King Asa and his army attack the Cushites. The Cushite people run away. King Asa and his soldiers chase the Cushites all the way to Gerar City outside of Judah. Many or all people from the region of Cush die, and the Cushites are not able to go on fighting. Yahweh and his army, which is the army of Judah, defeat the Cushites completely. The men of Judah carry away a large amount of plunder from the Cushites.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Asa, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel so grateful to Yahweh. I prayed to Yahweh and Yahweh defeated the army of Zerah; or
* I feel relieved that the people of Judah are safe again; or
* I feel safe because Yahweh is our God. Yahweh cares for us and blesses us with peace when we live as Yahweh says we should.

Continue the drama.

Asa and his army attack and defeat all the cities near Gerar City which are also outside of Judah. Asa's soldiers take plunder from the cities because the people in the cities have many valuable things. Asa's army also attacks the tents of the herdsmen and takes lots of sheep and camels. Then Asa and his army return to Jerusalem.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 14:2–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

**King** Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of Yahweh, Asa's God. Use the same word or phrase for king as you used in previous passages. For more information on king, refer to the Master Glossary.

**Yahweh** is God's personal name. Use the same name for Yahweh that you have used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

**God** is the general name for God, the creator of the universe. Use the same word or phrase you used in previous passages. Look up God in the Master Glossary for more information.

Asa removed the foreign altars and took away the high places. Asa also broke into pieces the pillars, or sacred stones people used to worship other gods. Asa also cut down the Asherah poles.

Stop here and look at the images of a high place, a sacred stone, and Asherah poles. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for **sacred stones** and **Asherah poles**. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Use the same words or phrases for **altar** and **high places** as you used in previous passages. For more information on "altar," refer to the Master Glossary.

The **kingdom** of Israel was at peace. Use the same word or phrase for kingdom that you have used previously, and refer to kingdom in the Master Glossary for more information.

Asa made the **cities** of **Judah** stronger. Asa and his workers could do all this because the land was peaceful. No army attacked King Asa during those years, because Yahweh gave Asa peace.

Use the same words for Judah and cities as you used in previous passages. Judah is in the Master Glossary.

Here, the word for **peace** is not the usual one. Instead, it comes from the same word as Sabbath, which means rest in the original language. Use the same word or phrase here for "peace" or "rest" that you used in 2 Chronicles 14:1\.

King Asa tells the people of Judah to seek Yahweh, "**the God of their fathers**." This means that Yahweh is the God that the ancestors worshipped. Asa orders the people of Judah to obey Yahweh's **laws** and **commandments**. Use the same words or phrases for "the God of their fathers," laws, and commandments, as you used in previous passages. For more information on laws and commandments, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Asa builds up **strong cities** while the land of Judah is at peace. Use the same word or phrase for "strong city" as you used in previous passages.

King Asa has an army of 300,000 men from the tribe of Judah. Each soldier carries a large shield and a spear. Asa also has 280,000 soldiers from the tribe of Benjamin. These soldiers carry small shields and bows. A bow was a wooden weapon that people used to shoot arrows at enemies from far away.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the picture of the items the soldiers of Judah carried—a spear and a large shield. Now look at the items the soldiers of Benjamin carried—a bow and a small shield. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **bow**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A Cushite named Zerah comes to fight King Asa's army with a huge army and 300 **chariots**.

Use the same word or phrase for chariot as you used in previous passages.

The men of Judah carry away a large amount of plunder from the Cushites. Plunder means the valuable things people take, like money, animals, or goods, from enemies after a battle.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **plunder**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Asa's army also attacks the tents of the herdsmen and takes lots of sheep and camels.

Herdsmen are people who take care of animals like sheep, goats, or cows and lead these animals to places where the animals can eat and drink.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **herdsmen**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

## 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 (id: eng-2ch-p30-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passage, the storyteller told us about when Jehoshaphat followed Yahweh and was a good king of Judah. Now, the storyteller starts to tell us of a time when Jehoshaphat makes mistakes and visits King Ahab in Israel. We can also find this story in 1 Kings 22:1–9, but with some differences.

Stop here and do this activity as a group: If you have already translated 1 Kings 22:1–9, listen to your translation of that passage. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller starts the story by telling us again that Jehoshaphat had lots of money and many people respected Jehoshaphat. Even though Jehoshaphat did not need money or respect, Jehoshaphat made an alliance, a formal relationship, with Israel by marrying his son to Ahab's daughter. The alliance meant Jehoshaphat and Ahab did not fight each other. The two kings would work together and support each other.

Stop here and do this activity as a group: Tell a story of a time when two people married or made a formal relationship to make two families or groups of people work together and support each other. Pause this audio here.

After Jehoshaphat married his son to Ahab's daughter, Jehoshaphat goes to visit Ahab. We do not know exactly how many years there were between the marriage and the visit, but it was probably more than three years. Jehoshaphat leaves Jerusalem and goes to visit Ahab in the city of Samaria, in Israel. Jehoshaphat probably travels to Samaria with a large number of people. In the time of King Jehoshaphat, it was normal for kings to travel with many servants and officials. When Jehoshaphat is in Samaria, Ahab tells his people to kill lots of sheep and "cattle," or oxen. Sheep and cattle are both large animals, and when people cook one of these animals, the animal will feed lots of people.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of sheep. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of cattle. Pause this audio here.

The people probably do not kill the animals for a sacrifice to please Yahweh. Ahab probably gives the sheep and cattle to Jehoshaphat and the people with Jehoshaphat as part of a big feast. The feast is to celebrate the visit of Jehoshaphat and all the people with Jehoshaphat. Ahab wants Jehoshaphat to feel special and important. Ahab wants Jehoshaphat to help Ahab attack Ramoth in Gilead.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of Israel, Judah, and western Syria. Find the cities of Jerusalem, Samaria, and Ramoth in Gilead. Pause this audio here.

You may remember that Ramoth Gilead was part of the land Yahweh gave to the tribe of Gad and was a city of refuge where the Levites lived. However, the people of Aram attacked and now control Ramoth Gilead. After the last war between Israel and Aram, the king of Aram said he would give Ramoth Gilead back to the king of Israel. The king of Aram did not give Ramoth Gilead back to Ahab, and now Ahab wants the city back. Syria is another name for Aram. The Aramean people are the same people as the Syrian people.

Ahab wants Jehoshaphat to help to fight the Arameans at Ramoth Gilead and to help get back control of Ramoth Gilead. Jehoshaphat tells Ahab that Jehoshaphat and Ahab are united like being one person. Jehoshaphat says that the fighting people of Judah and Israel are one people together. Jehoshaphat will support Ahab in the war to fight the Arameans. Jehoshaphat tells the king of Israel that the two kings must ask Yahweh for guidance before the kings do anything else. In the time of the kings of Israel and Judah, the kings used prophets to ask for guidance from God.

The king of Israel gathers the prophets so that the kings can ask for guidance. There are about 400 prophets. We do not know if the prophets were all men or if they were both men and women. The prophets were people who said they spoke messages from God. It is possible that the prophets all served the king of Israel. The king of Israel asks if the kings should go to war to fight against the people in Ramoth Gilead or hold back and not attack. The king of Israel does not expect the prophets to go to war.

The prophets tell the kings that God will give Ramoth Gilead into the king of Israel's "hand" or control. The prophets use polite language and do not address the kings directly. Jehoshaphat does not trust the prophets' answer. Jehoshaphat does not think any of the prophets bring a message from Yahweh. Jehoshaphat asks the king of Israel if all the prophets of Yahweh are gone or if there is still one prophet that the kings can ask for guidance. The king of Israel tells Jehoshaphat about the one prophet of Yahweh whom the kings can talk to. The king of Israel hates the prophet of Yahweh because, in all the time the prophet has brought messages, the messages for the king are never good news. The prophet always prophesies bad things to happen to the king of Israel. The king of Israel names the prophet as Micaiah, who is the son of Imlah. Imlah was probably Micaiah's father.

Jehoshaphat replies directly to the king of Israel but addresses him as the king. Jehoshaphat uses polite language to tell the king of Israel that the king should not say bad things about a prophet of Yahweh.

Stop here and do this activity as a group: Tell a story about a time when you needed to tell someone politely that the person was doing something wrong. Maybe the person was older than you or a very important person in your community. Pause this audio here.

The king of Israel calls one of his officials over to him and asks the official to bring Micaiah, son of Imlah, to the two kings. The king wants Micaiah to come to the two kings as soon as possible.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

**In the first scene:** The storyteller tells us that Jehoshaphat is rich, well respected, and has a formal relationship with Ahab.

**In the second scene:** Jehoshaphat visits Ahab in Samaria, and Ahab gives a big feast for Jehoshaphat. At the feast, Ahab persuades Jehoshaphat to fight with Ahab against Ramoth Gilead. Jehoshaphat wants to help Ahab but wants to hear from Yahweh first.

**In the third scene:** The king of Israel gathers 400 prophets and asks the prophets if Israel should fight Ramoth Gilead. The prophets tell the king of Israel to fight because God will give Ramoth Gilead to the king of Israel. Jehoshaphat wants to hear from a prophet of Yahweh. The king of Israel says that Micaiah is the only prophet of Yahweh. The king of Israel hates Micaiah because Micaiah always prophesies bad things for the king of Israel. The king of Israel asks an official to bring Micaiah to the two kings.

The characters in this passage are:

* The storyteller
* Jehoshaphat, king of Judah
* Ahab, king of Israel
* Jehoshaphat's people
* Four hundred prophets
* And the king of Israel's official

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the previous passage, the storyteller told us Jehoshaphat followed Yahweh, became powerful, and was a successful king of Judah. Now the storyteller wants to tell us about the time Jehoshaphat visits Ahab, the king of Israel. The storyteller begins the story by reminding us that Jehoshaphat is wealthy, with lots of money and valuable things. The storyteller also tells us that Jehoshaphat has a lot of honor, has respect from lots of people, and is well known by lots of people. Jehoshaphat has allied himself with Ahab; Jehoshaphat has made a formal relationship with Ahab by marrying Jehoshaphat's son to Ahab's daughter.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do you call a formal relationship between two leaders where the leaders will help each other and possibly fight to protect each other's countries? Pause this audio here.

A few years after Jehoshaphat and Ahab became allies, Jehoshaphat visits Ahab in Samaria. You may remember that the storyteller in 1 Kings tells us that Jehoshaphat visits Ahab in the third year after Aram made peace with Israel. But the storyteller in this story only gives a general idea of when Jehoshaphat visits Ahab. Jehoshaphat goes down from Jerusalem, which is on top of a hill, to Samaria, which is lower down. Samaria is north of Jerusalem.

Stop here as a group and, if needed, look at a map of Israel, Judah, and western Syria. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How will you say Jehoshaphat went down to see the king of Israel? Remember that "going down" means that Jehoshaphat traveled from a higher place to a lower place. Pause this audio here.

When Jehoshaphat visits Ahab, Ahab kills sheep and cattle to celebrate the visit and to provide food for a feast.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of sheep if needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of cattle if needed. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller tells us that Ahab urges Jehoshaphat to help Ahab attack Ramoth Gilead. The storyteller uses language to tell us that Ahab wants Jehoshaphat to do something that is not good.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about someone who tries to get someone to do something that is not good or the right thing to do? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller uses Ahab's and Jehoshaphat's titles as kings of Israel and Judah when the storyteller says what Ahab asks Jehoshaphat. Ahab wants Jehoshaphat and Jehoshaphat's fighting men to help attack the people at Ramoth Gilead. Now, the storyteller stops naming Ahab as the king of Israel. Jehoshaphat replies to say that the two kings are united and will work together as one fighting people. The people of Judah will join the people of Israel in a war against Aram at Ramoth Gilead.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: If you have one, what particular saying or phrase do you use to say that you and another person or group of people will do something together, like you are one person or group? Pause this audio here.

At the same time as Jehoshaphat agrees to fight with Ahab, Jehoshaphat also says that the kings should ask Yahweh for guidance. The storyteller stops naming Ahab and only uses the title "the king of Israel."

The king of Israel gathers together prophets. We do not know how long it takes for the prophets to come to the kings. The prophets are probably part of the people living in the king's household and probably come to the kings on the same day or the next day. The group of prophets probably included men and women. The king of Israel asks the prophets if Israel and Judah should go to war to attack and fight the people of Ramoth Gilead, or not go to war. The prophets all reply that God will give Ramoth Gilead into the king's hand. The prophets use the word "hand" to symbolize power. The prophets say the king of Israel will have power over Ramoth Gilead. The prophets do not call God by God's personal name.

Jehoshaphat asks if there is no prophet of Yahweh in the group that the kings can ask for guidance. Jehoshaphat thinks that it is possible that there are no prophets of Yahweh advising the king of Israel.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you ask someone politely if a person is in a town or village if you do not know if that person is still there or has gone away? Pause this audio here.

The king of Israel tells Jehoshaphat that there is one prophet whom the kings can use to ask questions to Yahweh. The king of Israel tells Jehoshaphat about the one prophet of Yahweh who is in Israel. The king of Israel says that he hates the prophet and sees the prophet as an enemy. The prophet's messages for the king of Israel are never good. The king of Israel names the prophet as Micaiah, son of Imlah. Jehoshaphat tells the king of Israel that the king of Israel should not speak in that way. The king of Israel should not say bad things about Micaiah because Micaiah is a prophet of Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you tell somebody not to say bad things

about another person? Pause this audio here.

The king of Israel asks one of his officials to come to the king and asks the official to bring Micaiah to the two kings.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* The storyteller
* Jehoshaphat, king of Judah
* Ahab, king of Israel
* Jehoshaphat's people
* Four hundred prophets
* And the king of Israel's official

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

The storyteller tells us that Jehoshaphat is rich, that everyone respects Jehoshaphat, and that Jehoshaphat has a formal relationship with Ahab.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the storyteller, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* Jehoshaphat is a powerful king of Judah; or
* I told you Jehoshaphat followed Yahweh. But Jehoshaphat made an alliance with Ahab, who did not follow Yahweh; or
* Now I will tell you about a mistake Jehoshaphat made.

Continue the drama.

Jehoshaphat visits Ahab in Samaria, and Ahab gives a big feast for Jehoshaphat and his people. At the feast, Ahab persuades Jehoshaphat to fight with Ahab against Ramoth Gilead. Jehoshaphat wants to help Ahab but wants to hear from Yahweh first.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Jehoshaphat, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* Ahab has made a big feast for us. Ahab is trying to impress us and make us feel welcome; or
* I am happy to help Ahab because our families are connected; or
* It is important to consult Yahweh. I do not want to fight if Yahweh does not tell us to fight; or
* I am worried that Ahab does not care about Yahweh.

Ask the person playing Jehoshaphat's people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We are very impressed by this amazing big feast for us; or
* We feel very welcome in Samaria.

Ask the person playing the king of Israel, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I want Jehoshaphat to help me get control of Ramoth Gilead and make it part of Israel again; or
* I am happy that Jehoshaphat wants to help me; or
* I have lots of prophets who will bring messages to me from God. I do not care which god the prophets talk to.

Continue the drama.

The king of Israel gathers 400 prophets and asks the prophets if Israel should fight Ramoth Gilead. The prophets tell the king of Israel to fight because God will give Ramoth Gilead to the king of Israel. Jehoshaphat wants to hear from a prophet of Yahweh. The king of Israel says that Micaiah is the only prophet of Yahweh. The king of Israel hates Micaiah because Micaiah always prophesies bad things for the king of Israel. The king of Israel asks an official to bring Micaiah to the two kings.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the king of Israel, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am excited. All the prophets say that I should attack Ramoth Gilead. God is with me and will give me the victory; or
* Why does Jehoshaphat care about Yahweh? Yahweh's prophet never says anything good to me. I do not want to talk to Yahweh's prophet; or
* If I want Jehoshaphat to help me, I will need to get Micaiah to come and prophesy.

Ask the person playing the 400 prophets, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We want the king to like us, so we tell the king, "Yes, go and fight Ramoth Gilead"; or
* You, the king of Israel, are powerful. Of course, you will win; or
* Listen to all of us. We can tell you what God is saying.

Ask the person playing Jehoshaphat, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* There are so many prophets, but I do not think these prophets speak messages from Yahweh; or
* I do not trust these prophets; or
* I must hear from Yahweh before I go with Israel and take my army to fight Aram in Ramoth Gilead; or
* The king of Israel does not respect Micaiah, Yahweh's prophet. I do not like what the king of Israel says about Micaiah.

Ask the person playing the king of Israel's official, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I must find Micaiah quickly; or
* I wonder what Micaiah will say this time. I hope Micaiah does not make my king angry.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 18:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Jehoshaphat has great **wealth** and **honor**. Wealth is when a person has lots of money and possessions. A person with honor is a person whom people respect and value because the person makes good choices and has good behavior. Use the same words or phrases for wealth and honor as you used in previous passages.

Jehoshaphat allied himself with Ahab through marriage. Jehoshaphat made a formal relationship between Judah and Israel by marrying Jehoshaphat's son to Ahab's daughter.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **allied through marriage**. Pause this audio here.

Ahab slaughtered **sheep** and **cattle** for Jehoshaphat. Use the same words or phrases for sheep and cattle as you used in previous passages. Ahab killed the animals for the group of visitors to eat as part of a feast.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "**slaughtered**," or killed, an animal. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The **king** of **Israel** asked the king of **Judah** to go to attack Ramoth Gilead. Use the same words or phrases for king, Israel, and Judah as you used in previous passages. For more information on king, Israel, and Judah, refer to the Master Glossary.

Jehoshaphat told the king of Israel to seek counsel or advice from **Yahweh**. Yahweh is God's personal name. In this passage, God is called Yahweh. Be sure to translate Yahweh in the same way as you have in previous passages, and remember that Yahweh is in the Master Glossary.

The king of Israel gathered the **prophets**. Use the same word or phrase for prophets as you used in previous passages. For more information on prophet, refer to the Master Glossary.

The prophets say that **God**, the most powerful being, will give Syria to the king of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for God as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

God will give Ramoth Gilead into the king's "**hand**" or into the king's power. Use the same word or phrase for "into the king's hand" as you used in previous passages.

The king of Israel says that Micaiah never **prophesies** anything good about the king. Use the same word or phrase for prophesies as you used in previous passages. For more information on prophecy, refer to the Master Glossary.

The king of Israel asks an official to bring Micaiah to the kings. An official is a person who serves the king and helps the king run the country. An official has high status in the king's household and does not do domestic tasks.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **official**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Speaking the Word
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
