## 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 (id: eng-2ch-p37-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, the army of Judah marched into the wilderness of Tekoa to face the armies of the Ammonites and the Moabites, and the army of the people of Mount Seir. Jehoshaphat tells the people to trust Yahweh, their God, and the singers march in front of the army praising Yahweh. As the people sing, Yahweh makes the Ammonites and Moabites turn against the men of Mount Seir, and then the Ammonites and Moabites fight each other until no one is left. When the army of Judah arrives, they find all the enemies already dead and collect plunder for three days. Then Jehoshaphat's army returns to Jerusalem with joy, and Yahweh gives Jehoshaphat's kingdom peace.

In this story, the storyteller summarizes King Jehoshaphat's reign in Judah. A different storyteller also tells this story in 1 Kings 22:41–50\.

Stop here and listen to your translation of 1 Kings 22:41–50 if you have already translated this passage. Pause this audio here.

Jehoshaphat rules the kingdom of Judah. Jehoshaphat is 35 years old when he becomes king of Judah, and Jehoshaphat rules in Jerusalem for 25 years, from about the year 872 to the year 848 before Jesus. Jehoshaphat's mother's name is Azubah. Silhi is the father of Azubah.

King Jehoshaphat follows the example of his father, Asa, and does not stop following it. Jehoshaphat does things that please Yahweh.

However, Jehoshaphat does not take down the high places, or shrines on the hilltops, where people worship other gods. But, you may remember that the storyteller said in an earlier story in 2 Chronicles 17:6 that Jehoshaphat removed the shrines on hilltops from Judah. This means that either Jehoshaphat did not finish his work or Jehoshaphat stopped watching carefully for new shrines on hilltops. For example, Jehoshaphat's father, Asa, also removed shrines on hilltops from Judah. But by the time Jehoshaphat ruled, people had built more of those shrines on hilltops. The people often worshipped Yahweh at the shrines on hilltops, but that was also wrong. Some people also worshipped false gods like Baal and Asherah there. Yahweh wanted the people to worship only Yahweh and not other gods, and Yahweh wanted Yahweh's people to only give offerings and sacrifices at the temple in Jerusalem. By worshipping at shrines on hilltops, the people of Israel show that they strongly turned toward idol worship and mixed the worship of Yahweh with idols. So, the storyteller partly blames the people of Judah because the people did not remove the shrines on the hilltops. The storyteller says that the people of Judah, even at this point in the story, still do not really want to follow the God of their ancestors.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Talk about the religions in your culture. How can you tell whether people are or are not fully obeying the god or gods of these religions? Pause this audio here.

Many other things happen while Jehoshaphat is king. From start to finish, Jehu, the son of Hanani, writes these things in a book or scroll called the history, or records, of Jehu. Jehu's writings are part of a bigger book called the "Book of the Kings of Israel." The name "Israel" here really means Judah. By saying "Israel," the storyteller possibly shows that the kingdom of Judah remains the true Israel—the nation that trusts Yahweh. Jehu is a prophet, and Jehu does not write only ordinary history like a royal record. Jehu's writings likely include prophecies, warnings, rebukes, and Yahweh's judgment of Jehoshaphat as a king. Jehu writes history as a prophet who writes under Yahweh's direction. There is no remaining copy of Jehu's writing.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Who records the history of rulers or kings in your people group? What things do these people record about the rulers and their time as leaders? Pause this audio here.

Now the storyteller talks about a specific event from King Jehoshaphat's reign. The storyteller says, "After this, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, makes an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel." Ahaziah becomes king of Israel in the 17th year of Jehoshaphat's reign and rules for two years. This means Jehoshaphat makes the alliance during that time, after Judah defeats the armies of Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir, and after the time of peace that follows. You will remember these events from the last story. Then the storyteller says, "He does evil." In the original language, we cannot tell if "he" means King Ahaziah of Israel or King Jehoshaphat of Judah. Many people think it is Ahaziah who does evil. These people say the word "evil" describes how Ahaziah usually acts, not just one bad choice. But others think it is Jehoshaphat who does evil. These other people say Jehoshaphat makes a serious mistake when Jehoshaphat chooses to join with Ahaziah. Still others say the word "evil" really describes Ahaziah, because the word is too strong to describe Jehoshaphat.

King Jehoshaphat agrees with King Ahaziah to build several large trading ships that can travel very far, even to a place called Tarshish. In 1 Kings 22, the storyteller says that Jehoshaphat builds "ships of Tarshish." "Ships of Tarshish" or "Tarshish ships" are names for big, strong trading ships people made for long sea trips. Other Old Testament storytellers use this phrase too. Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah build these ships in the city of Ezion Geber. Ezion Geber is an important port city on the north side of the Gulf of Aqaba in Edom, which is now under Judah's control. Jehoshaphat had gained control over the area around Ezion Geber after Jehoshaphat pushed back the attack from the Moabites, Ammonites, and the people of Mount Seir in the previous story. Long ago, King Solomon made a lot of money through sea trade from this port. This history likely makes Jehoshaphat want to start sea trade again, so Jehoshaphat joins with Ahaziah to build ships for trading.

Stop here and, as a group, find Tarshish and Ezion Geber on the map. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a ship of Tarshish. Pause this audio here.

Then the prophet Eliezer, the son of Dodavahu, warns King Jehoshaphat. Prophet Eliezar comes from the city of Mareshah in southern Judah. This is the only time the Bible mentions the prophet Eliezer. Eliezer prophesies or tells Jehoshaphat that Yahweh will destroy the ships Jehoshaphat builds because Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with King Ahaziah. Because of this, something destroys the ships, and the ships cannot sail to faraway lands. The storyteller does not say what exactly happens to the ships.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has six scenes.

**In the first scene:** The storyteller summarizes Jehoshaphat's reign. Jehoshaphat rules the kingdom of Judah. Jehoshaphat is 35 years old when Jehoshaphat becomes king of Judah, and Jehoshaphat rules in Jerusalem for 25 years. Jehoshaphat's mother's name is Azubah. Silhi is Azubah's father.

**In the second scene:** King Jehoshaphat follows the example of his father, Asa, and does not stop following it. Jehoshaphat does things that please Yahweh.

**In the third scene:** Jehoshaphat does not take down the shrines on the hilltops where people worship other gods. The people of Judah, even at this time in their story, still do not really want to follow the God of their fathers.

**In the fourth scene:** The storyteller finishes the story of King Jehoshaphat's rule. The storyteller says that many other things happen while Jehoshaphat is king. From start to finish, Jehu, the son of Hanani, writes these things in a book or scroll that people call the history, or records, of Jehu. Jehu's writings are part of a bigger book called the "Book of the Kings of Israel."

**In the fifth scene:** The storyteller talks about a specific event from King Jehoshaphat's reign when Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel. The storyteller then says, "He does evil," which likely refers to how Ahaziah usually acts. But some people think that the words point to Jehoshaphat, who makes a serious mistake when he chooses to join with Ahaziah. King Jehoshaphat makes an agreement with King Ahaziah to build large trading ships that can travel to faraway places like Tarshish. Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah build these ships in the port city of Ezion Geber.

**In the sixth scene:** The prophet Eliezer, the son of Dodavahu, warns King Jehoshaphat. Eliezer prophesies, or tells Jehoshaphat, that Yahweh will destroy the ships Jehoshaphat builds because Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with King Ahaziah. Because of this, something destroys the ships, and they cannot sail to faraway lands like Tarshish.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Jehoshaphat of Judah
* Yahweh
* The people of Judah
* Jehu, the son of Hanani, a prophet who records the details of Jehoshaphat's reign
* Ahaziah, king of Israel
* And prophet Eliezar, son of Dodavahu

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this story, the storyteller summarizes the rule of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. The storyteller also talks about these events in 1 Kings 22:41–50\. The storyteller follows the normal way of talking about a king's rule. The storyteller says how long Jehoshaphat rules and gives the name of Jehoshaphat's mother.

Jehoshaphat rules the kingdom of Judah. Jehoshaphat is 35 years old when Jehoshaphat becomes king of Judah. Jehoshaphat rules in Jerusalem for 25 years, from about the year 872 to the year 848 before Jesus. For the first three years, Jehoshaphat co\-reigns with Jehoshaphat's father, Asa. Jehoshaphat's mother's name is Azubah. Silhi is Azubah's father. People know Silhi is Azubah's father and not Azubah's mother because, in the Bible, when people call a woman the daughter of someone, the name is almost always her father's name. That was the normal way to show family lines. Also, the words in the original language make it clear that Silhi is a male.

Stop here and, as a group, discuss the following question: What do people in your culture say when they talk about a king's or ruler's time as leader? What important things about that person's rule do people talk about? What family members in the king's or ruler's family do people think are important to mention? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that Jehoshaphat walks in the way of Asa, his father, which means that King Jehoshaphat follows the example of his father, Asa. The word "father" here means biological father. The storyteller then explains how closely Jehoshaphat follows his father and says that Jehoshaphat does not turn away from the way of his father. This means that Jehoshaphat does not stop following his father Asa's example. Jehoshaphat does things that are right in the eyes of Yahweh, which means Jehoshaphat does things that please Yahweh.

Stop here and, as a group, discuss the following question: How will you say that Jehoshaphat walks in the way of his father Asa or follows Asa's example? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller now uses language that shows that the negative things that happen next contrast with the positive things in Jehoshaphat's reign that the storyteller has just talked about. However, Jehoshaphat does not take down the high places, or shrines on the hilltops, where people worship other gods. This is despite what the storyteller says in a story in 2 Chronicles 17:6 from an earlier part of Jehoshaphat's reign, where Jehoshaphat removes the shrines on hilltops from Judah. Therefore, Jehoshaphat either does not finish his work, or Jehoshaphat stops watching for new shrines on hilltops so that Jehoshaphat can destroy those shrines. So the storyteller partly holds the people of Judah responsible for not removing or rebuilding the shrines on the hilltops. The storyteller says that the people of Judah have not yet made their hearts ready to follow the God of their fathers. The word "fathers" here means ancestors, not biological fathers. This means that the people of Judah, even at this point in the story, still have not chosen to fully obey God.

Now the storyteller uses a common way he often uses in the books of 1 and 2 Chronicles to finish the story of a king's rule. The storyteller says that many other things happen while Jehoshaphat is king. From start to finish, Jehu, the son of Hanani, writes these things in a book or scroll that people called the chronicles, or records of Jehu. Jehu's writings are part of a bigger book that people called the "Book of the Kings of Israel." The name "Israel" here really means Judah. In 2 Chronicles, the storyteller often calls the southern Kingdom of Judah by the name "Israel."

Stop here and, as a group, discuss the following question: What is the usual way in your culture to finish telling the story of a king's rule? Pause this audio here.

Now the storyteller talks about a specific event from King Jehoshaphat's reign. The storyteller says, "After this, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, makes an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel." "After this" refers to the time after Judah defeats the armies of Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir, and after the time of peace that follows. Then the storyteller says, "He does evil." In the original language, we cannot tell if the storyteller is talking about King Ahaziah of Israel or King Jehoshaphat of Judah. It is more likely that the storyteller talks about Ahaziah, and the word "evil" describes how Ahaziah usually acts.

Stop here and, as a group, discuss the following question: How will you decide who the words "He does evil" are talking about? How will you translate these words? If you can keep this vague in your translation, that would be best. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that King Jehoshaphat makes an agreement with King Ahaziah to build ships to go to Tarshish. But the words "ships to go to Tarshish" may be a mistake. The storyteller probably means "ships of Tarshish." Ships of Tarshish were big, strong trading ships that could travel very far, even to a distant place called Tarshish. No one is sure of the location of Tarshish, but many consider Tarshish to be in the western Mediterranean region or the ancient city called Carthage. People made these ships from strong wood, often cedar or other durable timber. The ships usually had one large square sail, though some may have had two sails for longer journeys. Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah do not actually build the ships themselves, but Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah oversee their workers who build the ships. Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah build these ships in the city of Ezion Geber, an important port city on the north side of the Gulf of Aqaba in Edom, which is under Judah's control.

Stop here and, as a group, find Tarshish and Ezion Geber on the map. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a ship of Tarshish. Pause this audio here.

Then the prophet Eliezer, the son of Dodavahu, warns King Jehoshaphat. Prophet Eliezer comes from the city of Mareshah in southern Judah. Eliezer prophesies or tells Jehoshaphat that Yahweh will destroy the ships Jehoshaphat builds because Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with King Ahaziah. The storyteller says that because of this, something destroys the ships, and they cannot go to Tarshish. We do not know what happened, but Yahweh may have used natural events like a violent storm, strong winds, or rough seas to destroy the ships. Here, "Tarshish" does not mean the place Tarshish, but it means faraway lands. Because Yahweh destroys the ships due to Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahaziah, the ships can no longer sail to faraway lands.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

The storyteller summarizes Jehoshaphat's reign. Jehoshaphat rules the kingdom of Judah. Jehoshaphat is 35 years old when Jehoshaphat becomes king of Judah, and Jehoshaphat rules in Jerusalem for 25 years. Jehoshaphat's mother's name is Azubah. Silhi is Azubah's father.

King Jehoshaphat follows the example of his father, Asa, and does not stop following it. Jehoshaphat does things that please Yahweh.

However, Jehoshaphat does not take down the shrines on the hilltops where people worship other gods. Even at this point in the story, the people of Judah still do not really want to follow the God of their fathers.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Jehoshaphat, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am grateful. Yahweh has helped me to obey Yahweh all my life. I did my best to follow the example that my father, King Asa, had set; or
* I am very upset that I have not managed to get rid of all the shrines on hilltops where people worship other gods. My workers destroyed the shrines at first, but then the people of Judah rebuilt the shrines; or
* I am disappointed that the people of Judah, even now, do not want to follow Yahweh, the God of their fathers, with their whole hearts.

Continue the drama.

The storyteller finishes the story of King Jehoshaphat's rule. The storyteller says that many other things happen while Jehoshaphat is king. From start to finish, Jehu, the son of Hanani, writes these things in a scroll that people called the chronicles, or records, of Jehu. Jehu's writings are part of a bigger book that people called the "Book of the Kings of Israel."

The storyteller now talks about a specific event from King Jehoshaphat's reign when Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel. The storyteller then says that the way Ahaziah usually acts is evil. But some people think that the word "evil" points to Jehoshaphat, who makes a serious mistake when he chooses to join with Ahaziah. King Jehoshaphat makes an agreement with King Ahaziah to build large trading ships that can travel to faraway places like Tarshish. Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah build these ships in the port city of Ezion Geber.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Ahaziah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am happy that King Jehoshaphat decided to make an alliance with me to build several ships of Tarshish in the port city of Ezion Geber; or
* I hope that the ships will help me and King Jehoshaphat make a lot of money for our kingdoms when we trade with faraway countries. We will use the ships to sell and buy goods from distant lands, just like King Solomon did; or
* I am pleased that King Jehoshaphat follows Yahweh. Perhaps Yahweh will bless our alliance.

Continue the drama.

Then the prophet Eliezer, the son of Dodavahu, warns King Jehoshaphat. Eliezer prophesies, or tells Jehoshaphat, that Yahweh will destroy the ships Jehoshaphat builds because Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with King Ahaziah. Because of this, something destroys the ships, and they cannot sail to faraway lands.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Prophet Eliezer, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am afraid of King Jehoshaphat. I must tell Jehoshaphat that Yahweh is very unhappy about Jehoshaphat's alliance with evil King Ahaziah; or
* I trust that Yahweh will protect me when I tell Jehoshaphat that Yahweh will destroy the ships they build; or
* I love Yahweh because he always keeps his word. Yahweh destroyed the ships of Tarshish that Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah built, as Yahweh said he would do.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Jehoshaphat rules the **kingdom** of Judah. Jehoshaphat is 35 years old when Jehoshaphat becomes **king** of **Judah**. Although the storyteller just says that Jehoshaphat ruled over Judah, we know that Judah is a kingdom. You may choose to say "the kingdom of Judah" if you need to.

Use the same words or phrases for kingdom, Judah, and king as you used in previous passages. For more information on kingdom, Judah and king, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Jehoshaphat follows the example of his father, Asa, and does not stop following it. Jehoshaphat does things that please Yahweh.

The word **father** means biological father here. Use the same word for father as you used in previous passages.

**Yahweh** is God's personal name. Use the same name for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

However, Jehoshaphat does not take down the **shrines on the hilltops** where people worship other gods. The people of Judah, even at this point in the story, still had not set their **hearts** on God. In other words, the people did not really want to follow the God of their fathers. The God of their fathers is Yahweh, the **Creator God**. The word fathers here means ancestors, not biological fathers. Use the same word or phrase for "shrines on the hilltops" or **high places** as you used in previous passages. Use the same word for the Creator God as you used in previous passages. For more information on **God**, refer to the Master Glossary. If you use your word for heart in your translation, refer to heart in the Master Glossary.

From start to finish, Jehu, the son of Hanani, writes these things in a book or **scroll** called the history, or records, of Jehu. Jehu's writings are part of a bigger book called the "Book of the Kings of Israel." Use the same word or phrase for scroll as you have used in previous passages. Refer to scroll in the Master Glossary for more information.

Use the same words or phrases for **Israel** as you used in previous passages. For more information on Israel, refer to the Master Glossary.

Jehoshaphat made an alliance with King Ahaziah of Israel. Either Jehoshaphat or Ahaziah was **wicked**, or evil. Use the same word or phrase for wicked as you have used previously, and refer to wicked in the Master Glossary for more information.

Then the prophet Eliezer, the son of Dodavahu, warns King Jehoshaphat. Eliezer **prophesies**, or tells Jehoshaphat, that Yahweh will destroy the **ships** Jehoshaphat builds because Jehoshaphat makes an alliance, or agreement, with King Ahaziah. Use the same words or phrases for prophesy and ships as you used in previous passages. For more information on prophesy, refer to the Master Glossary.

## 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 (id: eng-2ch-p41-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the last story, Jehu killed King Ahaziah of Judah. Then King Ahaziah's mother, Athaliah, made herself queen of Judah and killed the rest of the royal family members so that no one could become king. But Ahaziah's sister, Jehosheba, who was married to Yahweh's high priest, Jehoiada, hid Ahaziah's baby son, Joash, in Yahweh's temple so that Athaliah could not find and kill Joash.

This story happens almost seven years later, when Joash is now seven years old. At this time, Jehoiada, the high priest, decides it is time to take action. So Jehoiada secretly meets with the commanders or leaders of the military. These men are Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of \[]{.mark}Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zicri. Jehoiada makes a covenant or special agreement with these men. Then these men travel all around the kingdom of Judah and gather all of the Levites and the heads of all the Israelite families and bring all of these men to Jerusalem, the capital city.

When this large crowd of men arrives in Jerusalem, all of the men gather at the house of Yahweh, the temple, where Joash is hiding. All of the men make a covenant or special agreement to make Joash the new king. Then Jehoiada, the high priest, speaks to all of the men. Jehoiada says that Ahaziah's son Joash will become the new king so that the promise Yahweh made to King David long ago will happen. You will remember that Yahweh had promised David that one of David's descendants would always be king over Israel.

Next, Jehoiada gives all of the men instructions. First, Jehoiada says that of all of the priests and Levites whose turn it is to serve Yahweh at the temple, a third of those men must guard the gates into the temple area. Another third of those men must guard the palace, and the last third must stand near the Foundation Gate, which was probably a gate in the wall that surrounded the temple and the royal palace. Jehoiada also says that all of the other men who are not priests or Levites must gather together in the temple courtyards, which are open areas just outside the temple. Jehoiada also reminds people that no one but the priests and Levites who are supposed to be working at the temple at that time may go into the temple itself. This is because Yahweh only allows the men who are holy or ceremonially clean to go into Yahweh's house. Finally, Jehoiada says the Levites must surround Joash while the Levites hold swords or sharp weapons. If anyone tries to come into the temple area, the Levites must kill that person. These Levites must bring Joash safely into the temple area, and these Levites must also protect Joash when the time comes to leave the temple. With all of these people in place to guard Joash in this way, no one will be able to harm Joash.

Stop here and look at a drawing of what the temple and royal palace area might have looked like. Look at the temple itself, the inner and outer courtyards of the temple, and the wall that protected the temple and palace from the rest of the city of Jerusalem. Pause this audio here.

So the Levites and all the men of Judah who have gathered together do exactly as Jehoiada has said. Each of the commanders gathers all of his men together, including the men who are to serve on the Sabbath and those who are not. Then Jehoiada gives all of the commanders of the Levites weapons, including spears and large and small shields that once belonged to King David's men. People had stored all of these weapons and shields at the temple. Then Jehoiada instructs all of these men to stand around Joash with the weapons, ready to protect Joash. So all of the men position themselves in a semi\-circle around the altar and the front of the temple, from the south side of the temple to the north side of the temple. You will remember that the temple faced to the east. So by standing in this way, the men fully protect Joash from anyone who might try to come near to harm Joash.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about an important person whom other people must protect. How do people organize themselves to protect the person? Where do the people stand, or how do the people move when they guard the person? What tools or weapons do the people carry? Pause this audio here.

Then Jehoiada and his sons bring Joash, King Ahaziah's son, out of the temple and put the king's crown on Joash's head. The men also give Joash a copy of the covenant, which is all of the written instructions or rules the king must obey as part of the king's agreement with Yahweh. Then the men proclaim or announce that Joash is now the king, and the men anoint Joash by pouring oil over his head. Finally, everyone shouts loudly, "Let the king live forever!"

Now, Athaliah, the queen, hears people running and cheering for the king. The storyteller does not tell us where Athaliah is at this time, but Athaliah is probably in the royal palace, which is near the temple. It seems that because Jehoiada and all the men kept the plans secret, Athaliah was not aware of these things until now. So when Athaliah hears all of the people shouting about the king, Athaliah probably feels very surprised and concerned. So Athaliah goes to the temple where all the people are gathered.

The storyteller does not explain how Athaliah gets past the guards into the temple area, but when Athaliah arrives, she sees Joash, the new king, standing beside the pillar at the entrance to the temple. The storyteller does not say what this pillar is, but we know from other passages in the Bible that there were two large pillars in front of the temple. Athaliah also sees the commanders of the military and the men who play the trumpets standing there with King Joash. And Athaliah also hears the people celebrating and playing loud sounds on the trumpets and musical instruments.

Athaliah tears her clothes or the robe Athaliah wears. You will remember that in that culture, people would rip or tear their clothes to show other people that they felt very shocked or upset. Then Athaliah says loudly, "Treason! Treason!" Treason is when you help your leader's enemies take away your leader's power or hurt your leader. So here, Athaliah seems to be saying that Jehoiada and everyone else who has helped make Joash the king have betrayed or been unfaithful to Athaliah as queen.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about someone in your community who felt very upset or sad because of something surprising and bad that people did. Tell what that person did to show how they felt. Pause this audio here.

Then Jehoiada tells the commanders or leaders of the military to take Athaliah away. Jehoiada tells the commanders to kill anyone who tries to follow behind to protect Athaliah or to set Athaliah free. Jehoiada tells the commanders not to kill Athaliah in the temple. To kill someone in the temple would make the temple ceremonially unclean, so Jehoiada is saying that the men must kill Athaliah outside. So the commanders force Athaliah to walk with them through the horses' entrance to the king's palace, and there the guards kill Athaliah.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has six scenes.

**In the first scene:** Jehoiada makes a covenant or agreement with the five men who are the commanders of the military. Then these men go to the different parts of the kingdom of Judah. The men gather all the Levites and the leaders of family groups and bring them all back to Yahweh's temple in Jerusalem.

**In the second scene:** Jehoiada speaks to the large crowd of men who have gathered at the temple. Jehoiada says the men will make Joash the new king. Jehoiada gives detailed instructions to organize all of the men to protect the temple area and Joash himself. Then all of the men organize themselves, and Jehoiada gives the men weapons to protect Joash.

**In the third scene:** Jehoiada brings Joash out of the temple, where the crowd can see Joash. The men put the crown on Joash's head and give Joash the written instructions for how to obey Yahweh. The men also anoint Joash with oil, and then everyone shouts, "Long live the king!"

**In the fourth scene:** Athaliah hears the noise that the people are making, so Athaliah goes to the temple to see what the people are doing.

**In the fifth scene:** When Athaliah arrives at the temple, Athaliah sees Joash standing by the pillar. Athaliah also sees the commanders and the people who are blowing trumpets standing beside the king and all the people celebrating. Then Athaliah tears her clothes and says, "Treason! Treason!"

**In the sixth scene:** Jehoidah commands the commanders to take Athaliah out of the temple. Jehoidah says not to kill Athaliah in the temple. The commanders follow Jehoidah's orders and then kill Athaliah.

The characters in this passage are:

* Jehoiada, the high priest
* Military commanders: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zicri
* Levites
* Heads or leaders of all of the Israelite families
* Joash, the new king
* God, whose name is Yahweh
* Priests, who are also Levites
* Athaliah, the queen
* People of Judah who are celebrating
* And trumpeters

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

We hear this same story about King Joash in 2 Kings 11:13–21, although some of the details of the story are different. So if you have already translated 2 Kings, you can go back and listen to 2 Kings chapter 11 to remember how you translated it.

Stop here and listen to 2 Kings 11:13–21\. Listen for any ways that this story in 2 Chronicles is either the same or different from the story in 2 Kings. Pause this audio here.

In the first scene, the storyteller says that in the seventh year, Jehoiada took courage. "The seventh year" means that nearly seven years have passed since the last story, when Jehosheba hid Joash away in the temple so that Athaliah could not find Joash and kill Joash. So now, in the seventh year, Jehoiada takes courage. This means that Jehoiada strengthens his position or takes some action to take control of the situation. Jehoiada begins by entering into a covenant with the commanders of hundreds of men, who are the top leaders of the military. This covenant means that Jehoiada makes an agreement with these men. These men's names are Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zicri. You will remember that in Bible times, people often said the name of a person's father as well as that person's own name so that everyone would know exactly which person they talked about.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your community, when more than one person has the same personal name, what else do you say when you talk about that person so that everyone knows exactly which person you mean? For example, do you also say that person's family name, the name of the person's father or mother, the name of the village or place where that person lives, or something else? Pause this audio here.

After Jehoiada and these commanders agreed about what they would do, each of the men went throughout the kingdom of Judah and gathered the Levites and the heads of Israelite families from each city. The storyteller does not say if Jehoiada and these men went to each place together or if the men went separately to different places. But we know that these men then brought all of the men they had gathered back to Jerusalem. We know this because, as the second scene begins, the storyteller says that when all of these people came to Jerusalem, everyone who had assembled made a covenant with the king in the "house of God," which means in Yahweh's temple. You will remember that a covenant is a special agreement that two people or groups of people make, where each one makes a promise either to do or not do certain things. The storyteller does not say exactly what the people agree to do or not do, but the people probably agree to protect Joash and to make Joash their new king. Then Jehoiada said to everyone gathered, "Behold, the king's son!" "Behold" is special language that means "Look!" or "Pay attention!" Jehoiada calls Joash "the king's son" because Joash is the son of Ahaziah, who had been Judah's king until Jehu killed King Ahaziah in a previous story. Then Jehoiada continues to speak and says that the king's son, meaning Joash, will reign, just as Yahweh promised David's sons, which means David's descendants. You will remember that "to reign" means to rule and have authority as king, so Jehoiada is saying that Joash will be the new king. Athaliah, who has been acting like the queen, is not one of David's descendants. But Joash is David's descendant. So when Joash becomes king, Yahweh's promise will happen. This shows us how important it is that Joash become king, and it also shows that Yahweh will support this plan.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How does someone become the head leader in your culture? Does a person become the next leader automatically because of the family they are born into, or do people talk together and choose who the next leader will be? What happens if someone who is not supposed to be the leader tries to make themselves the leader? Pause this audio here.

Now, Jehoiada tells everyone what they must do. First, Jehoida says that one\-third of the priests and Levites who are going on duty on the Sabbath day must serve as guards at the gates where people enter the temple area. You will remember that the priests and Levites help people worship Yahweh at the temple, and the Sabbath day is the special day of the week when everyone rests from their work. You will also remember that the priests and Levites each had certain days where they did their work, and certain days where they rested while other priests and Levites worked. So here, Jehoiada is saying that the priests and Levites who are to work on this day must divide up into three equal groups and then one of those groups must act as guards at the gates into the temple area to protect it. Jehoiada then says that another one of those three groups must guard the royal palace, which is where the king lives. And the final group must stand and protect the Foundation Gate. The storyteller does not say what the Foundation Gate is, but this is probably the gate in the wall that surrounds the temple and the royal palace within the city of Jerusalem.

Jehoiada also says that all of the other men in the crowd who are not priests or Levites must gather together in the temple courtyards, which are the open areas just outside the temple. Jehoiada says not to let anyone except the priests and Levites who are supposed to be working at the temple go into the temple itself, because only these men are holy or ceremonially clean and allowed to go into Yahweh's house.

Finally, Jehoiada says the Levites must surround Joash while they hold swords or sharp weapons. You will remember that a sword is a long, sharp weapon with a handle, and that soldiers use swords to kill people in battle. If anyone tries to come into the temple area, the Levites must kill that person. And the Levites must not only bring Joash safely into the temple area, but the Levites must also protect Joash when the time comes to leave the temple.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a sword. Pause this audio here.

After Jehoiada finishes giving these instructions to the people, the Levites, including the priests, who are a special group of Levites, do just as Jehoiada, the high priest, ordered. Each leader takes or gathers and organizes his men, both those men who were to go on duty on the Sabbath and those who were going off duty. Here, the storyteller says that Jehoiada had not said any of the men could leave when it was time to go off duty, so all of the priests and Levites are here to help.

Jehoiada gives the commanders of the Levites spears, as well as the large and small shields that had belonged to King David. You will remember that a spear is a sharp, pointed weapon that people make from metal and then attach to a long pole, and shields are something that soldiers carry to protect themselves from their enemy. People had stored these things at the temple, so Jehoiada now gets these things out of storage and gives them to the men to use.

Jehoiada stations or organizes all of these men, each with his weapon in his hand, into position so that they are all around Joash, the new king. These men stand near the altar and the temple from the south side of the temple to the north side. In this way, the men protect Joash so that no enemy can come near Joash from any side.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a spear and a picture of a shield. Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Jehoiada and the other men bring out Joash, the king's son. The men place the king's crown on Joash's head. You will remember that a crown is a special decorative item that a person wears on the top of their head. A crown shows that this person has power and authority that only the king would have.

The men also give Joash a copy of the covenant or laws that the king must obey as part of their agreement with Yahweh. People have written all of these instructions on a scroll, which is a very long piece of paper or animal skin that people roll up around a stick so that they can easily store it away or carry it from place to place.

Then the men announce that Joash is the king, and the men anoint Joash, which means the men pour oil over Joash's head to show that Yahweh set apart or specially chose Joash to serve as king.

And finally, everyone says loudly together, "Long live the king!" which is a way to say that the people want Joash to live a long life and serve as king for a very long time.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a scroll and a picture of a crown. Pause this audio here.

In the fourth scene, Athaliah hears the noise of people running and the loud noise of people cheering for the king. The storyteller does not say who is running or where Athaliah is at this time, but Athaliah is probably in the palace. And it may be that other people in the palace are also surprised to hear the crowd cheering and are running toward the temple to see what is happening. So Athaliah also goes to the temple.

In the fifth scene, when Athaliah arrives at the temple, Athaliah looks and sees the king standing by the pillar at the entrance to the temple. The storyteller does not say which pillar this is, but we know from 1 Kings 7:15–22 that Solomon's workers built two large, decorated pillars that stood in front of the temple. Athaliah also sees the commanders and the trumpeters, or the men whose job it was to blow the trumpets, standing beside the king. You will remember that a trumpet is a type of musical instrument that people use to make a loud noise. Athaliah also sees and hears all of the people celebrating and blowing trumpets, and Athaliah sees the musicians playing their musical instruments and leading the celebration.

Stop here and look at a picture of what the two columns in front of the temple might have looked like. Pause this audio here.

So when Athaliah sees all of these things, Athaliah immediately tears her clothes. This means that Athaliah pulls strongly against her outer robe so that the cloth tears apart. Then Athaliah cries out, or says in a very loud voice, "Treason! Treason!" This is another way to say, "You are traitors! You have betrayed me!" In other words, Athaliah accuses the people of being disloyal to Athaliah.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about a time when people betrayed or were disloyal to a leader by secretly helping someone else to become the new leader. What words do you use to describe what these people did? Pause this audio here.

In the sixth scene, the high priest, Jehoiadah, tells the military commanders to take Athaliah outside the temple courtyard. Jehoidah tells the men to do this with Athaliah between the rows of soldiers so that Athaliah cannot escape.

Jehoidah says to use a sword to kill anyone who follows Athaliah. Although Jehoidah does not say, Jehoidah probably means to kill anyone who follows closely behind Athaliah to try to protect her or free her from the guards. Although Jehoidah does not tell the commanders exactly what to do with Athaliah, Jehoidah says not to kill Athaliah in the temple. So the commanders know that Jehoidah means to kill Athaliah once they leave the temple area. The men lay hands on Athaliah, which means the men hold onto Athaliah like a prisoner so that Athaliah cannot escape. Then the men take Athaliah to the horses' entrance to the king's house or palace. You will remember that a horse is a large animal that people, such as kings or soldiers, would ride. So this was probably some sort of gate or entrance into the part of the palace where the guards kept the horses. Then, when the men arrive at this place, the men kill Athaliah.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a horse. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has six scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* Jehoiada, the high priest
* Military commanders: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zicri
* Levites
* Heads or leaders of all of the Israelite families
* Joash, the new king
* God, whose name is Yahweh
* Priests, who are also Levites
* Athaliah, the queen
* People of Judah who are celebrating
* And trumpeters

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

After nearly seven years, Jehoiada decided that it was time to take action. So Jehoiada made an agreement with the military commanders of hundreds of soldiers. Those men were Jeroham's son Azariah, and Jehohanan's son Ishmael, and Obed's son Azariah, and Adaiah's son Maaseiah, and Zicri's son Elishaphat. These men traveled to all of the cities in Judah and brought together all of the Levites and the heads of the Israelite families.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Jehoiada the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* Athaliah is a bad woman who murdered people so that Athaliah could be queen. But Yahweh never meant for Athaliah to be queen. Yahweh promised that one of David's ancestors would always be king in Israel. And that ancestor is Joash! or
* We have hidden Joash for almost seven years now. It is time to make Joash king!

Ask the people playing the commanders, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We respect Jehoiada and are happy to help Jehoiada carry out this plan; or
* We know that Athaliah will be angry and try to stop this plan, so we will keep this plan a secret and make sure no one takes the news back to Athaliah, the queen.

> Continue the drama.

When all of these people came to Jerusalem, these people made an agreement with Joash, the king's son, in God's house, the temple. Jehoiada said to all the men, "The king's son will be king as Yahweh promised David's descendants. Now this is what you must do. A third of you priests and Levites who are going to be on duty on the Sabbath are to guard the temple gates. Another third of you priests and Levites must guard the palace. And the other third of priests and Levites must stand at the Foundation Gate. The rest of you will remain in the open area or courtyard around Yahweh's temple. Do not let anyone enter the temple of Yahweh except the priests and Levites on duty. Those priests and Levites may enter the temple because they are ritually pure, but the others are to obey Yahweh's instructions and not enter. The Levites are to surround the king, and each man must hold a weapon in his hand. You must kill anyone who comes into Yahweh's house. Stay close to the king wherever the king goes."

So the Levites and all of the other people of Judah did what Jehoiada the priest told the people to do. Each one of the leaders took his men, both those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath and those who were going off duty, because Jehoiada the priest had not let any of them go home. Jehoiada gave the commanders of the Levites the spears and the large and small shields. These weapons had belonged to King David, and people had stored these weapons in the temple. Jehoiada stationed all the men with their weapons in their hands around the king. The men stood near the altar and the temple from the south side to the north side of the temple.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Jehoiada, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I know that Queen Athaliah will be very angry when she finds out that Joash is alive and that we are making Joash king. Athaliah will probably try to kill Joash if she can, so I must create a very good plan to protect Joash.

Ask the people playing the commanders, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The peoplemight answer things like:

* Jehoiada has made a very good plan. We have lots of men here with weapons to stand between Joash and anyone who might come close to hurt Joash. We have men at the gate of the wall to make sure no one can come inside. And we even have men at the palace to protect Joash when we are ready to go there with Joash later.

Ask the people playing the Levites who are guarding Joash, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We hope no one comes close to try to hurt Joash, but if someone does, we are ready to protect Joash; or
* We are glad that people kept all of these spears and shields here at the temple. These will help us protect Joash much better than if we only had our swords.

Continue the drama.

Then Jehoiada and Jehoiada's sons brought the king's son, Joash, and placed the crown on Joash's head. The men gave Joash a copy of the laws that instructed how Joash must rule as king, and they announced to everyone that Joash was now the king. The men also anointed Joash with oil, and everyone shouted, "Long live the king!"

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Joash, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am only a child, just seven years old. I have no idea how to be a king! or
* I am glad these men gave me these written instructions. Maybe if I do what the instructions say, I will know what to do, even though I am just a child and have never been a leader; or
* I always wanted to leave the temple and see what it was like outside, but it was never safe for me to leave before. Now that I can finally come outside, all of these people are looking at me. I feel overwhelmed!

Continue the drama.

When Athaliah heard the sound of people running and cheering for the king, Athaliah went to Yahweh's temple to see what people were doing there.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Athaliah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I hear people shouting about a king, but there is no king anymore. After Ahaziah died, I killed everyone in the family who could become the next king; or
* I do not know why people are shouting about a king, but I am worried. I had better go see what this is all about.

Continue the drama.

Athaliah looked and saw the king standing by the pillar at the door of the temple. Athaliah also saw the commanders of the military and the trumpeters who were beside the king. All the people were happy, and people were playing trumpets. The musicians were also playing instruments and leading people in the celebration. Then Athaliah tore her clothing apart and shouted, "You have betrayed me! You have betrayed me!"

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Athaliah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am shocked that every one of the leaders hid this from me. No one who knew this secret came to tell me! or
* I thought for sure I had killed every one of David's descendants who might challenge me as queen. I am shocked to find out that Joash is still alive.

Ask the people playing all the people celebrating, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We are so happy to have a proper king to rule and protect us! or
* We never liked having Athaliah as the queen. Athaliah is a bad woman who killed her own family to make herself powerful, so no one can trust Athaliah; or
* We know that Yahweh said one of David's descendants will also be our king. Joash is David's descendant and the person who was supposed to be king, so that must mean Yahweh will bless Joash and us, too.

> Continue the drama.

Jehoiada the priest sent out the army commanders of hundreds, who were in charge of the troops and said to these men, "Bring Athaliah out between the rows of guards so that she cannot escape. And kill anyone who follows Athaliah." Jehoiada the priest had said, "Do not kill Athaliah in Yahweh's temple." So the men caught Athaliah and killed her at the entrance of the Horse Gate that enters the palace courtyard.

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing the commanders, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We are used to fighting and killing enemies in battle, but to have to kill an older woman makes us feel uncomfortable, especially when Athaliah used to give us orders; or
* We do not like to kill Athaliah, but Athaliah killed her own family and tried to kill Joash too, so this is the right thing to do; or
* We never liked Athaliah. Athaliah was an evil woman, so we feel relieved and happy now that Athaliah is no longer alive to threaten Joash or any of us.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 23:1–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Jehoiada made a **covenant** with the commanders of hundreds of soldiers. \[A covenant is a strong and serious agreement where people or groups promise to do certain things for each other and trust each other to keep those promises.]{.mark} When people make a covenant, the people swear an oath and say, "I will keep my promise. If I do not, God may punish me." Use the same word or phrase for covenant as you used in previous passages. For more information on covenant, refer to the Master Glossary.

Then each of these leaders went throughout Judah and gathered the **Levites** and the heads of fathers' **households** of Israel. The Levites are people who belong to the tribe of Levi, one of the 12 tribes of Israel. The "heads of fathers' houses" refers to the men in each family and clan, or large family group, of Judah who were the leaders of those families and clans. Use the same words or phrases for Levites and "heads of fathers' houses" as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up Levites and household in the Master Glossary.

Sometimes the word **Israel** refers to all the descendants of Jacob together. It then means the same as Israelites, or as people of Israel. Other times, the word Israel refers to the land, or the territory, where the Israelites lived. You will remember that during this time, the land of Israel was divided into two kingdoms: people usually called the kingdom to the north "Israel" and the kingdom to the south Judah". However, in this story, the storyteller uses "Israel" to refer to Judah, the southern kingdom. Use the same word or phrase for "Israel" as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up Israelites in the Master Glossary.

Then all of these men came to **Jerusalem**. For more information, look up Jerusalem in the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for Jerusalem as you used in previous passages.

And the people gathered together in a special gathering or **assembly**, and made a covenant with the **king** at the **house of God**. A king is someone who rules over a city or territory, like a region or country. **God** is the general word for Yahweh, the true God who created everything. And the "house of God" is another way to refer to the **temple**. Use the same words or phrases for assembly, king, God, and "house of God" or temple as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up king, God, and temple in the Master Glossary.

Jehoiada said that **Yahweh** had promised that **David's** **sons** would always reign over Israel. Yahweh is God's personal name, and David refers to King David. Here, "sons" means David's descendants. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh, David, and sons or **descendants** as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up Yahweh, David, and descendant in the Master Glossary.

Jehoiada gives detailed instructions to the **priests** and the Levites. You will remember that the priests are Levites who are descendants of Aaron. The priests worked in the temple to serve Yahweh by offering sacrifices on behalf of the people, and the other Levites helped the priests to do that important work. Use the same word or phrase for priests as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up priest in the Master Glossary.

Jehoiada gave instructions for the Levites who were going on duty on the **Sabbath**. The Sabbath is the seventh day of the week for the Israelites. It is a day of rest and worship to God. Use the same word or phrase for Sabbath as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up Sabbath in the Master Glossary.

Jehoiada says not to let anyone go inside the temple except the priests and the **ministering** Levites, because these men are **holy**. To minister means to serve, and to be holy means to be ceremonially clean or set apart. Use the same words or phrases for minister and holy as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, see the Master Glossary.

The men stood around the **altar** and the temple from the south side of the temple to the north side. You will remember that the altar was the place where people made offerings and sacrifices to God. Use the same word or phrase for altar as you used in previous passages. For more information on altar, see the Master Glossary.

The men **anointed** Joash as king. Use the same word or phrase for anointed as you used in previous passages. For more information on anoint, see the Master Glossary.

The trumpeters were people whose job it was to blow a trumpet. Trumpets were long, straight instruments that people had made from hammered metal, either silver or bronze. People used these trumpets in times of war to sound the alarm, but people also used the trumpets to produce music in times of celebration.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a trumpet. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **trumpeter**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Jehoiada told the people to put anyone who followed Athaliah **to the sword**. Use the same word or phrase for killing people with a sword as you have used in previous stories.

Jehoiada told the priests to put Athaliah to death at the Horse Gate into the **palace**, or the king's house. Use the same word or phrase for palace that you have used previously.
