## 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 (id: eng-2ch-p50-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, the storyteller told us what happened during Jotham's time as king of Judah. Jotham followed Yahweh, completed many building projects, and defeated the Ammonites in war. When Jotham died, Jotham's son, Ahaz, became the next king.

Ahaz was 20 years old when Ahaz began to rule from Jerusalem. Ahaz ruled for 16 years as king.

Unlike Ahaz's ancestor, King David, Ahaz does not do what is right in the eyes of Yahweh. In other words, Ahaz does not live in a way that pleases Yahweh. Instead, Ahaz acts like the kings of the northern kingdom of Israel, who continually disobeyed Yahweh. The storyteller compares Ahaz to the northern kings to show how bad Ahaz truly was. Ahaz behaves so badly that Ahaz tells people to make metal statues of Baal, the Canaanite god of storms and fertility. The people pour melted liquid metals, such as gold, silver, bronze, or iron, into molds and allow the metal to cool and harden to make metal idols. The people then use the metal idols to worship the god Baal.

Stop here and look at a picture of a metal idol of Baal. In your culture, what kinds of objects or symbols do people use to show respect or devotion to spirits or gods? Pause this audio here.

Ahaz was so far from Yahweh that Ahaz made offerings in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem, and even burned Ahaz's own sons as a sacrifice.

Stop here as a group and look at a map that shows Jerusalem and the Valley of Ben Hinnom. Pause this audio here.

The people who lived in the land before the Israelites did many evil things. Specifically, the Ammonites burned their children in fire to worship their god Molech. But Yahweh took the land away from those people and gave the Israelites specific laws that forbid child sacrifices. The Israelites viewed child sacrifice as something hateful and a disgusting violation against Yahweh. When Ahaz sacrifices his son to the false god, Ahaz shows just how wicked Ahaz has become.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture talk about the difference between religious practices that cause people to live well and religious practices that cause harm? Pause this audio here.

Ahaz not only sacrifices his sons, but Ahaz also offers sacrifices and worships at the high places, on the hilltops, and under every green tree. The high places were places where people worshiped and made sacrifices to other gods who were not Yahweh, the one true Creator God. The people offered animals and burned incense, or sweet\-smelling spices, to their gods. The high places, hilltops, and beneath green trees were all common places for non\-Israelites to worship their gods. The Israelites considered these places to be unclean and unfit for worship to Yahweh.

Because of Ahaz's disobedience, Yahweh gives Ahaz into the hands of the king of Aram, which means Yahweh allows the king of Aram to defeat Ahaz. We know from 2 Kings 16 that Rezin was the King of Aram, or Syria. King Rezin's army not only defeats Ahaz, but he takes many of the people of Judah prisoner and forces them to move to the city of Damascus. Damascus was the capital city of Aram.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story of a time when a leader's choices led the whole community into trouble. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also allows Ahaz to be in the hand of, or under the power of, King Pekah of Israel. Pekah's army killed 120,000 experienced soldiers in Ahaz's army. Yahweh allows King Pekah to defeat Ahaz and his army because they did not worship Yahweh as their ancestors did, but instead worshiped false gods. During the battle, Zicri, a champion fighter from the clan of Ephraim, kills three important men. Ephraim was one of the tribes of Israel, and Ephraim belonged to the northern kingdom. Zicri kills Maaseiah, one of the sons of King Ahaz. It is unclear if Maaseiah was an actual son of the king or if this was a title. Zicri also kills Azrikam, the commander of the palace, or the official who was in charge of the palace and Elkanah, who was second in command to the king.

Once the soldiers from the northern kingdom of Israel win the battle, the soldiers take 200,000 women and children as prisoners. The women and children from Judah were also relatives of the Israelites, because they were descendants of Jacob. The Israelite soldiers take a large amount of valuables from the people of Judah and carry the plunder and the people back to the capital city of Samaria in Israel.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a map that shows Judah, Israel, and Syria, as well as the cities of Damascus, Jerusalem, and Samaria.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

**In the first scene:** Ahaz becomes the king of Judah when he is 20 years old, and Ahaz rules for 16 years. While Ahaz is king, Ahaz does not act in a way that pleases Yahweh. Ahaz orders people to make metal images to worship Baal. Ahaz goes to the valley of Ben Hinnom and sacrifices his sons in the fire to worship a false god. Ahaz makes offerings and worships false gods at the high places, on the hill tops, and under every green tree.

**In the second scene:** Yahweh allows Rezin, the King of Aram, or Syria, to come against King Ahaz and defeat him. The Aramian army defeats the people of Judah and forces many of the people to move to the city of Damascus.

**In the third scene:** Yahweh allows Pekah, the king of Israel, to come against King Ahaz. The Israelite army kills 120,000 strong soldiers of Judah. An Israelite soldier, Zicri, kills three important men during the battle: Maaseiah, Ahaz's son; Azrikam, the official in charge of Ahaz's palace; and Elkanah, the second in command to Ahaz.

**In the fourth scene:** The Israelite soldiers force 200,000 women and children from Judah to be prisoners, even though they are relatives. The Israelite soldiers take many valuable items from Judah, and the soldiers force the prisoners to go to their capital city, Samaria.

The characters in this passage are:

* Ahaz
* Ahaz's sons
* Rezin, king of Aram or Syria
* The Aramian army
* Pekah, king of Israel
* The Israelite army
* The men of Judah
* Zicri
* Maaseiah
* Azrikam
* Elkanah
* And the 200,000 women and children prisoners from Judah

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The storyteller uses the same format as previous passages to introduce Ahaz as the king of Judah. Ahaz became king when Ahaz was 20 years old, reigned from Jerusalem, and ruled as king for 16 years.

Unlike Ahaz's father, David, Ahaz did not do what was right in the eyes of Yahweh. It is important to remember that David was not the actual father of Ahaz, but rather, David was the ancestor of Ahaz. "Did not do what was right in the eyes of Yahweh" is special language that means Ahaz did not act in a way that was pleasing to Yahweh. Instead of serving Yahweh, Ahaz worshiped false gods.

Ahaz walked in the way of the kings of Israel. It is important to remember that here, Israel refers to the northern kingdom of Israel and not to the nation as a whole. The storyteller saw these Israelite kings as evil because most of them did not follow Yahweh. The storyteller is not referring to how Ahaz physically walked. Rather, the storyteller is saying that Ahaz acted like or imitated the kings of Israel because Ahaz had no desire to obey Yahweh.

Ahaz made cast idols for worshipping the Baals. Ahaz did not make the idols himself, but most likely ordered people to make the metal images for Ahaz. Baal was a Canaanite god of storms and fertility.

Ahaz also goes to the Valley of Ben Hinnom to burn incense and make offerings. Ahaz also sacrifices his sons in the fire to worship a false god.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of the Valley of Ben Hinnom. Pause this audio here.

It is important to remember that the Ammonite people often practiced child sacrifice to worship their god, Molech. Yahweh's law strictly forbade child sacrifice, so the Israelites saw it as a disgusting or detestable act against Yahweh. You will remember that detestable things are things that Yahweh hates.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about someone who did something absolutely horrible. Pay attention to the words and phrases you use to talk about this horrible thing. Pause this audio here.

When Ahaz sacrificed his sons, Ahaz acted like the people who used to live in the land of Israel before Yahweh allowed the Israelites to conquer the land. It is important to notice that the storyteller says Ahaz sacrificed more than one son, while 2 Kings 16 says Ahaz only sacrificed one son.

Ahaz offered sacrifices and burned incense, or sweet\-smelling spices, at the high places, on the hilltops, and under every green tree. It is important to remember that the high places, hill tops, and beneath green trees were all common places for non\-Israelites to worship their gods. This was another way to say that Ahaz made offerings at every place where people were not supposed to worship Yahweh.

The storyteller says it is because Ahaz continued to disobey Yahweh that Yahweh gave Ahaz into the hand of the King of Aram, or Syria. When someone is "in the hand" of someone else, that person is under the power of that person. In other words, Yahweh allows King Rezin to defeat King Ahaz and take many of Ahaz's people prisoner to the city of Damascus in Aram.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story of someone who was under the power or authority of someone else. Pay attention to what words or phrases you use to describe someone who is under the control of someone else. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also gives Ahaz into the hand of, or under the power of, King Pekah of Israel. During one battle, King Pekah's soldiers kill 120,000 experienced soldiers of Judah. Israel defeats Judah because Ahaz and the people of Judah had abandoned Yahweh, the God of their ancestors. The storyteller says this because the storyteller wants to remind us that Yahweh specially chose the people of Judah as his own people, and yet the people chose to reject Yahweh.

During the battle, Zicri, a champion fighter from Israel, kills three important men: Maaseiah, Ahaz's son; Azrikam, the official in charge of Ahaz's palace; and Elkanah, the second in command to Ahaz.

The Israelite army takes many valuable items from Judah, and the Israelite army forces 200,000 women and children of Judah to be prisoners. The Israelite army takes the valuables and forces the prisoners to go to Samaria, the capital city of Israel. It is important to remember that the people living in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were relatives because they were all descendants of Jacob.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* Ahaz
* Ahaz's sons
* Rezin, king of Aram or Syria
* The Syrian army
* Pekah, king of Israel
* The Israelite army
* The men of Judah
* Zicri
* Maaseiah
* Azrikam
* Elkanah
* And the 200,000 women and children prisoners from Judah

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Act out Ahaz becoming the king of Judah when Ahaz is 20 years old. Ahaz rules for 16 years. While Ahaz is king, Ahaz does not act in a way that pleases Yahweh. Ahaz has people make metal images to worship Baal. Ahaz goes to the valley of Ben Hinnom and sacrifices his sons in the fire to worship a false god. Ahaz makes offerings and worships false gods at the high places, on the hilltops, and under every green tree.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel offended. How could our king sacrifice his children to a false god? or
* I feel scared. If King Ahaz is this desperate, he must feel threatened by our enemies; or
* I feel sad. King Ahaz has completely walked away from Yahweh. Our nation will suffer because of King Ahaz's disobedience.

Continue the drama.

Act out Yahweh allowing Rezin, the king of Aram, to attack King Ahaz in Jerusalem and conquer him. The Syrian army defeats the people of Judah and forces many of the people to move to the city of Damascus.

Act out how Yahweh allows Pekah, the king of Israel, to come against King Ahaz. The Israelite army kills 120,000 strong soldiers of Judah. An Israelite soldier, Zicri, kills three important men during the battle: Maaseiah, Ahaz's son; Azrikam, the official in charge of Ahaz's palace; and Elkanah, the second in command to Ahaz.

Act out how the Israelite soldiers force 200,000 women and children from Judah to be prisoners. The Israelite soldiers take many valuable items from Judah, and the soldiers force the prisoners to go to Samaria.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the prisoners, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel shocked. These soldiers are our relatives! How could they do this to us? or
* I feel panicked. I do not want to leave my homeland; or
* I am afraid. I want to go back to my family.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:1–8 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Ahaz becomes the next **king** of Judah, and Ahaz rules from **Jerusalem**. A king is someone who rules over a city or territory, like a region or a country. Jerusalem was the capital city of the kingdom of Judah. Use the same words or phrases for king and Jerusalem as you used in previous passages. For more information on king or Jerusalem, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz does not do **what is right in the eyes of Yahweh**. In other words, Ahaz does not act in a way that pleases Yahweh. Yahweh is God's personal name and shows God's special relationship with his people. Use the same word or phrase for "what was right in the eyes of Yahweh" as you used in previous passages. For more information on **Yahweh**, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz walks in the ways of the kings of **Israel**. Here, Israel refers to the northern kingdom of Israel, not to the nation as a whole. Use the same word or phrase for Israel, meaning the northern kingdom, as you used in previous passages. For more information on Israel, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz even has people make metal **idols** for worshiping **Baal**. Baal refers to the male Canaanite god of fertility and storms. An idol is an object people made out of wood, stone, or metal in order to worship a god. Use the same word or phrase for Baal and idol as you used in previous passages. For more information on Baal and idols, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz burns incense to, or **sacrifices**, in the Valley of Ben Hinnom. In Jewish culture, people only burned incense or sacrificed on the altar in the temple. You may say that Ahaz burns incense in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, or you may say that Ahaz sacrifices or makes **offerings**. If you use sacrifices or offerings in your translation, refer to sacrifices or offerings in the Master Glossary for more information, and use the same words or phrases for sacrifices or offerings as you have used previously.

Ahaz also burns his children in the fire. Child sacrifice was something people in the nations in the land did before Yahweh forced those people out and gave the land to the Israelites. Yahweh considers these actions **detestable**. Use the same word or phrase for detestable as you used in 2 Chronicles 15:8\.

A **nation** is a group of people who live together in the same country and have the same ruler, such as the Ammonites. Here, "**Israelites**" refers to God's chosen people, the descendants of Jacob, who lived in the land of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for nation and Israelites as you used in previous passages. For more information on nation and Israelites, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz made offerings at every **high place, on the hilltops, and under every spreading tree**. These were all places where non\-Israelites worshiped false gods. This was another way to say that Ahaz made offerings at every place where people were not supposed to worship Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for "high place, on the hilltops, and under every spreading tree" as you used in previous passages.

So Yahweh gives Ahaz **into the hand of** the king of Aram and the king of Israel. "Into the hand of" means under the power of someone. In this case, Ahaz was under the power of his enemies, who defeated Ahaz in battle. Use the same word or phrase for "into the hand of" as you used in previous passages.

The king of Israel defeats 120,000 soldiers of **Judah**. Judah refers to the southern kingdom of Israel. The capital city of Judah was Jerusalem. Use the same word or phrase for Judah as you used in previous passages. For more information on Judah, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh allowed Israel to defeat Judah's soldiers because Judah had abandoned Yahweh, the **God** of their ancestors. God refers to God who created everything. God is the most powerful spiritual being who chose the Israelites as his special people. Use the same word for God as you have in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Zicri killed Azrikam, the officer in charge of the **palace**. The palace was the king's house. Use the same word for palace as you used in previous passages.

The Israelite soldiers defeat their relatives, take many valuables, and force 200,000 women and children to become prisoners. The Israelites take the prisoners and **plunder** to **Samaria**. Samaria was the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for plunder and Samaria as you used in previous passages. For more information on plunder and Samaria, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

## 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 (id: eng-2ch-p51-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the last story, we heard how King Ahaz of Judah, the southern kingdom, did not follow Yahweh but instead worshipped foreign gods. So Yahweh allowed Judah's enemies, including Israel, the northern kingdom, to defeat Judah. The soldiers of Israel killed many of Judah's soldiers. Israel's army also brought 200,000 people, including women and children, from Judah back to the city of Samaria as prisoners. In this story, we will now hear what Yahweh tells the people of Israel to do with those prisoners.

The story begins when one of Yahweh's prophets, Oded, comes out of the city of Samaria to speak to the army of Israel. The Israelite army has just returned from Judah with the prisoners. You will remember that Samaria is the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel.

Stop here as a group and look at a map that shows the southern kingdom of Judah and the northern kingdom of Israel. Find the city of Samaria on the map. Pause this audio here.

Oded tells the army that Yahweh was angry with Judah, and that is why Yahweh allowed the army of Israel to defeat Judah. But now, Yahweh is angry with Israel because Israel's soldiers killed Judah's people in a very angry and cruel way.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about some soldiers who fought a battle in a very angry and cruel way. What did those soldiers do that was different from how people normally expect soldiers to behave in battle? Pause this audio here.

Oded also says that the soldiers now plan to make all of these people from Judah Israel's slaves. You will remember that in the law that Yahweh gave to Moses, in the book of Leviticus, Yahweh allowed an Israelite to work as a servant to another Israelite for a time to pay off a debt. But Yahweh said the people were never to make another Israelite a slave. So it would be very wrong for the soldiers to do this.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do people think about slavery in your culture? If people take slaves, how do those people treat those slaves? Which types of people are you allowed to take slaves from? Would you ever take slaves from people who are related to you? Pause this audio here.

Oded also reminds the soldiers that although the people of Judah sinned, the people of Israel have sinned too. You will remember the story from earlier in this book and in 1 Kings of how the 10 northern tribes first formed their own kingdom, with Jeroboam as king. At that time, King Jeroboam created idols for the people to worship so that the people would not have to go to Jerusalem in Judah to worship at Yahweh's temple. So Israel has done the same kinds of sinful things that Judah has done.

Oded warns the soldiers that Yahweh is very angry with Israel, just as Yahweh was angry with Judah. Oded says the soldiers must release these people and let the people go back home to Judah.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, when an army wins a battle against another army, how do people explain why those people were able to win? Pause this audio here.

Four of Israel's leaders now speak to the soldiers and repeat the same warning Oded just gave. The leaders say that the soldiers cannot bring these prisoners to Samaria. The leaders say that the people of Israel are already very guilty of sin against Yahweh and that Yahweh is very angry.

So the soldiers let the prisoners go free. The soldiers also give everything the soldiers took during the battle to the leaders. Then, from those things, the leaders give the people from Judah clothing to cover their bodies and sandals to put on their feet. The leaders also give the people food and drink and take care of the people's wounds from the battle. The leaders give anyone who is unable to walk a donkey to ride. Then the leaders take all of the people back to the city of Jericho in Judah so the people can be with their relatives. People call Jericho the city of palm trees.

Stop here as a group and again look at the map of Israel that shows the southern kingdom of Judah and the northern kingdom of Israel. Find Jericho on the map. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of sandals, a donkey, and palm trees. Pause this audio here.

Finally, the leaders return to Samaria, their home in the kingdom of Israel.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

**In the first scene:** Oded, one of Yahweh's prophets, comes out of the city of Samaria to speak to the army of Israel as the army returns with prisoners from Judah. Oded says that Yahweh let Israel defeat Judah because Yahweh was angry with Judah. But Israel has sinned too, so Yahweh will punish Israel if they keep these people from Judah as prisoners.

**In the second scene:** Four of Israel's leaders speak to Israel's army. The leaders repeat Oded's warning.

**In the third scene:** Israel's army lets Judah's people go free.

**In the fourth scene:** Israel's leaders give the people from Judah clothes and sandals to wear and food and drink. The leaders also take care of the people's battle wounds. Then the leaders take all of the people back home to Judah.

The characters in this passage are:

* Oded, Yahweh's prophet
* Yahweh
* Soldiers from the northern kingdom of Israel
* All the people of the southern kingdom of Judah
* The prisoners from Judah
* And four leaders from the northern kingdom: Azariah, Jehohanan's son; Berekiah, Meshillemoth's son; Jehizkiah, Shallum's son; and Amasa, Hadlai's son

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

You will remember that in the last story, the army of Israel, the northern kingdom, killed many people in Judah during a battle. Then the army brought many prisoners back to the city of Samaria, in the northern kingdom.

Stop here as a group and again find the city of Samaria on the map of Judah and Israel, if needed. Pause this audio here.

Now, as the first scene begins, the storyteller explains that one of Yahweh's prophets, Oded, lives in Samaria. You will remember that a prophet is a person who gives messages from God to the people. Oded comes out of the city to meet the army as the army approaches Samaria. Then Oded speaks to the army. In the original language, Oded begins with a word that means "Look!" or "Pay attention!" Then Oded tells the army why Israel was able to defeat Judah in the battle. Oded says that Yahweh, the God of the people's ancestors, was angry with Judah. You will remember that although Yahweh has always been the Israelites' God, the people have worshiped other gods instead of Yahweh for a long time. So Oded probably calls Yahweh the God of the Israelites to remind the people that Yahweh is the God their ancestors worshiped.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: The storyteller refers to Yahweh as the God of the people's ancestors. How do you talk about who your ancestors worshiped, whether it was God or the local gods or spirits? Pause this audio here.

Oded says that it was because Yahweh was angry with Judah that Yahweh gave Judah into Israel's hand. This is special language that means that Yahweh gave the army of Israel power and control over Judah. But although Yahweh allowed this to happen, Israel's army killed the army of Judah in a very angry and cruel way, without mercy. Oded says this reached up to heaven, which is special language that means that God, who is in heaven, saw what the army did.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about soldiers who fight in a way that is very cruel or who show no mercy even when they win the battle? If needed, think about the story you told in step two and how you described the soldiers in your story. Pause this audio here.

Now, Oded says that the army plans to make these people of Judah and Jerusalem, both male and female, slaves to the people of the northern kingdom of Israel. You will remember that Judah is one of the tribes of Israel, but Judah is also the name of the southern kingdom. Jerusalem is the capital city of Judah. Jerusalem was also the capital city of all of Israel before the people divided into two different kingdoms. Jerusalem is where Solomon built Yahweh's temple. Oded asks the army a question that Oded does not expect anyone to answer. Oded asks the men, "But are you not also guilty of sins against Yahweh your God?" Oded asks this question to show the army that just like Yahweh punished Judah, Yahweh will also punish Israel if the army disobeys Yahweh and takes these people as slaves.

Oded tells the army to hear Oded, which means to pay attention to Oded. Oded says to send all of these prisoners back home. Oded reminds the army that these people are the men's relatives. You will remember from a previous story that most of the people who live in the southern kingdom are from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, but some people from other Israelite tribes also live in Judah. Either way, all of these people come from the same 12 tribes of Israel, and all of the people are related. Oded says the army must send all of the people back home because Yahweh's wrath or burning anger is on the army, which means that Yahweh feels very angry with the army and plans to punish the people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you talk about someone who feels very, very angry? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the storyteller says that some chiefs or leaders of Ephraim confront the soldiers. You will remember that Ephraim is one of the tribes that live in the northern kingdom, but here the storyteller uses Ephraim to mean the entire northern kingdom. The storyteller says these leaders are Azariah, Jehohanan's son; Berekiah, Meshillemoth's son; Jehizkiah, Shallum's son; and Amasa, Hadlai's son. These four leaders speak to the army and repeat the same warning that Oded just gave. The leaders say that the army must not bring the prisoners into the city, because if they do, it will make the people's sin and guilt before Yahweh even worse than it already is. The leaders say that the people are already very guilty and that Yahweh's wrath, or anger, is very great toward the people of the northern kingdom.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about people who deserve punishment because of the wrong things those people have done? Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, the soldiers release the prisoners and all the things the soldiers took during the battle. The soldiers do this in front of the leaders and all of the other people who have gathered together.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller says that the men whom people mentioned by name rise up and take the prisoners. We are not sure what the storyteller means by "the men whom people mentioned by name." The storyteller may use this phrase to refer to the four leaders, Azariah, Berekiah, Jehizkiah, and Amasa. Or the storyteller may mean that the leaders specifically choose other men to help the prisoners. Also, "rose up" does not mean that the men were first lying down. This is special language that means the men take action. First, the men give the prisoners clothes and sandals to wear from the spoils, or all the things the army took from Judah during the battle. The men also give the people food and drink because the people are probably very hungry and thirsty after the battle and the journey to Samaria. The men also anoint the people. This means the men put olive oil on people's wounds. Many people were probably injured in the battle, and at this time, people often used oil from olives, a type of fruit, to put on wounds as medicine.

Then the men carried the feeble people on donkeys. This means that people who were weak or injured and could not walk rode on donkeys, which are large animals with four legs. The men took all of the people, whom the storyteller reminds us are kinfolk or relatives of the men, to Jericho, which people call "the city of palm trees."

Stop here as a group and again find the city of Jericho on the map of Judah and Israel, if needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look again at pictures of sandals, a donkey, and palm trees, if needed. Pause this audio here.

Finally, the men returned home to Samaria in the northern kingdom of Israel.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* Oded, Yahweh's prophet
* Yahweh
* Soldiers from the northern kingdom of Israel
* All the people of the southern kingdom of Judah
* The prisoners from Judah
* And four leaders from the northern kingdom: Azariah, Jehohanan's son; Berekiah, Meshillemoth's son; Jehizkiah, Shallum's son; and Amasa, Hadlai's son

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Oded is one of Yahweh's prophets, and Oded lives in Samaria. Oded goes out to meet Israel's army as they return to Samaria. Oded says to the army, "Yahweh, the God of your ancestors, was angry with Judah. That is why Yahweh let you defeat Judah. But you killed the people with so much violence that even God in heaven is shocked. And now you want to make these people from Judah and Jerusalem your slaves. But you have sinned too, and you are guilty before Yahweh your God. Now listen to me! You have the same ancestors as these people you have captured. So free these people and let them go home. Otherwise, Yahweh will be very angry and will punish you."

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing Israel's army, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We must be a very good army, because we completely defeated Judah's army; or
* The gods that we worship must be very pleased with us, because we won a great victory today! or
* We will show these people from Judah how strong we are. We will take everything Judah's people have and make them our slaves.

Ask the people playing the prisoners from Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel very scared. These men killed many of our families in a brutal way, and we do not know what these men will do to us now; or
* Even though we often fight with our relatives, we did not expect these men to treat us this badly.

Ask the person playing Oded, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* These soldiers think they won this battle by their own strength, but it was Yahweh who let them win; or
* Yahweh was angry with Judah because they served other gods, but the northern kingdom is guilty of the same sins; or
* These people have served other gods for so long that I have to remind them that Yahweh is their God; or
* These soldiers think that they are successful today, but they do not realize that God is about to punish them.

> Continue the drama.

Now, four of the leaders of the northern kingdom of Israel speak to the army and tell the army that the army is doing wrong. These leaders are Azariah, son of Jehohanan; Berekiah, son of Meshillemoth; Jehizkiah, son of Shallum; and Amasa, son of Hadlai. These men tell the army, "Do not bring these prisoners here. If you do that, Yahweh will consider us guilty of sin. You are making our sins and faults even greater. We are already very guilty, and Yahweh is very angry with us."

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing the soldiers, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel surprised. We thought our leaders would be happy that we won the battle and that we brought back all of these good things and these people to be our slaves; or
* We feel shame. We were very strong and powerful in battle, but Oded and our leaders have made us look foolish; or
* We feel afraid. We thought the gods were happy with us, but now our ancestors' God, Yahweh, might punish us!

Ask the people playing the four leaders, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel afraid that Yahweh will punish our people; or
* All of this wealth and power that the army has taken will do us no good if Yahweh punishes us.

> Continue the drama.

So, in front of the leaders and all of the people, the soldiers let all of the prisoners go free, and the soldiers laid down all of the things they had taken during the battle.

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing soldiers, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We fought very hard to win, and we feel like we deserve to keep these things, but we do not want to receive punishment; or
* I think Oded was right. These people are our relatives, and we should not have been so harsh with these people.

Continue the drama.

The leaders choose some men to help the people from Judah. Out of all of the things the soldiers brought back from battle, the men take clothes and give them to the people from Judah who are naked. The men also give people sandals to put on their feet. The men give people food and drink, and the men put oil on people's wounds. The men put people who are weak on donkeys, and then the men bring all of these people, who are the men's relatives, back to Jericho, the city of the palms.

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing the people from Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We are surprised that the soldiers and the leaders listened to Oded; or
* We are so happy that we do not have to be slaves, and that we can go home.

Continue the drama.

> Then the men from Israel go back home to the city of Samaria.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Oded, a **prophet** of **Yahweh**, comes out to meet the army when the army comes back to **Samaria**. A prophet is a person who gives messages from God to the people. Yahweh is God's personal name. Use the same words or phrases for prophet, Samaria, and Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on prophet, Samaria, and Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Oded reminds the soldiers that Yahweh is the **God** of their **fathers**. In the Bible, "God" refers to God who created everything. This is the general word for God. Here, the word "fathers" means ancestors. Use the same words or phrases for God and fathers as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Oded says that the Israel army killed the Judah army in a rage that reached up to **heaven**. This is special language that means that God in heaven saw what the army did. Heaven refers to the place where God lives with his angels. Use the same word or phrase for heaven as you used in previous passages. For more information on heaven, refer to the Master Glossary.

Oded says the army now plans to make these people slaves, or to force these people to serve the Israelites. A slave is the property of a master. The master can sell the slave to someone else, just as he can sell his other property. A slave works without pay and is not free to leave their master. Some masters treated slaves cruelly. The storyteller just says that the Israelites want to make the people they captured from Judah serve them forcefully. You may need to say that the Israelites wanted to make the captives from Judah their slaves. If so, translate slave in the same way you have previously, and refer to **slave** in the Master Glossary for more information.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use to show that the soldiers wanted to force the people from Judah to serve the Israelites. Pause this audio here.

Oded reminds the army that these people are their **brothers**, which means relatives. Use the same word or phrase for brothers or relatives as you used in previous passages.

Some chiefs or leaders of **Ephraim** speak to the army. Ephraim is one of the tribes of Israel, but here Ephraim refers to the whole northern kingdom of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for Ephraim as you used in previous passages.

The leaders say that the people's **sins** and **guilt** are very great. Sin is rebellion against God. Guilt means that someone has done something wrong and deserves punishment. Use the same words or phrases for sins and guilt as you used in previous passages. For more information on sin and guilt, refer to the Master Glossary.

So the soldiers let go of the prisoners and the **plunder** in the presence of the **princes**, or high officials, and all of the **assembly**. Plunder means all of the valuable things that an army takes from the enemy in battle. "Princes" is another word for important leaders, and "assembly" means a large group of people who gather together for a special purpose. Use the same words or phrases for plunder, princes, and assembly as you used in previous passages.

The leaders give the people from Judah clothing, sandals, and food and drink from the plunder the army took during the battle. Sandals are a type of footwear with a leather sole that people tie to the bottom of their foot with leather thongs or straps.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **sandals**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The leaders anoint the people. To anoint someone means to pour sweet\-smelling oil over that person. Many times in the Bible, to anoint meant to pour oil over a person or object to show that the person or thing was holy, or dedicated to God. But here, to anoint means to put oil on people's wounds to help the wounds heal.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **anoint**. Look up anoint in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The men carry the feeble people on donkeys. To be feeble means to fall down from weakness or to be unable to walk. A donkey is a large animal with four legs that people in Israel often rode or used to carry heavy burdens.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for **feeble** and **donkeys**. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The leaders take the people back to Jericho, the "city of palm trees." These are date palm trees. Date palms are slow\-growing, evergreen trees with arching gray\-green fronds that can grow up to 10 feet long. This kind of palm tree grows a sweet fruit that people call dates.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "**city of palm trees**." If you have already translated this phrase in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Finally, the men return to Samaria in the northern kingdom of Israel.

Speaking the Word
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

## 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 (id: eng-2ch-p52-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the last story, we learned that Yahweh was angry with the kingdom of Judah because the people had done evil and worshiped other gods. As punishment, Yahweh began to allow Judah's enemies, including the northern kingdom of Israel, to defeat Judah in battle. Now, in this story, we will learn how Judah's king, Ahaz, continues to reject Yahweh and turn to foreign gods for help, and how this hurts Ahaz even more.

As the story begins, we learn that Judah's enemies have continued to attack and defeat Judah, so King Ahaz sends someone to take a message to the king of Assyria to ask for help. We know this is Tiglath Pileser III, who was king of Assyria from 744 B.C. to 727 B.C. Assyria was a country in northern Mesopotamia, the area that today is northern Iran.

Stop here as a group and look at a map that shows Assyria and Judah. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller specifically mentions how the Edomites had attacked Judah and carried away prisoners, and how the Philistines had raided or attacked some of Judah's cities in the lower hills to the west side of Judah and also to the south of Judah. You will remember that the Edomites lived in the land south of Judah, and the Philistines lived in the land west of Judah along the Mediterranean Sea. The storyteller says that the Philistines had taken control of the cities of Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo and also the smaller villages that surrounded those cities.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of Judah that also shows Edom and Philistia. Find each of these cities on the map. Pause this audio here.

Now we learn why these countries were able to defeat Judah. The storyteller says that Yahweh humbled the king of Judah, King Ahaz, because the king turned away from Yahweh and encouraged the people to do wicked things. And so, when King Ahaz sends word to the king of Assyria, Tiglath\-Pileser, to ask for help, Tiglath\-Pileser oppresses Ahaz instead of helping. Ahaz takes many expensive things from Yahweh's temple, from Ahaz's own house, and even from the leaders who work for King Ahaz, and gives these things to Tiglath\-Pileser as payment for his help, but this does not help Ahaz.

When all of these bad things happened, King Ahaz should have asked Yahweh for help, but instead, Ahaz asked the gods of Judah's enemies for help. Ahaz offered sacrifices to the gods that people worshiped in Damascus, the capital city of Aram, or Syria. Ahaz said that if those gods had helped Ahaz's enemies, then Ahaz would ask those gods to help Ahaz, too. But the storyteller says that those gods ruined Ahaz and Judah rather than helping.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell about a time someone tried to fix a bad choice they had made, but that person just made it worse. Pause this audio here.

Ahaz took all of the valuable things out of God's temple and destroyed those things. Ahaz also shut the doors of Yahweh's temple so that no one could go into the temple anymore. Instead, Ahaz had people build altars where people could worship foreign gods at the corner of every street in Jerusalem. And in every town in Judah, Ahaz had people build places to sacrifice to foreign gods there, too. All of these things made Yahweh, the God that Ahaz's ancestors worshiped, very angry.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Where do people worship God, or local spirits or gods, in your community? What are the right ways to worship those local spirits or gods? What happens if someone decides to worship another way? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller finishes his story by reminding us that people wrote other important stories about King Ahaz in the book, or scroll, about the kings of Judah and Israel. You will remember that this book is not in the Bible and no longer exists. The storyteller also says that when Ahaz died, people buried Ahaz in Jerusalem, but the people did not put Ahaz's body in the tomb of the kings of Israel. The storyteller probably says this to show that people did not honor Ahaz because Ahaz was wicked and disobeyed Yahweh. However, this is different than what we hear in 2 Kings 16, where that storyteller says that people buried Ahaz with his ancestors. We are not sure why these are different, but it may mean that the people buried Ahaz near his ancestors, but not in the royal tomb. Finally, after Ahaz died, Ahaz's son Hezekiah became the next king.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has six scenes.

**In the first scene:** The Edomites and Philistines have once again attacked and defeated Judah, so King Ahaz asks the king of Assyria to help protect Judah.

**In the second scene:** The storyteller reminds us that Yahweh allowed these enemies to defeat Judah because King Ahaz had turned away from Yahweh and caused the people to sin.

**In the third scene:** Instead of protecting Judah, Assyria causes trouble, even though Ahaz gives the king of Assyria expensive things from Yahweh's temple as payment.

**In the fourth scene:** King Ahaz sacrifices to the gods of his enemy, so that those gods will help Ahaz. But instead, those gods destroy Ahaz.

**In the fifth scene:** Ahaz destroys the objects in Yahweh's temple and shuts the doors to the temple so no one will worship there. Instead, Ahaz makes sacred places where people can worship foreign gods. All of these actions make Yahweh very angry.

**In the sixth scene:** The storyteller tells how King Ahaz dies and how Ahaz's son Hezekiah becomes the next king.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Ahaz of Judah
* Edomite army
* Prisoners from Judah
* Philistine army
* People who live in and near Judah's cities that the Philistines capture
* King Tiglath\-Pileser of Assyria and his army, although the storyteller does not mention the army
* Yahweh
* Foreign gods
* And Hezekiah, Ahaz's son

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, the storyteller begins by saying that at that time, King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help. Here, the phrase "at that time" does not refer to the same time as the last story, when Syria and the king of Israel attacked Judah. Instead, it refers to a later time when Edom and Philistia attacked. Also, although the storyteller only says Ahaz "sent word," we know that this means the king sent someone to take a message from Ahaz to the king of Assyria. The storyteller will say later in the story that this is King Tiglath\-Pileser.

Stop here as a group and again look at a map that shows Assyria and Judah, if needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about when one person sends another person to carry a message to a third person who is far away? How will you translate the way King Ahaz sends this message here? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that King Ahaz sent this message because the Edomites had again invaded Judah and taken people away as captives or prisoners. Also, the Philistines had attacked cities in the Shephelah and the Negev of Judah. The Shephelah refers to the land in Judah where the hills are not very high. The Shephelah is west of the hill country of Judah but east of the Mediterranean seacoast. The Shephelah is south of the Aijalon Valley in an area about 65 kilometers long and 20 kilometers wide. The Negev refers to the southern part of Judah, where the land is very dry, or like a desert.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of the Shephelah and the Negev wilderness. Pause this audio here.

The Philistines took control of Beth Shemesh. There are four different cities in the Old Testament called Beth Shemesh, but most people believe that this Beth Shemesh was located on the northwest border of Judah, about 24 kilometers west of Jerusalem. The Philistines also took Aijalon, which people believe was about 20 kilometers northwest of Jerusalem, and Gederoth, which people believe was \[about 18 kilometers southwest of Lod on the Ramle\-Al Mughar road. The Philistines took Soco with its villages.]{.mark} There are three different cities in the Old Testament called Soco, but this is likely the Soco located in the Shephelah, about 30 kilometers southwest of Jerusalem. The Philistines took Timnah with its villages. Timnah was located on the northern border of Judah, about 6\.5 kilometers north of Beth Shemesh. And finally, the Philistines took Gimzo, which was located in the lowland region near the Philistine plain, about 5 kilometers southeast of Lod off the Jerusalem road in the Aijalon Valley. The storyteller says that the Philistines settled in these cities and the villages around these cities, which means to live in those places permanently.

Stop here as a group and again look at a map of Judah that shows the likely location of each of these cities. Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the storyteller says that Yahweh humbled Judah because Ahaz, king of Israel, had encouraged the people to do wicked things, and because Ahaz himself had been unfaithful to Yahweh. You will remember that the nation of Israel was divided into two different kingdoms at this time. One of these kingdoms was the northern kingdom, which people called Israel. The other kingdom was the southern kingdom, which people called Judah. We know that Ahaz was the king of the southern kingdom of Judah, but the storyteller may call Ahaz the "king of Israel" to remind us that Ahaz is acting just as badly as the people of the northern kingdom, who worshiped other gods.

In the third scene, because Ahaz has done these wicked things, when Ahaz asks King Tiglath\-Pileser of Assyria for help, Tiglath\-Pileser instead comes against Ahaz, which means he attacks Ahaz instead of helping. In the original language, we are not sure if the storyteller says that Tiglath\-Pileser did not make Ahaz strong by helping Ahaz, or if the storyteller says that Tiglath\-Pileser could not overpower Ahaz or defeat him. Either way, we understand that Tiglath\-Pileser made things worse for Ahaz and not better.

The storyteller says that Ahaz took or stole things from Yahweh's house, the temple. Ahaz also took things from his own palace, the house where Ahaz lived as the king. And Ahaz also took things from the "princes" or leaders of Judah who worked for the king. Ahaz then gave all of these expensive things to Tiglath\-Pileser as a way to pay for Assyria's help, but the storyteller says this did not help Ahaz. In other words, Tiglath\-Pileser did not help, even though Ahaz paid Tiglath\-Pileser to help.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller says that when Ahaz is distressed, or when all these bad things happen, Ahaz acts even more unfaithfully to Yahweh. Ahaz makes sacrifices to the gods of Damascus that defeated Ahaz. Remember that Damascus is the capital city of Syria, so these are the gods that the Syrians worship. And Ahaz said, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped those kings, I will sacrifice to those gods so that those gods may help me too." Here, the storyteller may mean that Ahaz said this out loud to himself, or it may mean that Ahaz simply thought this thing. Either way, the storyteller tells us this so we will know why Ahaz made sacrifices to these other gods. However, the storyteller says these gods ruined Ahaz and all of Israel, which means that the gods only made things worse, not better. When the storyteller says Israel here, we do not know if he refers to Judah, the kingdom where Ahaz rules, or to the northern kingdom, where people also worshiped foreign gods.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about a person who does something that people would not expect. Then tell people what that person thought that caused the person to act that way. Pay attention to the way you explain this. Pause this audio here.

In the fifth scene, the storyteller says that Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut the vessels into pieces. You will remember that the house of God means Yahweh's temple in Jerusalem. The "vessels" refer to the various holy items in the temple that the priests used to worship Yahweh. Apparently, Ahaz destroys these things to prevent people from worshiping Yahweh. Then Ahaz closes the doors to the temple. This probably means that Ahaz locks the doors so that no one can enter the temple to worship Yahweh anymore. Instead, Ahaz makes altars in every corner in Jerusalem. This probably means that Ahaz commands people to build these altars, or places for people to worship these gods, in many places around the city of Jerusalem. Also, in every city of Judah, Ahaz makes high places to burn incense to other gods. High places probably refers to places on hills where people would make special shrines to foreign gods. The storyteller says that all of these things provoked Yahweh, the God of Ahaz's ancestors, to anger. This means that Yahweh felt very angry that Ahaz did all of this.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about a time when someone in your community did something that people thought angered God or the local gods or spirits. What did that person do? How did people talk about those things the person did? How did people feel about those actions? Pause this audio here.

In the last scene, the storyteller uses the same kind of formal talk he used to describe other kings. First, the storyteller says that everything that happened when Ahaz was king, and everything Ahaz did, is in the scroll or book of the kings of Judah and Israel. You will remember that a scroll is a type of ancient book where people wrote everything on one very long piece of paper and then rolled that paper around a stick. The storyteller says that Ahaz "slept with his fathers." This is a nice way to say that Ahaz died, just as Ahaz's ancestors before Ahaz did. People buried Ahaz in the city of Jerusalem, but people did not place Ahaz's body in the tombs of the kings of Israel. And finally, Hezekiah, Ahaz's son, succeeded Ahaz as king. This means that Hezekiah became the next king after Ahaz.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has six scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Ahaz of Judah
* Edomite army
* Prisoners from Judah
* Philistine army
* People who live in and near Judah's cities that the Philistines capture
* King Tiglath\-Pileser of Assyria and his army, although the storyteller does not mention the army
* Yahweh
* Foreign gods
* And Hezekiah, Ahaz's son

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Then King Ahaz sent people to King Tiglath\-Pileser, the king of Assyria, to ask for help. Ahaz did this because the Edomites had again come and attacked Judah and taken people away as prisoners. And at the same time, the Philistines had raided the cities and towns in Judah's low hills and also the Negev. The Philistines captured and settled in Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, as well as Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo, along with the villages around those cities.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Ahaz, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I keep losing battles to my enemies. I need to do something to stop this! or
* Now we have even fewer people and cities to protect ourselves; or
* I am not sure if I can trust the Assyrians, but I know they have a strong army. Maybe I can pay the Assyrians to help us.

Continue the drama.

Because of the evil things King Ahaz did, Yahweh made the kingdom of Judah low. Ahaz had led his people to do evil things, and Ahaz himself disobeyed Yahweh.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am the one who protects my people, but now my people worship other gods instead of me. These other gods cannot help the people! or
* I will stop protecting my people so that the people will see that these gods can do nothing for them; or
* Ahaz has rejected me, so now I will reject Ahaz.

Continue the drama.

King Tiglath\-Pileser of Assyria comes to Ahaz. But instead of helping, Tiglath\-Pileser gives Ahaz even more trouble. Ahaz takes some of the things from Yahweh's temple, from Ahaz's palace, and from the officials of Judah, and Ahaz gives these expensive things to Tiglath\-Pileser as payment. But this does not help Ahaz.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Ahaz, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I do not want to give these expensive things away, but if it can help save my kingdom, it is worth it!

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I allowed these things to happen so Ahaz would remember to obey and worship me. But instead, Ahaz steals things from my temple to pay a human king to help.

Ask the person playing King Tiglath\-Pileser, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* My army is bigger and stronger than Judah's. I cannot completely defeat Judah in battle, but I will gladly take these expensive things from them.

Continue the drama.

King Ahaz disobeyed Yahweh even more when all of these bad things happened. Ahaz made sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, who had defeated Ahaz in battle, because Ahaz thought, "The gods of the kings of Aram have helped those kings, so I will also sacrifice to those gods. Then those gods will help me too." But worshiping those gods ruined Ahaz and all the people of Judah.

Pause the drama. Ask the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* Our enemies stole some of our people and cities. We must do something to protect ourselves! or
* If Yahweh allowed these bad things to happen, maybe other gods can help instead; or
* We will do whatever our king tells us to do.

> Continue the drama.

King Ahaz gathered up and destroyed all of the sacred things from Yahweh's temple. Ahaz shut and locked the doors of the temple so that no one could go in to worship Yahweh anymore. Then Ahaz set up altars at the corner of every street in Jerusalem, and Ahaz built sacred places to burn sacrifices to foreign gods in every town in Judah. This made Yahweh, the God that Ahaz's ancestors worshiped, very angry.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* Ahaz continues to disobey me and treat me with great disrespect; or
* Ahaz not only disobeys me and worships other gods, but Ahaz makes other people disobey me too; or
* I will punish Ahaz and the people of Judah for doing these things.

> Continue the drama.

King Ahaz did many things while he was king, and people wrote about all of these things in the book "The History of the Kings of Judah and Israel." Then Ahaz died, and people buried Ahaz with his ancestors. People buried Ahaz in Jerusalem, but the people did not bury Ahaz in the tombs of the kings of Israel. After Ahaz died, Ahaz's son Hezekiah became the next king of Judah.

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* The good kings of Judah in the past always worshiped Yahweh, but Ahaz changed all of that; or
* It seems like all of the changes Ahaz made in Judah made things worse for us, not better; or
* We need to show respect, but Ahaz was not a very good king. So we will bury Ahaz in Jerusalem, but not in the tombs where people buried the most important kings.

Ask the person playing Hezekiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* My father stopped people from worshiping Yahweh, our ancestors' God; or
* My father thought these other gods would make us stronger, but worshiping those gods made everything worse; or
* I do not want to be like my father. My father did not leave a good legacy as king.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 28:16–27 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

As the story begins, **King** Ahaz sends a message to the king of Assyria to ask for help. Use the same word or phrase for king as you used in previous passages. King is in the Master Glossary.

Assyria was a country in northern Mesopotamia, the area that today is northern Iran.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **Assyria**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The **Edomites** had once again defeated Judah and carried away captives or prisoners. You will remember that the Edomites were the ancestors of Esau, Jacob's brother. Jacob, who God later named Israel, was the ancestor of the Israelites. Use the same word or phrase for Edomites as you used in previous passages.

The Philistines had also made raids and taken several **cities** in the **foothills** and the Negev wilderness. Translate cities the same as you have in previous passages. The foothills refer to the land in Judah where the hills are not very high. These foothills are west of the hill country of Judah but east of the Mediterranean seacoast. Use the same word or phrase for foothills as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of the foothills, if needed. Pause this audio here.

The Negev refers to the Negev wilderness, the southern part of Judah, where the land is very dry, or like a desert.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of the Negev wilderness, if needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the **Negev wilderness**. If you use the word for wilderness, refer to wilderness in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh **humbled** Judah. **Yahweh** is God's personal name, and to humble people means to make those people submit, to bring them low, or to make them lose face. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh and humbled as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh humbled Judah because King Ahaz had promoted wickedness or caused Judah to act sinfully. Wickedness means evil, or the opposite of good, and to sin means to rebel against God. But here, King Ahaz does not just do wicked or sinful things himself. Instead, Ahaz does wrong as the leader of Judah and causes other people to do sinful or wicked things.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **promoted wickedness** or **caused Judah to act sinfully**. Look up **wickedness** and **sin** in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

King Tiglath\-Pileser of Assyria **afflicted** Ahaz, even though Ahaz paid him with many things. To afflict means to oppress or restrict either physically or emotionally. This does not necessarily mean that the Assyrians made war with Judah, but it does mean that Tiglath\-Pileser made things even harder for Ahaz. Use the same word or phrase for afflicted as you used in previous passages.

King Ahaz **sacrificed** to the **gods** of Damascus. When the Israelites would make a sacrifice to Yahweh, it either meant to kill an animal and then burn the animal on an altar, or to give a gift to Yahweh of food items, oil, or sweet\-smelling spices. But here, King Ahaz instead makes sacrifices to the foreign gods of Judah's enemies. Use the same words or phrases for sacrifice and gods as you used in previous passages. For more information on gods and on the kinds of sacrifices that people made to Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz destroyed the **vessels** in Yahweh's **temple**. Vessels refer to the items the priests would use in the temple for worship. Use the same words or phrases for vessels and temple as you used in previous passages. For more information, look up temple in the Master Glossary.

Ahaz made **altars** all around Jerusalem. An altar is a place where people make offerings or sacrifices to God, but Ahaz made these altars to make offerings to foreign gods. Use the same word or phrase for altars as you used in previous passages. For more information on the kind of altar that people made to worship Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Ahaz also made **high places**. People from these other countries would often make the shrines or places where they worshiped their gods on naturally high places, like hills, so Ahaz did the same thing in Judah. Use the same word or phrase for high places as you used in previous passages.

People wrote about everything King Ahaz did in a **book** or **scroll** about the kings of Judah and Israel. You will remember that in that time, a book or "scroll" was usually a long piece of leather or paper that people wrote on and then rolled up around a stick. This way, people could easily carry or store the scroll until they wanted to read it. Use the same word or phrase for book or scroll as you used in previous passages, and refer to the Master Glossary for more information about scroll.

Ahaz **slept with his fathers**. Slept is a nice way to say that Ahaz died, and "fathers" means Ahaz's ancestors. Use the same word or phrase for "slept with his fathers" as you used in previous passages.

The storyteller says that people did not bury Ahaz in the **tombs** of the kings. A tomb is a place where people bury a dead body. These were often caves or rooms that people would hollow out of rock to hide the body from view. Use the same word or phrase for tomb as you used in previous passages. For more information about tomb, refer to the Master Glossary.

Finally, after Ahaz died, Ahaz's son Hezekiah **reigned** in Ahaz's place. To reign means to rule or act with power as king. Use the same word or phrase for reign as you used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
