## 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 (id: eng-2ch-p63-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, Manasseh became the king of Judah and sinned against Yahweh in many ways. Manasseh led the people to worship false gods and to practice divination, sorcery, and witchcraft. In this story, Yahweh allows the Assyrian army commanders to take Manasseh prisoner, and Manasseh repents of his sin. Then Yahweh brings Manasseh back to Judah, and Manasseh removes all the foreign gods and idols from the country.

King Manasseh did more evil than almost any other king of Judah. Yahweh speaks to Manasseh and the people of Judah and tells them to stop doing evil things. But Manasseh and the people do not do what Yahweh tells them to do. Because Manasseh does not listen to Yahweh, Yahweh allows the Assyrian army to attack Judah and capture Manasseh. The Assyrians take Manasseh as a prisoner from Jerusalem to the city of Babylon. At this time, the city of Babylon was part of Assyria. Babylon is about 1,450 kilometers from Jerusalem.

Stop here and look at a map that shows the locations of Jerusalem and Babylon. Pause this audio here.

When the Assyrians take Manasseh prisoner, the Assyrians put a ring in Manasseh's nose and bind him with bronze chains. The Assyrians do this to make sure that Manasseh will not escape. When the Assyrians put a ring in a person's nose, the Assyrians also attached the ring to a chain or a rope. Then an Assyrian soldier would hold onto the chain or the rope so that the prisoner could not escape. The Assyrian soldier could also pull on the rope to hurt the prisoner.

Stop here and look at a picture of an Assyrian carving that shows an Assyrian soldier holding a rope attached to a prisoner's nose ring. Pause this audio here.

The Assyrians also use bronze chains to make sure Manasseh cannot escape. People put chains around another person's legs or wrists, or sometimes both, to stop that person from running away.

The Assyrians do these things to Manasseh to make sure Manasseh cannot escape, but also to shame Manasseh. When Manasseh is a prisoner, Manasseh very likely feels ashamed, afraid, sad, and hopeless. Manasseh is probably worried about what will happen to Manasseh and to Manasseh's country. So Manasseh humbles himself, prays to Yahweh, and asks Yahweh to help Manasseh. Yahweh knows that Manasseh is truly sorry, so Yahweh causes the Assyrians to set Manasseh free. Manasseh goes back to Judah and again leads Judah as king. But the most important detail is that now, Manasseh knows that Yahweh is the one true God.

Stop here and tell a story about someone who first lived their life one way, then changed and was completely different. What caused the person to change his life? How did that person change? How did the change affect the people around that person? Pause this audio here.

After Manasseh goes back to Judah, Manasseh repairs the walls of Jerusalem. Manasseh repairs the wall and makes it higher, from the Fish Gate on the north side of Jerusalem to the Gihon spring on the southeastern side of Jerusalem, and also around a hill called Ophel.

Stop here and look at a drawing of Jerusalem that shows the location of the Fish Gate, the Gihon spring, and the hill called Ophel. Pause this audio here.

Manasseh also stations military officers in all the fortified cities of Judah. But the most important part of this story is that Manasseh proves that he really believes in Yahweh through Manasseh's actions. Manasseh removes all the foreign gods, idols, and altars in Jerusalem. Manasseh was the one who had built all of these things, but now Manasseh does the right thing and tears them down. Manasseh also tells the people to only worship Yahweh.

Stop here and tell a story about a leader who tried to make big changes in his community. Why did that person try to make the changes? How did the people respond? Was the leader successful in making the changes? Pause this audio here.

Manasseh also repairs the temple of Yahweh and makes peace or fellowship offerings and thank offerings to Yahweh. When the Israelites sacrificed a peace or fellowship offering, the Israelites sacrificed a male animal with no defects in the temple. The purpose of the peace offering was to establish or maintain good relations with Yahweh. In this case, because Manasseh had defiled Yahweh's temple before, Manasseh might feel that he needs to make some sacrifices in order to show that Manasseh was sorry.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your culture, if two individuals or groups have a serious conflict and then make peace, what actions do those people take to show that they are now at peace with each other? Can you tell a story about two groups who were once in conflict but then made peace and showed that peace through some kind of action or ritual? Pause this audio here.

Manasseh also sacrifices thank offerings to Yahweh. A thank offering was similar to a peace offering except that people also gave different kinds of bread in addition to an animal. People gave thank offerings to thank Yahweh for something Yahweh did. In this case, Manasseh probably wants to thank Yahweh for saving Manasseh from the Assyrians and bringing Manasseh back to Jerusalem. Manasseh tries to lead the people to worship only Yahweh in the right way. However, Manasseh does not remove all of the high places. Although the people still make sacrifices in these places, the storyteller says that the people only make sacrifices to Yahweh. The people still disobey Yahweh when the people do this.

Stop here and tell a story about someone who received instructions to do something but only did part of it. Why did that person only do part of it? What was the result? How did the person who gave the instructions feel? Pause this audio here.

People wrote about all of the things that Manasseh did in two books, or scrolls. One of those books is the "History of the Kings of Israel." In this case, when the storyteller says "Israel," the storyteller means both the kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah together. The storyteller also mentions another book called the "Records of the Hozai." Some Bible scholars think that the Hozai were a group of prophets, or seers. So sometimes people called this book "The Records of the Seers." No one knows where either of these books is now. Although Manasseh repented and believed in Yahweh later in his life, most of the things that Manasseh did as king of Judah were evil.

Manasseh died, and the people buried Manasseh in Manasseh's own house. This probably means that the people buried Manasseh in a tomb located somewhere in the palace, where the king and his family lived. Then Manasseh's son Amon became the next king of Judah.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

**In the first scene:** Yahweh warned Manasseh and the people of Judah, but they did not listen to Yahweh's warnings. So Yahweh lets the Assyrian army attack Judah and take King Manasseh as a prisoner. Manasseh humbles himself and prays to Yahweh, so Yahweh causes the Assyrians to set Manasseh free. Manasseh goes back to Jerusalem.

**In the second scene:** After Manasseh returns to Jerusalem, Manasseh is faithful to Yahweh. Manasseh removes all the foreign gods from Judah and stops most of the sinful practices that Manasseh had started.

**In the third scene:** Manasseh dies, and Manasseh's people bury him. Manasseh's son Amon becomes the next king of Judah.

The characters in this passage are:

* Yahweh
* Manasseh
* The people of Judah
* The commanders of the Assyrian army
* The military commanders of Judah
* The seers who spoke to Manasseh
* And Amon, Manasseh's son

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, the storyteller begins the story by saying that Yahweh spoke to Manasseh and his people. It is unclear whether "his people" means "Yahweh's people" or "Manasseh's people." Although both possibilities are true, Bible scholars think the storyteller means "Yahweh's people." Manasseh and the people did not listen to what Yahweh said to them. The storyteller does not mention how Yahweh spoke to Manasseh and the people, but later the storyteller does say that the seers, or prophets, spoke to Manasseh in the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel. But Manasseh and the people did not pay attention to what Yahweh said to them. Remember that in the original language, the word for "listen" not only means to hear the words that someone says, but to also act on those words or obey the person who is speaking.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your language, how do you describe a situation where one person hears the words that another person says but does not act on what that person said or obey that person's commands? Which of these could you use here? Pause this audio here.

Because Manasseh and the people did not listen to Yahweh, Yahweh sends the Assyrian army commanders to Jerusalem, and they capture Manasseh. The Assyrian army commanders probably brought the Assyrian army with them when they captured Manasseh. The storyteller sometimes talks about things people did and says that Yahweh did those things. This shows that Yahweh controls all events on earth. The king of Assyria probably decided to send his army commanders to Jerusalem to capture Manasseh and bring Manasseh to Babylon, but it was Yahweh who caused the king of Assyria to make that decision.

Stop here and discuss these questions: How confusing do you think it will be for your hearers to hear the storyteller say, "Yahweh sent the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria against Manasseh and the people of Judah"? If it is too confusing for people, how can you say it so that people will understand that a person made the decision, but Yahweh caused that person to make that decision? Pause this audio here.

The Assyrian army commanders force Manasseh to go to Babylon. The storyteller says that the Assyrians capture Manasseh with hooks. The storyteller probably means that the Assyrians put a hook in Manasseh's nose as they did to many of their prisoners. The Assyrians also put bronze chains on Manasseh. The Assyrians most likely did these things so that Manasseh could not run away.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your culture, how do you stop prisoners from running away? After you discuss this, look again at the picture of an Assyrian prisoner with a hook in his nose, and the picture of bronze chains. Decide how you will say that the Assyrians captured Manasseh with hooks and bound Manasseh with bronze chains. Pause this audio here.

The Assyrian commanders take Manasseh to the city of Babylon. At this time, the Assyrians controlled the city of Babylon and all the territory around Babylon.

When Manasseh is a prisoner, Manasseh probably feels sad, afraid, embarrassed, and angry. When Manasseh is in this terrible situation, Manasseh finally asks Yahweh for help. Manasseh pleads with Yahweh and humbles himself. This means that Manasseh is no longer proud and no longer rebels against Yahweh. Manasseh admits to Yahweh that the things Manasseh did were wrong.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words or phrases do you use for a situation where one person who is in trouble asks a more powerful person for help? Which of those could you use here? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller calls Yahweh "the God of his fathers." This phrase means "the God that Manasseh's ancestors followed."

When Manasseh prays, Yahweh hears Manasseh's words. Yahweh is moved by Manasseh's request. This means that Yahweh feels sorry for Manasseh and wants to help Manasseh.

Stop here and discuss these questions: what words or phrases do you have to describe a situation where one person feels sorry for another person and wants to help that person? Which of these could you use here? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh causes the Assyrians to release Manasseh so that Manasseh can go back to Jerusalem.

At the end of this scene, the storyteller says, "And Manasseh knew that Yahweh is God." This is the most important statement in this scene. This statement means that Manasseh finally realizes that Yahweh is the only God and that all other gods are false gods.

Stop here and discuss these questions: \[Manasseh not only knew that Yahweh is God. Manasseh also realized that all the other gods and idols Manasseh had previously worshiped were not really gods like Yahweh is God. Discuss how you can show this in the way you translate this part.]{.mark} Pause this audio here.

In scene two, the storyteller tells us what Manasseh did after Manasseh came back to Jerusalem from Babylon. First, Manasseh repaired the outer wall of the City of David. The storyteller does not tell us why Manasseh needed to repair the wall. It is possible that the Assyrian army damaged or destroyed part of the wall when they attacked and took Manasseh prisoner. It is also possible that Manasseh completed the wall that Hezekiah started building. Or, it is possible that Manasseh built a new wall.

The Fish Gate was a gate in the city wall on the north side of Jerusalem. The Ophel hill and the Gihon spring are on the southeastern side of Jerusalem. The Gihon spring is in a deep valley on the eastern side of Jerusalem. This valley is called the Kidron Valley. Many Bible scholars think that the part of Jerusalem that people called "The City of David" was between these two locations. So Manasseh needed to repair a large section of the city wall from the Fish Gate on the north side of the city to Gihon on the southeastern side of the city.

Stop here and look at a drawing of Jerusalem that shows the location of the Fish Gate, the Gihon spring, and the hill called Ophel. Pause this audio here.

Manasseh also stationed military commanders in all of Judah's fortified cities. A fortified city is a city with a wall and other structures for defense. The king usually kept soldiers in fortified cities to help fight off any attack. It seems like Manasseh put more commanders in these cities to make the country stronger.

Manasseh got rid of all the foreign gods that Manasseh had brought into Jerusalem. "Foreign gods" were the gods that people in other nations worshipped. The people made objects, or idols, to represent those gods. "Foreign gods" were any objects of worship other than Yahweh.

Manasseh removed the idol that he had placed in Yahweh's temple. An idol is a statue or object that represents a false god. Manasseh removed all of the altars that Manasseh had built on the hill where Yahweh's temple stood. Manasseh also removed altars from other places around Jerusalem. The people of Judah worshipped false gods at these altars, so Manasseh needed to remove and destroy them as well.

Next, Manasseh restored the altar inside Yahweh's temple. Yahweh said that this altar was the only place where the Israelites could make sacrifices to Yahweh. Then Manasseh sacrificed peace or fellowship offerings and thank offerings on the altar. To make these sacrifices, Manasseh would have brought live animals to the temple, usually a young bull or male sheep, as well as bread for the thank offerings. Manasseh killed the animal and cut it into pieces. Then, the priests burned part of the animal on the altar, while they cooked another part and ate the meat. The priests also burned the bread for the fellowship offering.

After Manasseh did all this, Manasseh commanded the people of Judah to serve Yahweh, the God of Israel. This means that the people of Judah should not worship any other gods, but only Yahweh. It seems that the people obeyed Manasseh's commands and stopped making sacrifices to idols. But the people did do one thing wrong. The people continued to make sacrifices to Yahweh at places of worship other than Yahweh's temple. The people sometimes called these places of worship "high places" because people often built these places on top of hills.

Stop here and discuss this question: How can you make it clear to your hearers that the people were not supposed to make sacrifices at the high places? Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, the storyteller says that people wrote down more stories about what Manasseh did. People wrote about Manasseh's prayer, which is probably the prayer that Manasseh prayed while he was a prisoner in Babylon. People also wrote down the messages that the prophets or seers gave to Manasseh. The prophets spoke in the name of Yahweh, which means that these prophets spoke on Yahweh's behalf. These stories are in the "Book or Scroll of the History of the Kings of Israel." Remember that the storyteller often calls the southern kingdom of Judah "Israel." This is a different book from the book of Kings in our Bibles.

Other stories about Manasseh are in a different book called the "Records of Hozai" or the "Records of the Seers." Bible scholars do not agree on what this book was. Nobody knows what happened to the "Records of Hozai." In this book, someone recorded stories about how Manasseh sinned, worshipped idols, and built high places. Manasseh made carved images of the goddess Asherah, which are sometimes called Asherah poles. Manasseh also made carved images of other false gods. "Carved image" is another way to say "idol." People usually carved idols out of wood or stone.

The storyteller does not tell us how much longer King Manasseh lived after Manasseh came back from Babylon. When Manasseh died, Manasseh's people buried him in his own house. This probably means there was a tomb located somewhere on the palace property. Then Manasseh's son Amon became the next king of Judah. The name Amon means "skilled."

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* Yahweh
* Manasseh
* The people of Judah
* The commanders of the Assyrian army
* The military officers of Judah
* The seers who spoke to Manasseh
* And Amon, Manasseh's son

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh warned Manasseh and his people, but they refused to pay attention. So Yahweh sent the commanders of the Assyrian army to invade Judah. The Assyrian commanders captured Manasseh, stuck hooks in Manasseh, put Manasseh in chains, and took Manasseh to Babylon. But while Manasseh was in great distress, Manasseh pleaded with Yahweh his God and sincerely humbled himself before the God of Manasseh's ancestors. And when Manasseh prayed, Yahweh listened to his plea and felt compassion for Manasseh. So Yahweh brought Manasseh back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh finally realized that Yahweh is the only one true Creator God!

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Manasseh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* My kingdom is strong and the Assyrians are far away. No one can harm me; or
* I feel so embarrassed! I was the king of Judah but now I am nothing but a prisoner. What will happen to me and my people? or
* I was wrong to be so proud and rebellious! I was wrong to worship idols! Have mercy on me, Yahweh! or
* I am so grateful that Yahweh was merciful to me in spite of all the evil things I have done. Yahweh truly is the only God!

Ask the people playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We should not listen to those arrogant prophets who claim to speak for Yahweh. It is better to worship as many gods as we can; or
* The Assyrians are invading! Maybe if we pray to the Assyrians' gods, those gods will stop the Assyrians from attacking us; or
* We feel terrified. The Assyrians captured King Manasseh and took him away. How will our people survive now? or
* We are amazed! King Manasseh has come back, and Manasseh says that Yahweh saved him. If Yahweh can forgive Manasseh, then Yahweh is truly a great and loving God.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I have spoken to Manasseh many times, and Manasseh will not listen to me. It is finally time to do something so that Manasseh will humble himself; or
* I warned my people over and over again, but the people keep on following their king and worshipping idols. The people will have to see the result of their rebellion or else the people will never repent; or
* I am so happy that Manasseh repented! Now I will bless Manasseh and bring him back to Jerusalem!

> Continue the drama.
> 
> After this, Manasseh rebuilt the outer wall of the City of David. Manasseh started west of the Gihon spring in the Kidron Valley to the Fish Gate. Manasseh also made the wall go around the hill of Ophel. Manasseh built the wall even higher than it had been before. And Manasseh stationed his military officers in all the fortified towns of Judah. Manasseh also removed the foreign gods and the idol from Yahweh's temple. Manasseh tore down all of the altars he had built on the hill where the temple stood. Manasseh tore down all the altars that were in Jerusalem and dumped them outside the city. Then Manasseh restored the altar of Yahweh. Manasseh sacrificed peace offerings and thanksgiving offerings on the altar. Manasseh also encouraged the people of Judah to worship Yahweh, the God of Israel. However, the people continued to worship at the pagan altars, but they only worshipped Yahweh their God.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Manasseh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I thought Jerusalem was strong before, but now I see that I was wrong. I need to make the city stronger and ready for an attack; or
* I feel terrible that I encouraged the people to worship false gods. I need to destroy all the foreign gods and lead the people back to Yahweh; or
* I want to show Yahweh that I am sorry for all the terrible things I did and am grateful for Yahweh's love and mercy. I will make many sacrifices to Yahweh; or
* I am the king and it is my responsibility to make sure the people are faithful to Yahweh. I will tell the people that Yahweh alone is God and that the people should not worship any other gods!

Ask the people playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We feel relieved that the king is rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. It will make the city safer; or
* We feel glad that Manasseh has restored the temple of Yahweh. We hope that Yahweh will bless us even more now; or
* King Manasseh said we should only make sacrifices at the temple, but the journey is too long. Let's just make sacrifices at the high place nearby; or
* I do not understand why we cannot worship Yahweh at the local shrine. Is that not just as good as the temple in Jerusalem?

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am very happy that Manasseh has genuinely repented. I love Manasseh so much, and Manasseh has returned to me; or
* I am glad that Manasseh destroyed all the idols and pagan altars, but the people are still worshipping at the high places. I feel sad that the people will not obey me completely; or
* If these people would be completely faithful to me, I would bless the people more than they could imagine!

> Continue the drama.
> 
> Everything else Manasseh did while he was king, including Manasseh's prayer to Yahweh his God and the words that the prophets spoke to Manasseh in the name of Yahweh the God of Israel, is in "The History of the Kings of Israel." Manasseh's prayer and plea to Yahweh, all of Manasseh's sin and unfaithfulness, and all the locations where Manasseh built high places and set up Asherah poles and other carved images before Manasseh humbled himself are in the "Records of the Seers." Manasseh died, and the people buried Manasseh in his own house. Then Amon, Manasseh's son, became the next king.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Manasseh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I regret all the terrible things I did in my life. I hope that the changes I made at the end will be enough to protect our people; or
* I feel so grateful for Yahweh's mercy. I did not deserve it, but Yahweh forgave me; or
* I hope that my son and my people will continue to worship Yahweh after I am gone.

Ask the people playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* Manasseh was once very evil, but at the end, Manasseh turned back to Yahweh. At least Manasseh finished his life well; or
* We feel amazed at how Yahweh forgives even the worst people. If Yahweh can forgive someone like Manasseh, then Yahweh can forgive anyone! or
* We wonder what Manasseh's son Amon will be like. Will Amon worship idols like Manasseh did when he was young, or will Amon be faithful to Yahweh?

Ask the person playing Amon, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am sad that my father is dead; or
* I am happy that I am now the king. I get to do things my way! or
* I will do whatever I have to do to keep the country safe and strong.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel happy that Manasseh turned back to me and that Manasseh ended his life well; or
* Although Manasseh was very sinful for most of his life, at the end, Manasseh returned to me and became a good leader for the people; or
* The next king is coming to the throne. Leaders come and go, but my purposes and my covenant with the people of Judah will never change.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:10–20 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

**Yahweh** spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen. So Yahweh brought against them the army **commanders** of the **king** of **Assyria**. The Assyrians took Manasseh prisoner, put hooks in him, bound him with **bronze** chains, and took him to **Babylon**. Be sure to use the same words for Yahweh, commander, king, Assyria, bronze, and Babylon that you used in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on Yahweh, king, and bronze.

Stop here and look again at the picture of bronze chains if needed. Pause this audio here.

When Manasseh was in great distress, Manasseh sought the favor of Yahweh\*\*,\*\* his **God,** and Manasseh humbled himself greatly before the God of his ancestors. When Manasseh **prayed** to Yahweh, Yahweh listened to Manasseh's plea and was moved by Manasseh's request. So Yahweh brought Manasseh back to **Jerusalem** and to his **kingdom**. Then Manasseh knew that Yahweh alone is God! Be sure to use the same words for God, pray, Jerusalem, and kingdom that you used in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on God, pray, Jerusalem, and kingdom.

Afterward, Manasseh rebuilt the outer wall of the City of David, west of the Gihon **spring** in the valley, as far as the entrance of the Fish Gate and going around the hill of Ophel. Manasseh also made the wall much higher. Manasseh stationed military commanders in all of Judah's **fortified cities**. Be sure to use the same words that you used in previous stories for spring and fortified city.

Manasseh threw away all the foreign **gods** and removed the **idol** from the **temple** of Yahweh. Manasseh also removed all the **altars** that Manasseh had built on the temple hill and in Jerusalem, and Manasseh threw them out of the city. Be sure to use the same words for gods, idol, temple, and altar that you used in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on gods, idols, temples, and altar.

Then Manasseh restored the altar of Yahweh and **sacrificed peace or fellowship offerings** and **thank offerings** on it. Manasseh told the people of **Judah** to serve Yahweh, the God of **Israel**. However, the people continued to sacrifice at the **high places**, but the people only made sacrifices to Yahweh their God. Be sure to use the same words you used for sacrifice, peace offerings, thank offering, Judah, Israel, and high places that you used in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on sacrifice, peace or fellowship offering, Judah, and Israel.

The "History of the Kings of Israel" records the rest of Manasseh's deeds as king. It includes Manasseh's prayer to God and the words the **seers** spoke to Manasseh in the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel. The "Records of the Hozai" also describe Manasseh's prayer, how God listened to his plea, and all his **sins** and actions that were unfaithful to Yahweh, or betrayed Yahweh. The records also list the places where Manasseh built high places, Asherah poles, and carved images before Manasseh humbled himself. Manasseh died, and his son Amon became king after Manasseh. Be sure to use the same words you used for seer and sins that you used in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on seer and sin. The entry for seer is under the entry for **prophet** in the Master Glossary.

## 2 Chronicles 33:21–25 (id: eng-2ch-p64-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 33:21–25 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:21–25 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:21–25 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, King Manasseh humbled himself before Yahweh and repented of worshipping false gods. Manasseh removed all the foreign gods and foreign altars from Israel. Then Manasseh died, and Manasseh's son Amon became the next king of Judah. In this story, Amon rules as king for only two years, and then Amon's officials kill Amon. And the people of Judah make Amon's son Josiah the next king.

Amon was 22 years old when he became the king of Judah, and Amon reigned for two years. Amon did the same evil things that his father, Manasseh, had done for most of Manasseh's life. Amon made sacrifices to idols and worshipped the idols. Unlike Manasseh, Amon did not repent of his sin. Instead, the storyteller says that Amon was even more guilty than his father, Manasseh.

Amon ruled as king for only two years because Amon's servants, or officials, gathered together and decided to kill Amon. In this story, the word servants probably means Amon's court officials. The storyteller does not tell us why the officials decided to kill Amon. The storyteller does tell us that the officials killed Amon right in Amon's own house.

Stop here and tell a story about a leader who was such a bad leader that his own people decided to kill him. Why did the followers kill this leader? What happened to the people who killed the leader? Who became the next leader? Pause this audio here.

After these officials killed King Amon, the people of the land killed all those officials. The storyteller does not tell us the reason why the people of the land decided to kill the officials.

After the people of the land killed the officials who murdered King Amon, the people made Amon's son Josiah the next king of Judah.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 33:21–25 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

**In the first scene:** Amon became the king of Judah and reigned for two years. Amon worshipped idols and rejected Yahweh, just like Amon's father Manasseh did. Then Amon's officials plotted against Amon and killed him.

**In the second scene**: The people of Judah killed the officials who murdered Amon. Then the people made Amon's son Josiah king of Judah.

The characters in this passage are:

* Amon
* Yahweh
* Amon's servants, or officials
* The people of the land of Judah
* And Josiah

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Amon became king when he was 22 years old, and Amon reigned as king for two years. King Amon did evil in the eyes of Yahweh, just like Amon's father Manasseh had done. The storyteller says this in the same way that the storyteller said it in previous stories.

The most important detail to the storyteller was that Amon served the same idols that Amon's father Manasseh had served. These idols were images of the gods of the nations around Israel. When the storyteller says that Amon served the idols, it means that Amon worshipped those idols and made sacrifices to the idols.

Amon did not humble himself before Yahweh like his father Manasseh had done. This means that Amon never repented of worshipping false gods, and Amon never turned back to follow Yahweh's laws. Instead, Amon multiplied his guilt. This might mean that Amon sinned even more than his father Manasseh sinned, or the storyteller might have meant that Amon's guilt was very great. When Amon disobeyed Yahweh and worshipped other gods, Amon became guilty of doing great wrong against Yahweh, and Amon deserved punishment.

Amon's servants, or officials, conspired against Amon. In this context, the servants were Amon's officials. This means that some of Amon's officials made a secret plan to kill Amon.

Stop here and tell a story about a group of people who got together and made a secret plan to do something against the law. What words do you use to describe what those people did? Could you use any of those words here? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller does not say how many officials conspired against Amon. The officials killed Amon right in his own palace.

Stop here and discuss this question: What special words does your language have for when someone kills a leader or another important person? If your language does not have a word like this, it is fine to use the normal word for "killed." Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the people of Judah killed all of the officials who conspired against King Amon. The storyteller does not say why the people did this. Then the people made Amon's son Josiah the next king of Judah. The name Josiah means "Yahweh supports," in the sense that Yahweh helps Josiah or Yahweh approves of Josiah. If you have already translated the book of 2 Kings, then you have already decided how to translate the name "Josiah."

If necessary, stop here and listen to the beginning of 2 Kings chapter 22 to remember how you translated the name "Josiah." Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Amon was 22 years old when he became king, and Amon ruled in Jerusalem for two years. Amon disobeyed Yahweh, just like Amon's father Manasseh had done. Amon worshipped the idols that Amon's father had made and made sacrifices to those idols. Amon's father, Manasseh, had turned back to Yahweh, but Amon refused to do that. Instead, Amon sinned even more than Amon's father.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Amon, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* My father was foolish to stop worshipping all of the gods. I want to start worshipping all of the gods again; or
* I feel angry that my father removed all of the altars and foreign gods. I do not want to worship only Yahweh. I want to worship other gods too! or
* Now I am the king, and I get to decide what happens in this country; or
* My father was weak at the end of his life. I am going to do what I want, and the prophets of Yahweh cannot stop me.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am sad because I showed mercy to Amon's father, but Amon did not understand. Now Amon is worshipping foreign gods; or
* I am angry. Amon's father put the people on the right path, but now Amon has started worshipping other gods again; or
* I feel disappointed that Amon does not understand that I am the only God and there is no other.

Continue the drama.

Some of Amon's officials made a plan and killed Amon in his own house. But the people of Judah killed the servants who had murdered Amon. And the people made Amon's son Josiah the next king.

Ask the people playing Amon's officials, "What are you feeling or thinking?" Those people might answer things like:

* Amon is a terrible king. Amon is worse than his father was! We need to do something about Amon; or
* We want to get rid of King Amon, but is it worth the risk? If anyone catches us, we will be in big trouble; or
* We know that it would be wrong to kill Amon, but it is probably better for the people if Amon does not continue to be the king.

Ask the people playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We are confused. Our kings cannot seem to decide who we should worship; or
* We are angry and scared. Manasseh finally stopped worshipping idols, but now Amon is worshipping the idols again; or
* I am worried about the new king, Josiah. If these corrupt officials killed Josiah's father, what might the officials do to Josiah if they do not like him? or
* Although Amon was a terrible sinner, Amon's servants had no right to kill Amon.

Ask the person playing Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am sad that my father is dead; or
* I am scared. My father trusted those officials, and those officials killed my father. What is going to happen to me? or
* I need Yahweh to help me. I want to be a good king, but this is a scary place.

## 2 Chronicles 34:1–7 (id: eng-2ch-p65-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:1–7 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.

6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:1–7 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, Amon was king of Judah for two years. Then Amon's officials killed Amon, and the people of Judah made Amon's son Josiah the next king. In this story, Josiah becomes king when he is eight years old. Eight years later, Josiah begins to follow Yahweh and destroys all of the idols and pagan altars in the land.

The storyteller begins this story by giving us the usual information about the new king. Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and Josiah ruled for 31 years. Josiah ruled in Jerusalem, the capital city. The storyteller immediately lets us know that Josiah was a righteous king. Josiah lived his life in a similar way to Josiah's ancestor King David. Josiah was faithful to Yahweh and always did what pleased Yahweh. Josiah never worshipped false gods and idols or did any of the other things that Yahweh did not allow.

Stop here and tell a story about a person who always lived in a very good way, as one of that person's ancestors did. How do you describe this person? Pause this audio here.

After Josiah had been king for eight years, when Josiah was around sixteen years old, Josiah began to seek God. This means that Josiah decided that he would always do what Yahweh wanted Josiah to do, obey Yahweh's commands, and make Yahweh happy.

Josiah knew that Yahweh did not want Josiah to worship other gods. Josiah also knew that Yahweh did not want the people of Israel to worship other gods. In addition, because Josiah was the king, it was Josiah's job to lead the people and show the people how to obey Yahweh. So Josiah decided to go through the land of Judah and destroy every idol and every place where the people worshipped false gods.

Josiah did these things throughout the land of Judah. But Josiah also destroyed idols in the territory that belonged to the tribes of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali.

Stop here and look at a map of Israel that shows the territory that belonged to each tribe. Pay attention to the location of the tribes of Judah, Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali. Pause this audio here.

The territory of Simeon was located inside the territory of Judah, so it was probably easy for Josiah to control this territory. The territories of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Naphtali were north of the kingdom of Judah. The territories of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Naphtali used to be a part of the northern kingdom of Israel. Eighty\-two years before Josiah became king, the Assyrian army defeated and took over the kingdom of Israel. But when Josiah was king, the Assyrian empire had become weak and did not strongly control the land of Israel. So Josiah was able to destroy the idols in these parts of the former kingdom of Israel as well.

Stop here and discuss this question: Tell a story about a time when another group took over the territory of your people. How did your people feel about this? Pause this audio here.

Josiah was quite thorough when Josiah destroyed the idols in the land. Josiah not only tore the idols down, but Josiah also cut the idols to pieces, smashed them, and crushed them. Josiah made sure that he completely destroyed the idols, and no one could ever use the idols again. Josiah tore down the altars of Baal. Baal was a storm god, and many of the nations around Israel worshipped Baal. Josiah also tore down and destroyed the symbols of the goddess Asherah. Many people in the nations around Judah also worshipped Asherah.

Josiah also destroyed the incense altars in the land. Incense is a sweet\-smelling substance. The Israelites burned incense as part of their worship of Yahweh, but the Israelites were only allowed to burn incense inside Yahweh's temple. The nations around Judah burned incense to worship their false gods. This is the main reason why Josiah destroyed all the incense altars in the land.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your area, what sweet\-smelling things do people burn to worship their gods? How do people worship their false gods, spirits, the sun and stars, or other things? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller adds an unusual detail. The storyteller says that Josiah burned the bones of the priests on their altars. These priests were not servants of Yahweh. These priests led people to worship false gods. When Josiah burned the bones of these priests on the same altars they had used, it was a way to show that those priests were not worthy of respect. It was also a way to show that the false gods the priests worshipped were powerless. By doing this, Josiah defiled these altars and made the altars unfit for worship.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your culture, how do people treat a dead body with respect? How common is it in your culture to burn the body of a dead person? What are some things that would be disrespectful to do to a dead body? When your people hear that Josiah burned the bones of these priests, what might people think? Will people understand that Josiah meant to insult the dead priests and the gods they worshipped? Pause this audio here.

When Josiah burned the bones of the pagan priests on their altars, Josiah did what Yahweh said would happen many years ago in a prophecy. About 300 years before Josiah was king of Judah, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, King Jeroboam, built an altar to worship idols in the town of Bethel. A prophet came to Jeroboam while Jeroboam was burning incense to worship the idols. The prophet told Jeroboam that a descendant of David named Josiah would sacrifice the pagan priests and burn their bones on that altar. The town of Bethel was located in the territory of Ephraim, so Josiah certainly went there and did exactly what the prophet said Josiah would do. This was probably a very serious insult to those priests. The Israelites always buried the body of a dead person. The Israelites believed that burning a dead person's body was a way to show no respect to that person.

All of Josiah's activities purified Judah and Jerusalem. This means that after Josiah did these things, Yahweh considered Judah and Jerusalem to be ritually pure again. When the Israelites worshipped false gods, the Israelites made the nation impure. Josiah wanted the nation to be pure again, so Josiah removed all the idols from the land.

After Josiah finished purifying the territories of Judah, Simeon, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Naphtali, Josiah went back to Jerusalem.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:1–7 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

**In the first scene:** The storyteller summarizes the reign of King Josiah.

**In the second scene:** After Josiah had been king for eight years, Josiah began to seek Yahweh. Josiah destroyed all the idols and pagan altars in Judah and even in the territory of some other tribes of Israel.

The characters in this passage are:

* Josiah
* Josiah's servants
* The people of Judah
* The people in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali
* And Yahweh

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Josiah became king of Judah when Josiah was eight years old. Because Josiah was so young, Josiah probably received help from other people in order to rule Judah. Josiah ruled in Jerusalem for 31 years.

The storyteller summed up Josiah's time as king of Judah by saying that Josiah did right in the sight of Yahweh. This means that Josiah always did the things that Yahweh approved of. Josiah walked in the ways of his ancestor, King David. This means that Josiah followed the example of King David, and Josiah lived his life in the same way that David did.

Stop here and discuss this question: In your language, how do you describe a situation where one person behaves exactly like another person? Pause this audio here.

Josiah followed David's example and did not turn away to the right or the left. This means that Josiah always followed Yahweh's way of doing things.

Stop here and discuss this question: In your language, how do you describe a person who always does what is right and never does what is wrong? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the storyteller described Josiah's efforts to remove all the false gods from the land of Judah and part of the old kingdom of Israel. When Josiah was about 16 years old, Josiah began to seek God. This means that Josiah devoted himself to worshipping Yahweh and did not worship any other gods. Josiah tried to worship Yahweh in the same way that Josiah's ancestor, King David, did.

Four years later, when Josiah had been king of Judah for 12 years, Josiah began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of all forms of idol worship. "Purge" means to eliminate, drive out, or destroy something completely. In this story, "purge" also means to purify, or make clean, so that the land is acceptable to Yahweh again. When the people of Judah and Israel worshipped idols, Yahweh saw the people as impure. So Josiah had to make the land and the people pure again.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words or phrases do you have in your language that mean to eliminate, drive out, and destroy something? Which of these words or phrases could also mean to make something clean or pure again? Which of these words or phrases could you use here? Pause this audio here.

Josiah destroyed the high places because the people often worshipped idols in the high places. The storyteller says that Josiah did all of these things, but the storyteller probably means that Josiah gave the orders for people to do this. Josiah probably helped the people do these things as well. Josiah destroyed the Asherah poles because they represented a false god. Josiah destroyed the altars of Baal because people used these altars to worship a false god. Josiah destroyed all the carved and metal idols because Yahweh told the people not to worship those things. A carved idol is an idol that people carved from wood or stone. A metal idol was an idol that people made by melting metal and then shaping the metal to look a certain way when the metal cooled.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words do you have in your language to describe an object that people make when they melt metal and then shape the metal as it cools? Which of these could you use here? Pause this audio here.

Next, the storyteller says that "they" tore down the altars of the Baals in Josiah's presence. It is not clear who "they" are, but it probably means the people of Judah or possibly the government officials who served Josiah. The storyteller makes a point to say that Josiah was personally present when the people tore down some, if not all, of the altars to Baal. This shows that it was very important to Josiah to make sure that people completely destroyed the altars of Baal.

The people also cut down the incense altars that were above the altars of Baal. You will remember that the people around the nation of Judah burned incense to their false gods as a way of worshipping those gods.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How could you translate this so that it is clear that people used the incense altars to worship these idols? Pause this audio here.

The people, or Josiah's servants, took the Asherah poles, carved idols, and metal idols, broke them into pieces and ground them into powder. This was a way for the people to completely destroy these objects. Then, Josiah had his people scatter the powder on the graves of people who worshipped those idols. It is not clear exactly why the people did this, but it is most likely some way to express that the gods those people worshipped were nothing. It might also be a way to insult the people who had once worshipped those idols. We also do not know if these idol worshipers were already dead or if Josiah and his servants killed the idol worshipers.

Stop here and discuss these questions: When you hear that Josiah's people scattered the ashes of the smashed idols over the graves of people who worshipped those idols, what does this cause you to think of? What words would you use to describe this action? What do you think that your people will think about this action? How could you describe this action to make sure your people understand that it shows the idols were nothing? Pause this audio here.

Next, Josiah and his followers burned the bones of the priests who had worshipped the false gods. This was probably a very serious insult to those priests. Many scholars think that this also means that Josiah and his servants killed the pagan priests.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your culture, do people think it is disrespectful to burn the body of a dead person? If not, how can you help your hearers understand that when Josiah burned the bones of the pagan priests on the idol altars, Josiah insulted both the priests and the idols? Pause this audio here.

Josiah also did all these things in the territories of the tribes of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali. The territory of the tribe of Simeon was located inside the territory of Judah. The territories of the tribes of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Naphtali were all located north of Judah.

The storyteller adds that there were ruins around the cities in Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali. The Assyrian army had destroyed many buildings and cities in the land many years earlier.

Stop here and discuss: Describe places that you know about that people have destroyed in war. How will you translate the ruins in the Israelite territories? Pause this audio here.

Josiah did all the same things in the territories of the old northern kingdom of Israel that Josiah did throughout the land of Judah. Once Josiah finished these activities, Josiah went back to Jerusalem. Josiah had traveled throughout Israel because it was very important for Josiah to make sure that his servants thoroughly purged, or purified, the land.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and Josiah ruled for 31 years in Jerusalem. Josiah did what was pleasing to Yahweh. Josiah followed the example of Josiah's ancestor David and always obeyed Yahweh's laws.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I want to be a good king, but I am so young. If I do everything that Yahweh says to do, Yahweh will help me to be a good king; or
* I feel scared because the whole country is counting on me to lead them in the right direction; or
* I am glad that I can count on Yahweh to help and protect our people.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* Because Josiah is a good and faithful servant, the people will return to faithfulness to me.

> Continue the drama.

In the eighth year that Josiah was king, while Josiah was still young, he began to earnestly follow the God of his ancestor David. In the 12th year of Josiah's reign, Josiah began to destroy all the high places, Asherah poles, carved idols, and metal idols in Judah and Jerusalem. With Josiah present, people tore down the altars of the false god Baal and chopped down the incense altars that were high above them. Josiah told the people to break the Asherah poles, carved idols, and metal idols into pieces and grind them into powder. Then Josiah told the people to scatter the powder on the graves of the people who had made sacrifices to those idols. Josiah also burned the bones of the pagan priests on the altars of the idols they worshipped, in order to insult them. And so Josiah purified the land of Judah and Jerusalem.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel very happy to watch while my people destroy these detestable idols and altars; or
* I feel relieved that we are removing all these idols from the land. Now these idols will not tempt the people to worship false gods; or
* These pagan priests were foolish to disobey Yahweh and worship false gods. I will show everyone what happens to people who turn away from Yahweh; or
* I am grateful that Yahweh has put me in a position of power so I can lead the nation to worship Yahweh properly again.

Ask the people playing Josiah's servants, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We are very happy that we finally have a king who will make sure our nation stops worshipping idols; or
* We are very pleased to take these idols and cut them up into pieces! or
* I feel angry because the king's servants just tore down the altar of my favorite god! or
* I still want to worship all the gods. I will have to be very careful and hide what I am doing.

Ask the people playing the people of Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel angry and worried. These are the gods we trust! Why is the king destroying them? or
* We feel confused. For so long, our people have worshipped many gods. Why is the king now making us worship Yahweh only? or
* King Josiah is serious about serving Yahweh alone. Maybe we should be too; or
* We are so happy that we finally have a king who loves Yahweh! Maybe this is the new beginning we have been hoping for.

Continue the drama.

Josiah did the same thing in the towns in the territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and even as far north as the territory of Naphtali. Josiah did this in all the devastated territory around those cities, too. Josiah destroyed the pagan altars and the Asherah poles, and Josiah crushed the idols into dust. Josiah cut down all the incense altars throughout the former kingdom of Israel. Then Josiah returned to Jerusalem.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am so grateful to Yahweh, who has given me an opportunity to purify the land of Judah; or
* I am glad that I am able to help the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali destroy the idols and return to faithful worship of Yahweh; or
* I am relieved that I can be sure that there is no more idol worship in the land that I control.

Ask the people playing the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel shocked and afraid. King Josiah just destroyed all our gods. What will happen to us now? Is Yahweh really more powerful than all these other gods? or
* We feel hurt and angry. King Josiah has destroyed everything we know; or
* King Josiah has no right to destroy our gods and tell us what to do! or
* Maybe Josiah is right that we should only worship Yahweh.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am so pleased with Josiah. Josiah loves to honor me and is showing all the people that I alone am the one true God; or
* I am grieved that the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali have been suffering for such a long time because of their sin. Now I will bless those people if they are faithful to me; or
* I will use Josiah's faithfulness as an example to the people. The people must see that I bless people when they obey me. The worthless idols cannot bless people.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:1–7 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Josiah was eight years old when he became **king**, and Josiah ruled in **Jerusalem** for 31 years. Josiah did what pleased **Yahweh** and followed the example of his ancestor **David**. Josiah did not stray from following the way that pleased Yahweh. Be sure to use the same words that you used for king, Jerusalem, Yahweh, and David in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on king, Jerusalem, Yahweh, and David.

After Josiah had been the king for eight years, while he was still a young man, Josiah began to seek the **God** of his ancestor David. After Josiah had been king for 12 years, Josiah began to purge **Judah** and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, and other **idols**. Be sure to use the same words that you used in previous stories for God, Judah, and idols. See the Master Glossary for more information on God, Judah, and idol.

Stop here and decide what word you will use for "**purge**." If you choose to use a word or phrase that means to purify or make clean, refer to **purify** in the Master Glossary for more information. Pause this audio here.

In Josiah's presence, the people tore down the **altars** to **Baal** and cut to pieces the **incense** altars that were high above them. Josiah and the people smashed the Asherah poles and all the other idols, ground them up into powder, and scattered the powder over the **graves** of people who had made **sacrifices** to the idols. Be sure to use the same words that you used in previous stories for altar, Baal, incense, grave, and sacrifice. See the Master Glossary for more information on altar, Baal, grave, and sacrifice.

Josiah also burned the bones of the pagan **priests** on the altars of the idols they **worshipped**. So Josiah purified Judah and Jerusalem. In the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and even as far north as the land of Naphtali, and in the ruined areas around those towns, Josiah tore down the altars and the Asherah poles. Be sure to use the same words that you used in previous stories for priest and worship. See the Master Glossary for more information on priest and worship.

If you need a reminder on how you decided to say the names of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, or Naphtali, stop here and listen to the beginning of 1 Chronicles chapter 2\. Pause this audio here.

Josiah crushed those idols into dust and cut to pieces all of the incense altars throughout the land of **Israel**. Then Josiah went back to Jerusalem. Be sure to use the same word that you used for Israel in previous stories. See the Master Glossary for more information on Israel\*\*.\*\*
