## 2 Chronicles 34:8–21 (id: eng-2ch-p66-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 34:8–21 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:8–21 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:8–21 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous story, King Josiah began to rule when Josiah was eight years old. After eight years as king, Josiah began to follow Yahweh, and Josiah destroyed all the idols and pagan altars in the land. In this story, Josiah begins to repair the temple of Yahweh, and Hilkiah the priest finds the Book of the Law. Shaphan the scribe reads the Law to King Josiah, who feels very sad because he knows that his ancestors had not obeyed Yahweh's Law.

This story begins when Josiah had been king of Judah for 18 years. Josiah was now around 26 years old. Josiah had finished removing all of the idols and pagan altars from Judah and from part of the territory of Israel. Then Josiah decided to repair the temple of Yahweh in Jerusalem. Josiah needed to repair the temple because the previous kings of Judah had not taken care of it, and the temple was now in poor condition.

Stop here and describe a building in your area that is in poor condition. Why is this building in poor condition? Who is responsible for fixing the building? Describe this building to each other and compare this building to how it looked when it was new. Pause this audio here.

To pay for the repairs, Josiah will use the money that the doorkeepers collected at the temple. We do not know why the doorkeepers had collected money at the temple. This money was probably the temple tax that Moses commanded every Israelite male over 20 years old to pay. The people gave this money to help care for the place of worship, first the tabernacle and then the temple. The people may have given this tax to the doorkeeper when the people came to the temple in Jerusalem. The doorkeepers were responsible for making sure only authorized people entered Yahweh's temple. The doorkeepers also helped to care for the temple. It is also possible that the Levites living in the different regions collected the tax for the people and brought it to the doorkeeper in Jerusalem. The people of Judah, plus people from the territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Benjamin, and the entire remnant of Israel, gave money to repair the temple in Jerusalem. Although enemies had conquered the northern kingdom of Israel many years before, some Israelites still survived and lived in the land of Israel. These Israelites were the "remnant," or those Israelite people who still lived in Israel.

Stop here and tell a story about a time when your community collected money or materials for something that would benefit everyone. Why was it important to your people to collect money or materials for this cause? Who were the leaders of this project? How long did it take to raise the money or collect the materials? How did your people feel about it? Pause this audio here.

All of the temple doorkeepers were Levites, and they were important officials. The Levites were one tribe of Israel, and the Levites had the special responsibility to take care of the temple and lead all of the activities at the temple.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your culture, which jobs or responsibilities belong only to one family, clan, or tribe? How do your people feel about this? How do the members of that family, clan, or tribe feel about this? How important is that job or responsibility to your people? Pause this audio here.

Josiah sent three officials to oversee repairs to the temple. These men gave the money from the temple doorkeepers to Hilkiah the high priest. Hilkiah gave the money to the men who were overseeing the work on the temple. The storyteller named four overseers, all of whom were Levites. These men's names were Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Meshullam. The Levites were all descended from Levi, one of Jacob and Leah's sons. Levi had three sons, Merari, Kohath, and Gershon, and each son's descendants were a family group. In this story, Jahath and Obadiah came from Merari's family, and Zechariah and Meshullam came from Kohath's family. The Levites were in charge of watching over the workers fixing the temple. The Levites made sure the wood and stone workers did their jobs well. The workers did their jobs honestly and used the money the right way.

While Shaphan, Maaseiah, Joah, and Hilkiah were bringing out the money to the workers in the temple, Hilkiah found a book. Though many translations call this a book, this was actually a collection of scrolls. A scroll is a long strip of material on which people would write down stories, laws, histories, family lines, or anything else that people wanted to remember. Usually, people would write on strips of papyrus or parchment. This book contained the Law of Yahweh. These are the instructions that Yahweh gave the Israelites about how the people should live and how they should worship Yahweh. Sometimes people called this law "the Law of Moses," because Yahweh told these things to Moses and then Moses wrote them down.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What stories are especially important to your people? Which of these important stories tell your people about what rules people should follow? Have your people written any of these stories in books? What might happen to your people if you did not have these stories? Pause this audio here.

Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan. Shaphan took the book and went to see King Josiah. First, Shaphan told Josiah that he had given the money to the workers in the temple and that the workers were doing the work they were supposed to do. Then Shaphan told Josiah that Hilkiah had found a book in the temple. This strongly implies that Hilkiah, the other priests, the people, and King Josiah had not heard the words in the Book of the Law before. So Shaphan read the book out loud to King Josiah.

Stop here and discuss these questions: Do your people have a story that involves a book that people lost and then found again? If so, tell that story now. If not, tell any story about an important object that someone lost and then someone found again. Why was the object so important to the people in the story? Why was the object lost? What happened after someone found the object again? Pause this audio here.

When Josiah heard what the Book of the Law of Yahweh said, Josiah felt very sad. Josiah was sad because Josiah realized the people of Judah had not done all the things that the Law of Yahweh required. To show how sad Josiah was, Josiah tore Josiah's clothes.

Stop here and discuss this question: When someone in your culture feels very sad, what does that person do to show other people that they are very sad? How often do people do this thing? Pause this audio here.

Josiah realized that the people of Israel and Judah had not been obeying Yahweh's instructions for a long time. Josiah became very worried for himself and the people. The Law of Yahweh said that Yahweh would bless the people if the people obeyed Yahweh's commands, but that Yahweh would punish the people if the people disobeyed Yahweh's commands. Josiah suddenly understood that because the people had disobeyed for many years, something very bad was going to happen.

Stop here and tell a story about a time when you knew something bad was going to happen. How did you feel? How did other people in that situation feel? Did you try to stop the bad thing from happening? What was the result? Pause this audio here.

So Josiah sent Hilkiah, Shaphan, Shaphan's son Ahikam, Micah's son Abdon, and Asaiah the king's servant to ask Yahweh what to do. Josiah did this because he wanted to know how Yahweh felt about the situation and what Yahweh wanted Josiah and the people to do.

Stop and discuss these questions: In your culture, when someone is worried or has a big problem, who does that person ask for advice? How easy is it to ask other people for advice? Who do you think gives good advice, and who gives bad advice?

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:8–21 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

**In the first scene:** Josiah chooses people to oversee the temple's repair. These men give the money the Levites collected to Hilkiah, the high priest. The workers make the repairs faithfully.

**In the second scene:** Hilkiah the priest finds the Book of the Law in the temple and gives it to Shaphan the scribe. Shaphan takes the book and reads it out loud to King Josiah.

**In the third scene:** When Josiah hears what the Book of the Law says, Josiah is very sad. So Josiah sends his servants to ask Yahweh what to do.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Josiah
* Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah
* Hilkiah, the high priest
* The Levites
* The people of Manasseh, Ephraim, and all the remnant of Israel
* The people of Judah and Benjamin
* The people who live in Jerusalem
* The overseers in the house of Yahweh: Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Meshullam
* The workmen in the house of Yahweh
* Ahikam, Abdon, and Asaiah
* And Yahweh

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, after Josiah had been the king for 18 years, Josiah began to repair the temple of Yahweh. Josiah may have wanted to repair the temple as part of Josiah's process to purify the land and the temple, or Josiah may have started to repair the temple after Josiah had purified the land and the temple. You should follow the translations that you have in your area's major languages. In the previous story, Josiah purified the land by destroying all the idols and foreign altars, not only in Judah but also in the territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Naphtali, and Simeon. The storyteller does not mention how Josiah purified Yahweh's temple. The storyteller might assume that his audience understands that this means Josiah removed any false gods or idols from Yahweh's temple.

Stop here and discuss this question: When your people hear that Josiah purified the temple, what will they think this means? Pause this audio here.

Josiah needed money, wood, and stone to repair Yahweh's temple. Josiah would use the money that the doorkeepers collected at the temple. The doorkeepers had collected money not only from the people of Judah and Jerusalem, but also from the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all the remnant of Israel. The doorkeepers were probably storing the money they collected in one of the temple's storerooms.

Stop here and look at a map that shows the location of the territory that belonged to each of the tribes of Israel. Pay attention to the location of the territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Benjamin. Pause this audio here.

Some Levites worked as doorkeepers or gatekeepers in the temple. The remnant of Israel is the small group of people from the northern kingdom of Israel who were left in the land after the Assyrian army attacked them. The Assyrians killed many Israelites, took some of the Israelites prisoner, and left a few of the Israelites alive in the destroyed land.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How will you talk about the "remnant" of Israel? Pause this audio here.

Josiah sent three officials to repair Yahweh's temple. These officials were probably responsible for coordinating the work as Josiah's official representatives. The officials were Shaphan the son of Azaliah, Maaseiah, and Joah the son of Joahaz. Later in the story, the storyteller says that Shaphan was a scribe. A scribe was a person who could read and write. The scribes had very important religious jobs, such as making copies of the Law that Moses had given to the Israelites. But the scribes also worked for the king.

Stop here and discuss which word you will use for "scribe." Pause this audio here.

Maaseiah was a very important official. Many Bible scholars think Maaseiah was the governor, the most important government official in Jerusalem.

Stop here and discuss this question: What words do you have for the person who is the most important government official of a city? Pause this audio here.

Joah was a recorder. A recorder was something different from a scribe. Like a scribe, a recorder could read and write. But it seems that a recorder had a very special and specific job to write down things that the king said and did. The recorder might have also been responsible to tell other government officials what the king said and did. You should choose a word for "recorder" that is different from the word that you use for "scribe."

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words do you have for a person who can read and write, who is also a very important government official? Which of these words could mean a person who writes down what the king or highest leader says? Which of these words could you use here? Pause this audio here.

Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah gave the money that the doorkeepers had been collecting to Hilkiah the high priest. The high priest was the leader of all the priests in Yahweh's temple. The high priest was the most important priest who had very important responsibilities in Yahweh's temple. In this story, King Josiah also trusted the high priest to make sure that the workers repairing Yahweh's temple did a good job.

Stop here and discuss: Think of a group of people in your culture who do a special religious job. What words or phrases do you have for the person who is the religious leader of this group? Think about how you might say "high priest" in your language. Pause this audio here.

King Josiah needed craftsmen or skilled workers to repair Yahweh's temple. A smaller group of overseers managed all of the workers in the temple. The overseers' job was to make sure that the workers did their work correctly.

Stop here and discuss this question: What words do you have in your language for someone who oversees the work of other people? Pause this audio here.

The workmen gave the money to carpenters and builders to buy the materials to repair the temple of Yahweh. A carpenter is someone who knows how to make things out of wood. A builder is a more generic term for someone who knows how to build things. The builder might be able to build things out of wood, stone, or even other materials. The builders could work with quarried stone, which is stone that the workers have already cut into the desired shape.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words or phrases do you have for stone that someone has already cut into a specific shape? If you do not have a word or phrase for this, how can you make sure that your hearers know that people had already cut this stone into the desired shape? Pause this audio here.

Timber is another word for wood. The workers used the wood to make joists and beams. A beam is a large, thick, long piece of wood that the workers used to build the roof of the house. Bible scholars are not sure what the joists were. Some translations call these "braces," "couplings," or "binders." A joist might have been a smaller piece of wood that people used to attach two larger pieces of wood together.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words do you have for a large, thick, and long piece of wood that you use to make the roof of a house? What words do you have for a smaller piece of wood that you use to attach two larger pieces of wood together? If you do not have words for these things, how can you describe these items so that your readers will understand what they are? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that the kings of Judah let these buildings become ruins. The storyteller does not mean that all of the kings of Judah allowed the temple of Yahweh to become ruined. The storyteller probably means that only certain kings of Judah allowed the temple to become ruined. It is acceptable here to say something like "the houses which some of the kings of Judah had allowed to become ruined."

Stop here and describe a building in your area that people have not taken care of and is now in bad condition. What words or phrases do you use to describe this building? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that the workers did their work faithfully. This means that the workers were honest, did a good job, and did not steal or waste the money the workers received.

Stop here and discuss this question: How do you describe a worker who is honest and does a good job? Pause this audio here.

Next, the storyteller names some of the men who were the overseers of the work to repair the temple. Jahath and Obadiah were Levites who were descended from Merari, one of the three sons of Levi. Zechariah and Meshullam were Levites who were descendants of Kohath, another son of Levi. These Levites supervised the burden bearers and all the workmen. A burden bearer was probably a worker who helped move heavy objects from one place to another. Stones and beams of wood were large and heavy, and these objects probably required many men to move them from one place to another.

Stop here and discuss this question: In your language, what words do you have for a worker who helps to move heavy objects from one place to another? Pause this audio here.

Next, the storyteller mentions that all of the Levites were skilled at playing musical instruments. We do not know if the phrase "all of these Levites" refers to the Levites that the storyteller has just told us oversee the work, or if this is a separate group of Levites. It might seem odd that the storyteller says this in the middle of a story about repairing the temple. Bible scholars are not sure why the storyteller says this. But the storyteller does say this, and you should work this statement into your story in the most natural way possible. Some of the Levites were scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.

In the second scene, Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah were still at the temple with Hilkiah the high priest. These men were in the process of giving the money to the overseers and the workmen so that they could repair the temple of Yahweh. While Shaphan, Maaseiah, Joah, and Hilkiah were doing this, Hilkiah found the Book of the Law of Yahweh. Bible scholars do not agree on exactly what this book was, but scholars do agree that the book contained at least part of the five books of Moses, which are the first five books in the Bible. These books are called the books of Moses because Moses wrote these books down. The Book of the Law of Yahweh included instructions for how to worship Yahweh.

Hilkiah told Shaphan that Hilkiah found the Book of the Law. Then Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan. Shaphan took the book with him when Shaphan went to report to King Josiah. First, Shaphan told King Josiah that the workers in the temple of Yahweh were doing what Josiah wanted the workers to do. Shaphan specifically told Josiah that the overseers had given the money for repairs to all of the supervisors and workers. This is the information that Josiah was expecting to hear from Shaphan. Then Shaphan told Josiah that Hilkiah had found a book in the temple. Shaphan read the book out loud to Josiah. Be sure to say this in a way that is clear to your listeners that Shaphan did not read the book silently but read it out loud so that everyone could hear.

In the third scene, when Josiah heard what the Book of the Law of Yahweh said, Josiah felt very sad. Josiah showed that he felt very sad by tearing Josiah's clothes. If your hearers will not understand that Josiah tore his clothes because Josiah felt sad, it is acceptable to say something like, "Josiah tore his clothes to show that he was sad."

Stop here and discuss these questions: How clear will the meaning be when your hearers hear the statement "Josiah tore his clothes"? Will you add a statement to clarify that Josiah tore his clothes to show that Josiah was sad? Pause this audio here.

Josiah was sad because Josiah realized that he and his people had failed to obey many of Yahweh's commands. Then Josiah gave an order to some of his officials. Josiah gave this order to Hilkiah the high priest and to Shaphan the scribe, but Josiah also included Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, and another man named Asaiah. The storyteller does not tell us what job Ahikam and Abdon did, but the storyteller does say that Asaiah was Josiah's attendant. An attendant is simply a person who helps the king in whatever way the king needs.

Stop here and discuss this question: What words do you have for a person who helps another person in whatever way that person needs help? Pause this audio here.

Josiah told Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, and Asaiah to inquire of Yahweh. To inquire of Yahweh simply means to talk to Yahweh and find out what Yahweh wants. When an Israelite wanted to inquire of Yahweh, that person usually asked a prophet. Josiah wanted his officials to find out what Yahweh had to say about the words in the Book of the Law. "The words of this book" actually mean the teachings or instructions that are in the book.

Josiah said that their ancestors had not kept the word of Yahweh. To keep the word of Yahweh means to obey Yahweh's instructions. Josiah realized that Yahweh was probably angry with the people because the people's ancestors had not obeyed the instructions in the Book of the Law.

Stop here and discuss these questions: What words or phrases do you have in your language that mean to obey the instructions that a person of higher status gives you? Which of these could you use here? Pause this audio here.

Josiah also said that Yahweh has poured out his wrath against the people. This is just a special way to say that Yahweh is very angry with the people of Judah and Israel.

Stop here and discuss these questions: In your language, how do you say that one person is very angry at another person? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:8–21 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Josiah
* Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah
* Hilkiah, the high priest
* The Levites
* The people of Manasseh, Ephraim, and all the remnant of Israel
* The people of Judah and Benjamin
* The people who live in Jerusalem
* The overseers in the house of Yahweh: Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Meshullam
* The workmen in the house of Yahweh
* Ahikam, Abdon, and Asaiah
* And Yahweh

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

After Josiah had been the king for 18 years, and he had finished cleansing all the idols from the land and from the temple of Yahweh, Josiah sent three officials to repair the temple of Yahweh, Josiah's God. The officials' names were Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the highest official of Jerusalem, and Joah son of Joahaz, who kept the government records. These three men went to see Hilkiah the high priest. The men gave Hilkiah the money that the doorkeepers of the temple had collected from the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, and the rest of Israel, as well as from those who lived in Judah, Benjamin, and Jerusalem.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel excited that we are finally going to repair the temple of Yahweh and make it look as beautiful as it once did; or
* I am grateful that Yahweh has made it possible for me to be the one who will make Yahweh's temple look wonderful again; or
* I hope that when the people see the repaired temple of Yahweh, the people will remember that Yahweh is the one true God.

Ask the people playing Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* We feel happy that the people gave so much money to repair the temple of Yahweh; or
* We feel proud of our people. Our people were very generous and donated this money to make the temple of Yahweh look good again; or
* I hope that when the people see the repaired temple of Yahweh, the people will remember that Yahweh is the one true God.

> Continue the drama.
> 
> Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah gave the money to the men appointed to oversee the work on Yahweh's temple. The overseers paid the men who repaired and restored the temple. The overseers also gave money to the carpenters and builders to purchase prepared stone, wood for the braces, and beams for the buildings that the recent kings of Judah allowed to become ruined. And the workers did their work honestly. The workers' overseers were Jahath and Obadiah, who were Levites from the clan of Merari, and also Zechariah and Meshullam, who were Levites from the clan of Kohath. The Levites, who were all skilled at playing musical instruments, were also in charge of the men who transported the materials and supervised all the workmen doing various jobs. And some of the Levites were scribes, officials and doorkeepers.
> 
> Stop here. Ask the people playing Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, Meshullam, and the Levites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel honored that the king has trusted us to lead this great work; or
* We feel so happy that King Josiah is restoring the temple; or
* This is a holy task. We must make sure that the work goes well and that the workers use the money wisely; or
* Once the people see a beautiful temple, maybe it will help the people return to worshiping Yahweh!

> Ask the people playing the workers in the temple of Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel proud that we get to use our skills to make this temple beautiful again; or
* This is not an ordinary building project. We are repairing the house of God; or
* We must be very honest and work hard. Yahweh will know if we do not do this the right way; or
* We want to show the king and the overseers that we are trustworthy and faithful.

> Continue the drama.
> 
> While the overseers were bringing out the money that the Levites collected at the temple of Yahweh, Hilkiah the high priest found the Book of the Law of Yahweh, which Moses wrote. Hilkiah told Shaphan the scribe, "I have found the Book of the Law in Yahweh's temple!" Then Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan. Shaphan took the book to the king and said, "Your officials are doing everything you assigned them to do. We gave the money that the Levites collected to the supervisors and the workmen." Shaphan also told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." So Shaphan read the book to the king.
> 
> Stop here. Ask the person playing Hilkiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I have heard about a book of the Law of Yahweh, but I have never seen it. Could this be it? or
* I feel worried that our people have disobeyed Yahweh's law; or
* I am in awe. These are the very words of Yahweh that Moses himself wrote! This could change everything for our people; or
* The king must hear the words of this book.

> Ask the person playing Shaphan, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* This might be the most important discovery of my lifetime! or
* I am excited that we are about to find out more information about how to please Yahweh; or
* What will the king do when the king hears the words of this book?

> Continue the drama.
> 
> When Josiah heard what was in the Book of the Law of Yahweh, Josiah tore his clothes in sorrow. Josiah immediately called together Hilkiah, Shaphan, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, and Josiah's servant Asaiah. Josiah said, "Go and speak to Yahweh on my behalf and on behalf of all the remnant of Israel and Judah. Ask Yahweh about the contents of this book. For Yahweh must be very angry at us because our ancestors have not obeyed Yahweh's instructions. We have not been doing everything that this book says we must do."
> 
> Stop here. Ask the person playing Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am sad because I did not know that we were supposed to do all these things; or
* I am afraid because Yahweh would be right to punish us for disobeying Yahweh's instructions; or
* I must find out what Yahweh wants me to do about this situation; or
* It is my responsibility as the king to show the people how to obey Yahweh's law.

> Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am pleased with Josiah's humility and repentance. Josiah is really sad that the people have not obeyed me; or
* Now that the people have found the Book of the Law, we will see if they will obey it or not; or
* Although the people have disobeyed me for a very long time, I will have mercy on anyone who repents and begins to live the right way.

The high priest was the leader of all the priests in the temple of Yahweh. The high priest was the most important priest who had very important responsibilities in Yahweh's temple.

## 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 (id: eng-2ch-p67-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passage, Hilkiah, the high priest, found the Book, or Scroll, of the Law in the temple, and King Josiah's scribe read the book to King Josiah. Josiah was very sad because the Israelite people had not obeyed Yahweh's commands in the Book of the Law. Josiah ordered Hilkiah and some other men to go to a prophet to ask Yahweh for wisdom.

Stop here and listen as a group: If you have already translated 2 Kings 22:14–23:14, which contains the same information, listen to your translation now. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Hilkiah the high priest and some other men go to ask Yahweh for wisdom through a prophetess, or female prophet, whom people call "Huldah." Josiah wants these men to find out what Yahweh says about the Israelite people's disobedience to Yahweh's law. A prophet gives messages from God to the people. People call Huldah's husband "Shallum." Shallum's father is Tokhath, and Shallum's grandfather is Hasrah. In 2 Kings 22, people call Tokhath by the name "Tikvah," and people call Hasrah by the name "Harhas."

Hasrah is the keeper of the wardrobe for the temple. The wardrobe may be the special clothing people wear at religious functions. Hasrah probably takes care of the clothing that priests and Levites wear when they serve in the temple. Priests are people who serve God in the temple. Levites are Levi's descendants who serve the priests. Huldah lives in a part of Jerusalem that people call the New Quarter or the Second Quarter, but we are not sure exactly where this part of the city is. Jerusalem is the most important city in Israel.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of the country of Judah, including the city of Jerusalem. Pause this audio here.

Huldah tells the men to tell King Josiah what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says about the Israelite people's disobedience. Yahweh will cause disaster, or bad things, to happen in the country of Judah and will punish the people in Jerusalem and Judah. All the curses from the Book, or Scroll, of the Law will come true. In the Book of the Law, Yahweh promised to bless the people if the people obeyed Yahweh's commands, but Yahweh promised to curse the people if they did not obey Yahweh's commands. This is the same Book of the Law that Hilkiah found in the temple.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about a time when people knew that if they did certain kinds of things, their god would bless or curse the people. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will bring disaster or bad things because the people of Israel and Judah rejected Yahweh and offered incense to other gods and idols that the people made. Yahweh is very angry with the people of Judah, and Yahweh's wrath will make Yahweh act against the people of Judah.

However, Huldah has a separate message from Yahweh specifically for King Josiah. When Josiah heard Yahweh's words in the Book of the Law, Josiah humbled himself and tore his robes and wept. Because Josiah regretted what his people had done and humbled himself, Yahweh promises that Yahweh will not send disaster on the land and the people right away. Josiah will go to his ancestors in peace. Yahweh will allow Josiah to die, and Josiah's people will bury Josiah peacefully before Yahweh sends disaster. Josiah will not have to see the bad things that Yahweh will send to the country and the people.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story where someone promises to punish a group of people, but the person delays their actions to protect someone or a group of people that they like. Pause this audio here.

The men report all of Huldah's words to King Josiah. King Josiah commands all the elders, or older leaders, in Jerusalem and the rest of Judah to meet with Josiah, so they all come together and go to Yahweh's temple. The rest of the people who live in Jerusalem, people who live in the other towns in Judah, the priests, and the Levites all join Josiah and the elders at the temple. All kinds of people go with Josiah to Yahweh's temple, from the least important to the most important person in Jerusalem and Judah. In the story in 2 Kings 22, the storyteller says prophets, not Levites, go to the temple with Josiah. Yahweh often speaks to the Israelites through prophets, and Levites are men from the tribe of Levi who assist the priests in the temple. Because all of the people in Jerusalem and Judah go to the temple, most likely both the Levites and prophets probably join King Josiah and all the rest of the people at the temple.

Josiah reads out loud everything that Yahweh says in the Book of the Covenant. When people make a covenant, people make a solemn promise that they cannot break. The Book of the Covenant describes Yahweh's covenant with the people of Israel. The Book of the Covenant and the Book of the Law are the same book. You will remember that Hilkiah found this book in the temple.

After Josiah finishes reading, Josiah stands in the place that people reserve for the king by the pillar. Kings probably stand in this place when they make important official announcements and speak with authority. Throughout the Old Testament, storytellers describe leaders who make covenants between Yahweh and the people. Each time a leader makes a new covenant or renews an old covenant, the leader stands in front of all the people and reads the covenant out loud. When Josiah renews this covenant, Josiah reminds the people how Yahweh makes covenants with Yahweh's people, the Israelites.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a pillar. Pause this audio here.

Josiah promises to obey Yahweh and to keep Yahweh's commands, testimonies, and statutes completely and faithfully with all Josiah's heart and soul. By promising to obey all of Yahweh's words, Josiah renews the covenant with Yahweh.

Josiah orders all the people who are present to promise to keep the covenant as well. So the people from Jerusalem and Judah obey the covenant they made with God, the God of their ancestors. An ancestor is someone from whom a person descended. Yahweh has been the God of the Israelite people through many generations of ancestors. Because Josiah orders the people to keep the covenant, the people obey Yahweh again.

King Josiah removes all the detestable idols from the whole country of Israel. Josiah requires everyone in Israel to serve Yahweh their God. Throughout Josiah's lifetime, the people do not turn away from following Yahweh, the God of their ancestors.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

**In the first scene:** The high priest Hilkiah and other men go to speak with the prophet Huldah in Jerusalem. Huldah tells the men that Yahweh promises to bring disaster on Judah and its people because the people rejected Yahweh and served other gods. However, Huldah says Yahweh will not punish the people until after Josiah dies because Josiah responded with humility.

**In the second scene:** When the men tell Josiah about Yahweh's words through Huldah, Josiah calls all the people of Judah, from the least to the greatest, to come to the temple in Jerusalem. Josiah reads the words of Yahweh's covenant from the Book of the Covenant out loud. Then Josiah and all the people renew the covenant with Yahweh.

**In the third scene**: Josiah removes all the idols from Judah and Israel. As long as Josiah lives, the people obey Yahweh, the God of Israel.

The characters in this passage are:

* Hilkiah
* Men whom Josiah sends with Hilkiah
* Huldah
* Yahweh
* King Josiah
* Elders of Judah and Jerusalem
* Priests and Levites
* And all the rest of the people who live in Jerusalem

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Hilkiah the high priest and some other men go to inquire, or to find out, what Yahweh says about something. The men go to the prophetess Huldah. Huldah's husband is Shallum, whose father is Tokhath and whose grandfather is Hasrah. Hasrah was the keeper of the wardrobe for the temple. Huldah lives in a part of Jerusalem that people call the New Quarter.

Because Huldah is a prophetess, Huldah speaks the message of Yahweh. Huldah tells the men, "This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says." In the Bible, prophets use language like this to introduce an important message from Yahweh. Huldah wants the men to know that Yahweh has a serious message for King Josiah. When Huldah speaks to the men, the men should understand that they are listening to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story where one person speaks for another person. In the story, people should understand that they are hearing words from the second person even though the first person is speaking. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group: You just told a story about one person who speaks for another person. How did you help your audience understand who is speaking and whose words that person speaks? Pause this audio here.

Through Huldah, Yahweh says, "I will cause bad things to happen in this country and will punish the people in it. All the curses that someone read to Josiah from the Book of the Law will come true. I will do this because the people from Israel and Judah rejected me and burned incense to other gods. I am angry because of all the idols that the people made. I will pour out my anger on Jerusalem, and no one will be able to stop it. My anger is like a fire that no one can put out."

Yahweh is angry because the people disobeyed Yahweh's commands when the people burned incense to other gods and created idols. Yahweh will cause disaster or bad things to happen to the people in Jerusalem. Yahweh will pour out or show all of Yahweh's anger to the people of Jerusalem. The storyteller describes Yahweh's anger with special language that compares anger to a fire that no one can quench or put out.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How do you talk about anger in your culture? What kinds of words or phrases will help you describe Yahweh's anger here? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh keeps speaking through Huldah, but now Yahweh has a different message specifically for King Josiah. Yahweh says, "This is what I say about the words you read in the Book of the Law. You were sorry when you heard the words from the book, and your heart was tender, so you humbled yourself before me when you heard what I will do to the people from Judah and Jerusalem. You tore your clothes in sorrow and wept in front of me. I heard you, so now I will let you die, and your people will bury you peacefully. You will not be alive when I bring all the bad things to the people of Judah and Jerusalem."

When the storyteller says Josiah's heart was tender, the storyteller means Josiah cared and felt sad because the people of Judah and Jerusalem disobeyed Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How do you talk about the way a person dies peacefully in your culture? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the king's men return to Josiah and report all of Yahweh's words. King Josiah commands all the elders in Jerusalem and the rest of Judah to meet with Josiah, so they all come together and go to Yahweh's temple. The rest of the people who live in Jerusalem, people who live in the other towns in Judah, the priests, and the Levites all join Josiah and the elders at the temple. All kinds of people go with Josiah to Yahweh's temple, from the least important to the most important person in Jerusalem and Judah.

Josiah reads out loud all the words that Yahweh wrote in the Book of the Covenant, which is the same Book of the Law that Hilkiah the high priest found in the temple. You will remember that this was really a scroll, or a long piece of parchment that someone turned around a long stick. King Josiah stands in his place by the pillar and renews the covenant with Yahweh. Josiah promises to follow Yahweh and to faithfully keep Yahweh's commands, testimonies, and statutes. These three words—commands, testimonies, and statutes—together refer to everything that Yahweh says. Josiah promises to obey every word that Yahweh says, and Josiah will obey with all Josiah's heart and soul. In the Bible, the storyteller uses a person's heart as special language for the place where a person's thoughts, feelings, and decisions happen. A person's soul represents the invisible part of a person, or a person's thoughts, feelings, and desires. Josiah promises to follow Yahweh completely and faithfully.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about someone who obeys someone else completely and faithfully. How do you describe a person who obeys like this? Pause this audio here.

After Josiah renews the covenant, Josiah orders all the people who are present to make a similar promise. So the people from Jerusalem promise to obey the covenant they made with God, the God of the people's ancestors.

In the third scene, Josiah removes all the detestable idols that people made in the entire land of Israel. You will remember that something that is detestable is something that Yahweh hates very much. Josiah requires every person in the land of Israel to worship Yahweh their God. As long as Josiah lives, the people obey Yahweh, the God of their ancestors.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* Hilkiah
* Men whom Josiah sends with Hilkiah
* Huldah
* Yahweh
* King Josiah
* Elders of Judah and Jerusalem
* Priests and Levites
* And all the rest of the people who live in Jerusalem

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Hilkiah the high priest and some other men go to inquire of Yahweh through the prophetess Huldah. Huldah's husband is Shallum, whose father is Tokhath and whose grandfather is Hasrah, the keeper of the temple wardrobe. Huldah lives in a part of Jerusalem that people call the New Quarter.

Huldah tells the men, "This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: 'I will cause bad things to happen in this country and will punish the people in it. All the curses that someone read to Josiah from the Book of the Law will come true. I will do this because the people from Israel and Judah rejected me and burned incense to other gods. I am angry because of all the idols that the people made. I will pour out my anger on Jerusalem, and no one will be able to stop it. My anger is like a fire that no one can put out.'"

Yahweh continues to speak with a different message specifically for King Josiah. Yahweh says, "This is what I say about the words you read in the Book of the Law. You were sorry when you heard the words from the book, and you humbled yourself before me when you heard what I will do to the people from Judah and Jerusalem. You tore your clothes in sorrow and wept in front of me. I heard you, so now I will let you die, and your people will bury you peacefully. You will not be alive when I bring all the bad things to the people of Judah and Jerusalem."

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing Hilkiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am afraid of Yahweh's anger; or
* I am afraid that King Josiah may become angry with us because we bring a serious message from Yahweh.

Ask the person playing Huldah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I am fearful that these men might not believe that the words I speak belong to Yahweh; or
* I feel angry that my people have disobeyed Yahweh and received Yahweh's great anger and punishment.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel very angry because my people rejected me; or
* I feel sad because I must punish my people because they failed to keep my covenant, even though I remained faithful to them; or
* I feel hopeful because King Josiah responded to me with such humility.

Continue the drama.

The men return to Josiah and report Yahweh's words. King Josiah commands all the elders in Jerusalem and the rest of Judah to meet with Josiah, so they all come together and go to Yahweh's temple. The rest of the people who live in Jerusalem, people who live in the other towns in Judah, the priests, and the Levites all join Josiah and the elders at the temple. All kinds of people go with Josiah to Yahweh's temple, from the least important to the most important person in Jerusalem and Judah.

Josiah reads out loud all the words that Yahweh wrote in the Book of the Covenant, which is the same book that Hilkiah the high priest found in the temple. King Josiah stands in his place by the pillar and renews the covenant with Yahweh. Josiah promises to follow Yahweh and to faithfully keep Yahweh's commands, testimonies, and statutes. Josiah promises to obey every word that Yahweh says, and Josiah will obey with all Josiah's heart and soul. Josiah promises to follow Yahweh completely and faithfully.

After Josiah renews the covenant, Josiah orders all the people who are present to make a similar promise. So the people from Jerusalem promise to obey the covenant they made with God, the God of their ancestors.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel sad that my people disobeyed Yahweh; or
* I feel relieved that Yahweh will not make me see the disaster that Yahweh will bring to my people; or
* I feel sad that I must die and will not be able to continue to encourage my people to obey Yahweh.

Ask the people playing all the people of Jerusalem and Judah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel fearful that we will experience Yahweh's anger; or
* We feel hopeful that maybe Yahweh will not punish us if we continue to obey Yahweh as Josiah requires.

Continue the drama.

Josiah removes all the detestable idols that people made in the entire land of Israel. Josiah requires every person in the land of Israel to worship Yahweh their God. As long as Josiah lives, the people obey Yahweh, the God of their ancestors.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 34:22–33 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Stop here and listen as a group: If you have already translated 2 Kings 22:14–23:14, which contains the same information, listen to your translation now. Pause this audio here.

**King** Josiah sends Hilkiah the **high priest** and some other men to see the prophetess Huldah. A king is someone who rules over a city or a territory. Priests were people who worked in the temple in Jerusalem. The high priest was the most important priest. Once every year, the high priest offered a sacrifice on behalf of the people for forgiveness of sins. A **prophet** is a person who gives messages from God to the people, and a prophetess is a female prophet. Use the same word or phrase for king, high priest, and prophet as you used in previous passages. For more information on king, high priest, and prophet, refer to the Master Glossary.

Huldah's husband is Shallum, who is Hasrah's grandson. Hasrah is the "keeper of the wardrobe." The wardrobe probably describes the special clothing people wear at religious functions. Hasrah probably takes care of the clothing that priests and Levites wear when they serve in the temple.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **keeper of the wardrobe**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Huldah lives in the city of **Jerusalem**. Jerusalem is the most important city in Israel, and people built Yahweh's temple in Jerusalem. Use the same word or phrase for Jerusalem as you used in previous passages. For more information on Jerusalem, refer to the Master Glossary.

As a prophet, Huldah speaks words or messages from **Yahweh**, the **God** of **Israel**. Yahweh is the name God gives himself. This name reminds people of the covenant that God made with the Israelites during the time of Moses. God created everything and is the most powerful spiritual being. Israel is the name of the territory where the Israelites lived. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh, God, and Israel as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, God, and Israel, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh tells Josiah's men that Yahweh will bring **disaster** on the land of Judah and the people who live there. A disaster is a sudden event that causes great damage or loss of life. Use the same word or phrase for disaster as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh also says that all the curses Yahweh wrote will come true. To curse someone means to wish that something bad would happen to that person. When God curses people, God promises to make bad things happen to those people.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **curse**. Look up curse in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh feels very angry with the people because the people burned incense to other gods. Yahweh says he will pour out Yahweh's strong anger, or **wrath,** on the people. In the Bible, "God" refers to the most powerful spiritual being who created everything. However, sometimes people worship other spirit beings or idols as if they have power. God told the people of Israel not to worship or follow any other **gods** but Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases for wrath and gods as you used in previous passages. Refer to the Master Glossary for more information about wrath and gods.

Yahweh says that Yahweh will not make Josiah see the disaster Yahweh will bring on the people because Josiah **humbled** himself before Yahweh. Josiah believed Yahweh's commands were more important than Josiah's desires. Yahweh will allow the people to bury Josiah in **peace**. When people live in harmony with one another without fighting, those people live in peace. Because Josiah did not fight with Yahweh about the people's disobedience, Josiah will die in peace. Use the same words or phrases for humbled and peace as you used in previous passages. For more information on peace, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Josiah called together all the **elders** of Jerusalem and the rest of Judah to come to the **temple**. All the rest of the people of Judah, including the **priests** and **Levites**, also meet at the temple. The elders in a community are people with authority in a community. The temple is the place where the Israelites worshiped God. Priests are people who serve God in the temple. Levites are descendants of Levi who serve the priests. Use the same words or phrases for elder, temple, priest, and Levite as you used in previous passages. For more information on elder, temple, priest, and Levite, refer to the Master Glossary.

Josiah read out loud all of the Book of the Covenant. At this time, people wrote books on a scroll, which is a long roll of material like paper that people write on and then roll up. When people make a covenant, they make a solemn promise to each other that those people cannot break.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a scroll. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "Book, or **Scroll**, of the **Covenant**." If you have already translated this word or phrase in another book of the Bible, use the same word or phrase that you have used there. For more information on scroll and covenant, refer to the Master Glossary.

Josiah promises to keep Yahweh's **commands**, **testimonies**, and **statutes** with all of Josiah's **heart** and **soul**. When a storyteller uses commands, testimonies, and statutes all together, the storyteller talks about all that Yahweh says. A person's heart is special language for the place where a person's thoughts, feelings, and decisions happen. A person's soul represents the invisible part of a person, or a person's thoughts, feelings, and desires. Use the same words or phrases for commands, testimonies, statutes, heart, and soul as you used in previous passages. For more information on commands, testimonies, statutes, heart, and soul, refer to the Master Glossary.

Josiah required all the people to promise to keep the covenant to Yahweh, the God of their **ancestors**. An ancestor is someone from whom a person descended. Use the same word or phrase for ancestor as you used in previous passages.

Josiah removed all the **idols** from the land of Israel. An idol is an object that people make in order to worship a god. Use the same word or phrase for idol as you used in previous passages. For more information on idol, refer to the Master Glossary.
