## 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 (id: eng-2ch-p68-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passage, a prophet told King Josiah's men that Yahweh would send disaster on the people because the people had rejected Yahweh. However, because King Josiah responded to Yahweh with humility, Yahweh would not send the disaster until after Josiah died. Josiah and all the people renewed the covenant with Yahweh, and Josiah required all the people to obey Yahweh.

If you have already translated 2 Kings 23:21–23, which has some of the same information, stop here as a group and listen to your translation. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, King Josiah commands all the people to celebrate the Passover festival to honor Yahweh. Passover is an important annual Jewish festival that reminds the people of how Yahweh rescued the people from Egypt. People also call Passover the "Feast of Unleavened Bread" because Passover happens on the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, so people celebrate Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread at about the same time. To celebrate Passover, the people eat roasted lamb along with bitter herbs and unleavened bread, or bread that people make without yeast. Yahweh gave instructions about the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the Israelites through Moses.

If you have already translated Exodus 12:1–28 and Deuteronomy 16:1–8, where Yahweh tells the people how to celebrate Passover, stop here as a group and listen to your translations. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a lamb, a picture of bitter herbs, and a picture of unleavened bread. Pause this audio here.

On the 14th day of the first month in the Jewish calendar, people kill lambs for the Passover festival in Jerusalem. The storyteller says that the people kill the Passover lamb, but we know the people slaughter many lambs or goats as Passover offerings. People call the first month in the Jewish calendar "Abib," and this month occurs in the spring.

Josiah chooses priests to do specific work in the temple and encourages the priests to serve well. Priests are descendants of Moses' brother Aaron, the first high priest, and priests are part of the Israelite tribe of Levi. Priests work in Yahweh's temple and offer sacrifices to Yahweh on behalf of the people. Josiah then speaks to the Levites. People called the descendants of Levi who were not from Aaron's family line, and were therefore not priests, "Levites." Yahweh consecrated or gave the Levites the special duty to serve Yahweh in the temple, and the Levites taught the Israelites in the temple and helped the priests take care of the temple. Levites do not offer sacrifices to Yahweh. Priests and Levites work together to serve Yahweh in the temple.

Josiah tells the Levites to leave the ark in the temple that King Solomon, King David's son, built. You will remember from a previous passage that the "ark," or ark of the covenant, is a symbol of Yahweh's presence. Before Solomon built the temple, the priests carried the ark from place to place. The priests set the ark on poles, and the priests carried the ark by putting the poles on the priests' shoulders. However, now the ark should stay in the temple. We do not know if someone moved the ark out of the temple or if Josiah wants the Levites to know they should not take the ark out of the temple in the future.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the ark in the temple and a picture of the ark with the poles the priests used to carry the ark. Pause this audio here.

Josiah also tells the Levites to serve Yahweh their God and to serve the Israelite people well. Josiah tells the Levites to be ready to do the work that King David and David's son Solomon assigned to each Levite division. David and Solomon wrote instructions and organized families of Levites into larger groups that people call divisions. Each division takes responsibility for specific duties in the temple.

Josiah tells each division of Levites to stand in specific places throughout the temple. When the Israelite families who are not priests or Levites enter the temple for Passover, the Levites will be available to help. The Levites will kill the Passover lambs, and then the Levites will consecrate themselves to make themselves pure. The Levites probably wash themselves in a special way to make themselves pure. Once the Levites make themselves pure, the Levites will prepare the lambs to be Passover offerings for the lay people. The Levites will do all these things according to the instructions that Yahweh gave through Moses.

From Josiah's own herds of animals, Josiah gives enough animals for all the lay people to make Passover offerings. Josiah gives 30,000 lambs and young goats for the Passover offerings. Josiah also gives 3,000 cattle. People probably use the lambs and goats for Passover offerings, and people use the cattle for other offerings during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which continues for several days after the Passover ends.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a lamb, a young goat, and cattle. You will remember that cattle can include cows, bulls, and oxen. Pause this audio here.

Josiah's other leaders also give freely to the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah the high priest, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the officials in charge of Yahweh's temple, give the priests 2,600 lambs and goats along with 300 cattle. The leaders of the Levites, including Conaniah and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, along with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, give 5,000 lambs and 500 cattle to the Levites.

The priests and Levites finish preparations and stand in their places in the temple in their divisions as King Josiah ordered. The Levites kill the lambs for the Passover offerings and give the blood to the priests. The priests splash the blood on the altar while the Levites remove the skin from the animals.

At the same time that the Levites kill and skin the Passover offerings, the Levites kill and set aside other animals that the Levites prepare to be burnt offerings. When people make burnt offerings, a priest offers an entire animal on the altar until the entire animal burns up. These offerings are not the same as the Passover offerings that the priests make. The Levites will give these animals that will be burnt offerings to the family divisions of non\-Levite people so that the people can offer them according to Yahweh's commands in the Book, or Scroll, of Moses. The Book of Moses probably refers to the first five books in the Old Testament. The Levites also set aside the cattle for families to use for other offerings to Yahweh.

The Levites roast lambs for the Passover offerings over a fire according to Yahweh's instructions. The Levites boil pieces of the cattle for other holy offerings in pots, caldrons, and pans. The other holy offerings may be fellowship or peace offerings, in which the priests burn the fat of the animal on the altar but boil the rest of the animal so that the priests and lay people may eat the animal. The Levites serve the meat from the Passover and other offerings to the non\-Levite people immediately.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a pot, caldron, and pan. Pause this audio here.

After the Levites serve the lay people, the Levites prepare for the Passover for themselves and for the priests. The priests make offerings on the altar from the morning until the sun goes down, so the Levites prepare animals for the priests to make offerings for themselves.

Previously, King David, along with Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, King David's seer, assigned specific places for musicians to stand in the temple many years before this. Asaph, Hemam, and Jeduthun were musicians who served King David and led the temple musicians. A seer understands messages from God like a prophet. We are not sure if only Jeduthun was David's seer, or if Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun were all seers for King David. Now, the musicians or singers, who are descendants of Asaph, stand in the places Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun had assigned many years before. The musicians and doorkeepers, or Levites who guard the temple, do not need to leave their assigned places because the rest of their fellow Levites prepare the offerings for them.

At that time, the priests and Levites prepare everything they need to worship Yahweh. They celebrate the Passover festival and make burnt offerings on Yahweh's altar. The people do all this as King Josiah commanded them. All the people present from Israel and Judah celebrate the Passover feast on the first day and then celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread for the next seven days.

No one had celebrated the Passover festival in this way since the time of the prophet Samuel, who lived during the time of King David. Many previous kings in Israel celebrated the Passover festival, but none of the former kings celebrated Passover like King Josiah. Josiah celebrates the Passover with the priests, the Levites, and all the people of Jerusalem, Israel, and Judah in Jerusalem during the 18th year that Josiah rules as king.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

**In the first scene:** Josiah orders all the people to celebrate the Passover feast. Josiah assigns priests and Levites to serve in specific places in their family divisions in the temple. Josiah also tells the Levites to leave the ark in Yahweh's temple and to help the Israelite laypeople celebrate Passover.

**In the second scene:** King Josiah provides lambs and cattle for Passover and other offerings. Josiah's officials, who take care of the temple along with the leaders of the Levites, also provide lambs and cattle for sacrifices.

**In the third scene:** The priests and Levites stand in their places in the temple to help the rest of the Israelite people make offerings and sacrifices to Yahweh. The Levites also make all the preparations for the rest of the Levites and priests, and the musicians and gatekeepers stay in their places because the Levites make preparations for them.

**In the fourth scene:** All the Israelites celebrate Passover according to Yahweh's commands that day, and the people celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread for the next seven days. No one had celebrated Passover in this way since the time of the prophet Samuel. Josiah celebrates Passover with the priests, Levites, and all the people from Jerusalem and Judah and Israel in the 18th year that Josiah rules as king.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Josiah
* Priests
* Levites
* Israelites who are not Levites
* Officials in charge of the temple: Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel
* Levite leaders: Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad
* Musicians
* And doorkeepers

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Josiah commands all the people to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem. The Levites kill the lambs for Passover offerings on the 14th day of the first month of the year in the Israelite calendar, which happens in our month of March or April. Yahweh had already told the people to celebrate Passover on this day each year. Josiah chooses priests to perform specific duties in the temple and encourages the priests to serve Yahweh and the Israelite people well.

Josiah then gives orders to the Levites. Yahweh consecrated or set the Levites apart for a special duty to serve Yahweh in the temple alongside the priests. Josiah tells the Levites, "Place the ark in the temple that King David's son Solomon built. Do not carry the ark on your shoulders anymore. Now, get ready to serve Yahweh and the Israelite people. King David and his son Solomon wrote down instructions for you to organize your families into divisions. Each division should stand in its place in the temple to help the laypeople. You Levites will kill the lambs, make yourselves pure, and prepare the lambs for the Israelite laypeople as Yahweh commanded through Moses."

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story where one person gives commands to another person about what that person will do in the future. How do you talk about actions that will happen in the future but have not happened yet? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the storyteller pauses the action to talk about how Josiah and Josiah's leaders provide animals for offerings. King Josiah provides from his own flocks 30,000 lambs and goats as Passover offerings for the lay people. Josiah also provides 3,000 cattle from his own herds for other offerings. Josiah's officials freely give more Passover offerings and cattle for the priests and Levites. Hilkiah the high priest, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the officials in charge of the temple, give the priests 2,600 Passover offerings and 300 cattle. The leaders of the Levites, including Conaniah with his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, along with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, give the Levites 5,000 Passover offerings and 500 cattle.

In the third scene, the storyteller continues the action. The priests and Levites obey Josiah's instructions and stand in their places in the temple so they can help the Israelite laypeople. The Levites kill the Passover offerings and probably put the blood in bowls to hand to the priests. The priests splash the blood on the altar while the Levites remove the skin from the Passover animals. The Levites kill and set aside other animals that the Levites prepare to be burnt offerings, and the cattle that the Levites will boil for other offerings. The Levites give these other animals to the laypeople according to their family divisions so the people can offer the animals the way Yahweh commands in the Book of Moses.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story where one person gives instructions to another person, but then the storyteller stops the action to give more details. Then the second person continues the action when he obeys the instructions from the first person. How will you help your audience understand the timing of this story? Pause this audio here.

Stop and do this activity as a group: Act out the order of events in this passage to make sure you understand when each event happens. Pause this audio here.

The Levites roast the Passover offerings over a fire as Yahweh commanded, but the Levites boil the cattle in pots, caldrons, and pans. A pot is a deep, round utensil with a wide opening that people use to boil food in water. A caldron is a deep, round\-bottomed, two\-handled cooking pot. A pan is probably a wide bowl. People use pots, caldrons, and pans to boil food in water. The Levites serve the meat from the Passover offerings and the meat from the boiled cattle to the laypeople right away. After the Levites finish all the preparations for the laypeople, the Levites make preparations for themselves and for the priests. The Levites do this because the priests are busy at the altar offering burnt offerings and fat portions to Yahweh from morning to evening. Burnt offerings refer to animals that the priests burn completely on the altar. The people eat the meat from some of the other animals they offer to Yahweh, but the people give the fat portions to the priests to burn on the altar. So the Levites make the preparations for themselves and for the priests, Aaron's descendants.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In this story, the storyteller talks about Passover offerings, burnt offerings, and other offerings. Discuss how you will describe the differences between these types of offerings. Pause this audio here.

The musicians or singers, who are descendants of Asaph, stand in the places that King David Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, King David's seer, assigned to the musicians many years before. The doorkeepers, Levites who guard the gates of the temple, do not leave their places because their fellow Levites prepare everything for the doorkeepers.

In the fourth scene, all the priests and Levites worship Yahweh at that time. The priests and Levites help all the Israelites who are present to celebrate Passover and make burnt offerings on Yahweh's altar as King Josiah ordered. The Israelites who participate celebrate Passover and then celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The Feast of Unleavened Bread began on the day of Passover and lasted seven days. No one had celebrated Passover in this way since the time of the prophet Samuel. None of the kings from Israel or Judah celebrated the Passover as Josiah does with the priests, the Levites, and the people from Jerusalem, Judah, and Israel. The people celebrate this Passover during the 18th year that Josiah rules as king.

Stop here and discuss as a group: No one before Josiah celebrated Passover in the same way that Josiah celebrated. Josiah obeyed Yahweh's instructions about how to celebrate Passover very closely, and no one else had obeyed so carefully. How will you talk about how no one celebrated Passover "in the same way" as Josiah? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text
------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Josiah
* Priests
* Levites
* Israelites who are not Levites
* Officials in charge of the temple: Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel
* Levite leaders: Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad
* Musicians
* And doorkeepers

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Josiah commands all the people to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem. The Levites kill the lambs for Passover offerings on the 14th day of the first month of the year in the Israelite calendar. Josiah chooses priests to perform specific duties in the temple and encourages the priests to serve Yahweh and the Israelite people well. Josiah then gives orders to the Levites. Yahweh consecrated or set the Levites apart to serve Yahweh in the temple alongside the priests. Josiah tells the Levites, "Place the ark in the temple that King David's son Solomon built. Do not carry the ark on your shoulders anymore. Now, get ready to serve Yahweh and the Israelite people. King David and his son Solomon wrote down instructions for you to organize your families into divisions. Each division should stand in its place in the temple to help the laypeople. You Levites will kill the lambs, make yourselves pure, and prepare the lambs for the Israelite laypeople as Yahweh commanded through Moses."

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel confident that the priests and Levites will obey my instructions to celebrate Passover the way Yahweh commands; or
* I feel pleased that the Israelite people will be able to make Passover offerings with the Levites' help; or
* I feel hopeful that, because we make these sacrifices, Yahweh might forgive the people and not punish them so severely.

Ask the people playing the priests and Levites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We are happy to serve Yahweh in the temple in the way that Yahweh commands; or
* We feel excited to obey King Josiah and to help our people celebrate Passover in the right way at the right time.

Continue the drama.

King Josiah provides from his own flocks 30,000 animals for the laypeople to make Passover offerings. Josiah also provides 3,000 cattle from his own herds for other offerings. Josiah's officials freely give more Passover offerings and cattle for the priests and Levites. Hilkiah the high priest, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the officials in charge of the temple, give the priests 2,600 Passover offerings and 300 cattle. The leaders of the Levites, including Conaniah with his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, along with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, give the Levites 5,000 Passover offerings and 500 cattle.

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing the officials in charge of the temple and the leaders of the Levites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel happy to give some of our animals for our fellow priests and Levites to use in their offerings; or
* We feel certain that Yahweh will be pleased with our generous gifts; or
* We feel hopeful that King Josiah will think well of us because we choose to be generous just like the king.

Continue the drama.

The priests and Levites obey Josiah's instructions and stand in their places in the temple so they can help the Israelite laypeople. The Levites kill the Passover lambs and hand the blood to the priests, who splash the blood from the lambs on the altar while the Levites remove the skin from the lambs. The Levites set aside the animals that the Levites prepare to be burnt offerings and the cattle that the Levites will boil for other offerings. The Levites give these animals to the Israelites according to their family divisions so the people can offer the animals in the way Yahweh commands in the Book of Moses. The Levites roast the Passover lambs over a fire as Yahweh commanded, but the Levites boil the cattle in pots, caldrons, and pans. The Levites serve the meat from the Passover lamb and the meat from the boiled cattle to the Israelites right away.

Ask the people playing the Israelites who are not Levites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel grateful that the priests and Levites help us make offerings to Yahweh; or
* We feel excited to celebrate Passover together in the way Yahweh commands.

Continue the drama.

After the Levites finish all the preparations for the Israelites, the Levites make preparations for themselves and for the priests. The Levites do this because the priests are busy at the altar, presenting burnt offerings and fat portions to Yahweh from morning to evening. So the Levites make the preparations for themselves and for the priests, Aaron's descendants. The musicians or singers, who are descendants of Asaph, stand in the places that King David, along with Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, King David's seer, assigned to them. The gatekeepers do not leave their places because their fellow Levites prepare everything for the gatekeepers.

Pause the drama. Ask the people playing musicians and gatekeepers, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

* We feel grateful that our fellow Levites take care of the preparations for Passover so we can keep serving in our assigned places; or
* We feel excited to serve Yahweh in our specific ways.

Continue the drama.

At this time, the priests and Levites complete everything they need to worship Yahweh on Passover and to make burnt offerings on Yahweh's altar. The priests and Levites do all this as King Josiah commanded them. All the people present from Israel and Judah celebrate the Passover feast and then the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days. No one had celebrated the Passover feast in this way since the time of the prophet Samuel. Josiah celebrates the Passover with the priests, the Levites, and all the people of Jerusalem, Israel, and Judah in Jerusalem during the 18th year that Josiah rules as king.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing King Josiah, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

* I feel peaceful because my people obey Yahweh and celebrate Passover exactly the way Yahweh commands; or
* I feel pleased because I obeyed Yahweh, and I know Yahweh will not punish me; or
* I feel hopeful that maybe Yahweh will not act so harshly and will not send disaster because the people obeyed by celebrating Passover according to Yahweh's commands.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

If you have already translated 2 Kings 23:21–23, which has some of the same information, stop here as a group and listen to your translation. Pause this audio here.

King Josiah commands the people to celebrate **Passover** in Jerusalem to honor **Yahweh**. The people kill **lambs** for Passover on the 14th day of the first month of the year. Passover is an important Jewish festival that reminds the Israelites of how Yahweh rescued the Israelites from Egypt. People also call Passover the **Festival or Feast of Unleavened Bread** because people celebrate both feasts at the same time. **Jerusalem** is the most important city of the Jewish people. Yahweh is the name God gives himself, and this name reminds people about the covenant God made with the Israelites at the time of Moses. A lamb is a young sheep, or an animal with four legs, hooves, and a thick, woolly coat. In the Bible, people often offer lambs as sacrifices to Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases for Passover, Festival of Unleavened Bread, Jerusalem, Yahweh, and lamb as you used in previous passages. For more information on Passover, Jerusalem, and Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a lamb if necessary. Pause this audio here.

King Josiah chooses **priests** to perform specific duties in the **temple**. Priests were from the Israelite tribe of Levi, and all the priests came from Aaron's family line. Priests were people who worked in the temple. Priests offered sacrifices on behalf of the people and taught the people how to live. The temple is the place where the Israelites worship God, and priests offer sacrifices in the temple. Use the same words or phrases for priest and for temple as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest and temple, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Josiah also gives orders to the **Levites**. Levites were people who belonged to the Israelite tribe of Levi but not to Aaron's family line. Levites helped the priests take care of the temple and taught the people of **Israel**. Israel is the name of the territory where the Israelites lived. Yahweh **consecrated** or set the Levites apart for special service to Yahweh. People may also consecrate themselves when they perform rituals to make themselves pure. Use the same words or phrases for Levite, Israel, and consecrate as you used in previous passages. For more information on Levite, Israel, and consecrate, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Josiah tells the Levites to leave the sacred or **holy** **ark** in the temple and not to carry the ark on their shoulders. People dedicate or set apart holy objects to Yahweh. The "ark," or the ark of the covenant, is a wooden box that is a symbol to the Israelites of Yahweh's presence. Use the same words or phrases for holy and ark as you used in previous passages. For more information on **holy** and **ark of the covenant**, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the ark in the temple if necessary. Pause this audio here.

Josiah tells the Levites to stand in the **Holy Place** to get ready to serve Yahweh their **God** and the Israelite people. The holy place can refer to any place in the tabernacle where the priests did their work. God is the most powerful spiritual being. Josiah tells the Levites to be ready to do the work that **King** **David** and David's son **Solomon** assigned to each Levite division. David and Solomon wrote instructions and organized families of Levites into larger groups that people call divisions. Each division takes responsibility for specific duties in the temple. David was the second king of Israel, and Solomon was David's son and the next king after David. A king is someone who rules over a city or territory. Use the same words or phrases for God, Holy Place, David, Solomon, and king as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, Holy Place, David, and king, refer to the Master Glossary.

Josiah tells the Levites to stand in specific places in the temple so they can help the "people who are not Levites." To celebrate Passover, the Israelites who are not Levites need the priests and Levites to help the people make offerings to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will talk about \*\*"\*\*people who are not Levites." If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Josiah, the officials in charge of the temple, and the leaders of the Levites provide **lambs** and **young goats** to be Passover offerings and **cattle** for other holy **offerings**. These animals are for the laypeople, priests, and Levites. Lambs and young goats are animals with four legs that people use for meat and milk. In the Bible, people sometimes sacrifice lambs or young goats as an offering to Yahweh for Passover. Cattle refers to more than one cow or ox. Cows and oxen are both four\-legged animals with hooves that people use for meat, milk, and to carry heavy loads. An offering is a gift or sacrifice that people offer to God, usually in the temple. People can make offerings for many reasons. Use the same words or phrases for lamb, young goat, cattle, and offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a goat and cattle, if necessary. Pause this audio here.

The Levites **slaughter** the lambs for Passover and give the blood to the priests, who **splash** the **blood** onto the **altar**. Slaughter is a special word that people use to talk about killing an animal for sacrifice. The priests splashed or threw the blood onto the altar from the bowls of blood. An altar is a place where people make offerings or sacrifices to God. In the Bible, blood symbolizes the breath of life. Blood was an important part of the sacrifices the Israelites made to God. Use the same words or phrases for slaughter, splash, altar, and blood as you used in previous passages. For more information on altar and blood, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Levites set aside the animals for **burnt offerings** so the people could make sacrifices according to the Book of Moses. A burnt offering is a form of sacrifice that people bring to God. When a person brings a burnt offering to God, that person burns an animal completely on the altar. People make burnt offerings to show their devotion to God. The Book of Moses probably refers to the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible, which Moses wrote. Use the same words or phrases for "burnt offering" and "Book or **Scroll** of Moses" as you used in previous passages. For more information on burnt offering and scroll, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Levites roast the Passover offerings over fire, but the Levites boil the cattle for other offerings in pots, caldrons, and pans. A pot is a deep utensil with a wide opening that people use to boil food in water. A caldron is a deep, round\-bottomed, two\-handled cooking pot. A pan is probably a wide bowl.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a pot, a caldron, and a pan. Discuss what words or phrases you will use for **pot**, **caldron**, and **pan**. Since these objects all have the same use, you may use the same general word for pot, caldron, and pan if you would like. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The Levites make preparations for Passover for the priests, who are **descendants** of Aaron. A person's descendants are his children, grandchildren, and all future generations from the same family line. Use the same word or phrase for descendants as you used in previous passages. For more information on descendants, refer to the Master Glossary.

The **musicians** and **doorkeepers** did not leave their assigned places because the Levites made preparations for them. A musician is a person who plays a musical instrument or sings. A gatekeeper is a person who guards the entrance to a specific place. Use the same words or phrases for musician and doorkeeper as you used in previous passages.

Josiah and the people celebrate the Passover in the way that Yahweh commands. No one had celebrated Passover in this same way since the days that Samuel the **prophet** lived. A prophet is a person who gives messages from God to the people. Samuel the prophet lived around the time of King David. Use the same word or phrase for prophet as you used in previous passages. For more information on prophet, refer to the Master Glossary.

## 2 Chronicles 35:20–27 (id: eng-2ch-p69-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

In this step, hear 2 Chronicles 35:20–27 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:20–27 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:20–27 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passage, King Josiah commanded all the priests, Levites, and people from Israel and Judah to celebrate the Passover festival in Jerusalem to honor Yahweh. No one had celebrated Passover in the same way since the time of the prophet Samuel.

If you have already translated 2 Kings 23:28–30, which contains some of the same information, listen to your translation as a group. Pause this audio here.

This passage probably takes place about 13 or 14 years after King Josiah restored the temple and celebrated Passover with all the people. Neco, the king of Egypt, comes with his army to the city of Carchemish near the Euphrates River. Carchemish is on the west bank of the Euphrates River. From another story in the Bible, we know that King Neco probably goes to Carchemish to help the king of Assyria fight against Babylon. Assyria was a powerful kingdom that had previously conquered the kingdom of Israel. Even though the Assyrians did not conquer the kingdom of Judah, the Assyrians still sometimes showed that they were powerful and required the people of Judah to serve them by paying the Assyrians money. The kings of Judah did not like Assyria. Babylon was a kingdom that eventually conquered Assyria and later conquered the kingdom of Judah. The King of Egypt probably wants to help Assyria fight against Babylon because King Neco does not want the Babylonians to come to Egypt.

Stop here as a group and look at a map that includes Egypt, Judah, Carchemish, Assyria, Babylon, and the Euphrates River. Pause this audio here.

King Josiah takes the Israelite army to fight against King Neco. Josiah probably goes to fight against Neco because King Josiah does not want Neco to help the people of Assyria. Josiah may support the Babylonians instead of the Assyrians, or Josiah may want to keep the Egyptians out of Judah. But Neco sends men to tell Josiah that Neco does not want to fight against Josiah. Neco asks Josiah what disagreement exists between Neco and Josiah. Neco does not plan to attack Judah because Neco plans to fight against another enemy nation. Neco even tells Josiah that God told Neco to hurry. Neco says God is on the Egyptians' side and Josiah should not oppose Neco. If Josiah interferes, God will destroy Josiah.

However, King Josiah does not stop his attack against King Neco. Josiah puts on different clothes so that no one will recognize Josiah. Josiah does not listen to God's words through Neco. Instead, Josiah takes his army to the plain of Megiddo to fight against King Neco's army. People also call the plain of Megiddo the Jezreel Valley. The city of Megiddo is in the Jezreel Valley about 40 kilometers southwest of the southern tip of the Sea of Galilee. Megiddo is along the main route from Egypt to Syria. The nation that controls Megiddo has access to trade routes that go north, south, and east, so many armies fight important battles at this location.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of the city of Megiddo in the Jezreel Valley. Pause this audio here.

During the battle, some of King Neco's soldiers fight with arrows. People call these soldiers archers. Archers use a bow to shoot arrows. A bow is a curved piece of wood connected by a taut string. Arrows have wooden shafts with a sharp point made of wood or metal at one end. Some of Neco's archers shoot at and hit King Josiah with arrows. In the story in 2 Kings 23:28–30, the storyteller says Neco kills Josiah, but here the storyteller says Neco's archers actually kill Josiah.

King Josiah tells some of his officers to take Josiah away from the battlefield because Josiah has a severe injury. The officers take Josiah out of his chariot and place Josiah in Josiah's other chariot. A chariot is a two\-wheeled vehicle that horses pull, and people often use chariots during battle. Josiah's first chariot probably carried only one or two people. The other chariot may be bigger to carry supplies during battle. Josiah's officers probably move Josiah to the second chariot to provide more space and comfort for the injured king.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a bow and arrow and a chariot. Pause this audio here.

Josiah's officers take Josiah back to Jerusalem, where Josiah dies. In the 2 Kings story, the storyteller says Josiah dies in Megiddo, but Josiah probably did not die right away. Josiah probably receives a severe wound in Megiddo and dies slowly on the way to Jerusalem. Josiah's people bury Josiah in the royal cemetery near Josiah's ancestors. In a previous passage, a prophet told Josiah that Josiah would die peacefully and that Josiah's people would bury Josiah with Josiah's ancestors. Josiah dies close to Jerusalem, and Josiah dies in the presence of his own soldiers. In this way, Josiah's death was peaceful, and the people bury Josiah with honor. All the people who live in Jerusalem and in the other towns in Judah mourn Josiah's death.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How do people mourn the death of a leader in your culture? Pause this audio here.

The prophet Jeremiah writes laments or funeral songs to honor Josiah. Jeremiah was a prophet who gave the people messages from God. Jeremiah lived around the same time as Josiah. People use laments to mourn the death of someone or to grieve the loss of something. Israelite tradition requires all the male and female singers to remember and honor Josiah with these songs from the time of Josiah's death through the time the storyteller writes about Josiah. Someone writes these funeral songs in the book or scroll that people call The Book of Laments. This is not the book that Jeremiah wrote that people call Lamentations in the Old Testament. We do not have a copy of the Laments book today.

Josiah did many other things while Josiah was king of Judah. Josiah remained faithful to Yahweh because Josiah obeyed the Law of Yahweh. People find the Law of Yahweh in the first five books of the Old Testament. Because Moses wrote these books, people sometimes call these books the Law of Moses. People wrote down all the things Josiah did, from the beginning to the end of Josiah's reign as king, in the "Book or Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah." This is not the same book as 1 and 2 Kings in the Old Testament. We no longer have a copy of the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 35:20–27 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

**In the first scene:** Some time after Josiah restored the temple and celebrated Passover, Neco, king of Egypt, brings the Egyptian army to the city of Carchemish. King Josiah goes to meet Neco for battle, but Neco sends messengers to tell Josiah that Neco does not want to fight Josiah. God told Neco to hurry and fight another enemy, and if Josiah interferes, God will destroy Josiah.

**In the second scene:** King Josiah refuses to listen to God's words through Neco. Josiah goes to battle against Neco, but Neco's archers shoot Josiah with arrows. Josiah tells officials to take Josiah away from the battle because Josiah is injured, and the military officers take Josiah back to Jerusalem, where Josiah dies.

**In the third scene:** All the people mourn for Josiah. The prophet Jeremiah writes a lament about Josiah. Tradition still requires singers to sing these songs of lament about Josiah. Someone writes these songs in The Book of Laments.

**In the fourth scene:** Josiah did many other things while he was king, and Josiah remained faithful to obey Yahweh's law. Someone writes down all the things that Josiah did as king, from the beginning to the end of Josiah's reign, in the book about the kings of Israel and Judah.

The characters in this passage are:

* King Josiah
* King Neco of Egypt
* Neco's messengers
* Josiah's soldiers and officers who took Josiah back to Jerusalem
* Neco's soldiers
* People from Jerusalem and Judah
* And Jeremiah

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, around 13 or 14 years after Josiah restored the temple and celebrated Passover, King Neco of Egypt brings soldiers towards the city of Carchemish on the Euphrates River. Josiah marches out to meet Neco in battle. But Neco sends messengers to King Josiah, who say, "King of Judah, what reason do we have to fight? I have not come to fight against you today. I want to fight against another enemy. God told me to do this quickly. I am doing what God told me to do, so do not fight against me. If you do fight me, God will destroy you." Neco is at war with another house. In this case, a "house" can describe a family or another nation. When Neco asks Josiah the question about what reason they have to fight, Neco does not actually expect Josiah to answer the question. Neco wants to emphasize that Neco does not wish to fight Josiah and the people of Judah.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How do people in your culture emphasize important points that they want other people to understand? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, despite Neco's message, Josiah refuses to turn away from battle against Neco. Josiah puts on different clothes so no one will recognize Josiah in the battle. Josiah refuses to listen to the words that Neco spoke. The storyteller says Neco's words are from the "mouth of God." The storyteller uses special language to say that what Neco says are God's own words. Josiah takes his army and goes to fight against Neco near the plain of Megiddo. A plain is a large area of flat land with few trees. However, Neco's archers shoot arrows that hit and severely injure Josiah.

Josiah tells his servants, "Take me away from the battle because I am severely injured." The servants that Josiah speaks to are probably Josiah's military officers. Josiah's officers take Josiah out of his chariot and move Josiah to Josiah's other chariot. The officers bring Josiah to Jerusalem, and Josiah dies. Josiah's people bury Josiah in the royal cemetery close to Josiah's ancestors, and all the people from Jerusalem and Judah mourn for Josiah. When people bury the body of a king, the people put the dead body in a natural cave or room that someone carved out of a rock.

In the third scene, the prophet Jeremiah writes laments, or funeral songs, for Josiah. Male and female singers still sing these laments at the time the storyteller writes about Josiah. The singers do this according to tradition to honor Josiah. Someone writes the laments that Jeremiah wrote in The Book of Laments.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Tell a story about people who mourn for someone who dies. How do people in your culture talk about a person whom they respect and want to honor after that person dies? Pause this audio here.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller uses a common formula to summarize Josiah's reign. In the Bible, storytellers often talk about all that a king does during his reign in this same way after the king dies.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your culture, after a ruler dies, how do people talk about the things the ruler did while the ruler was alive? Pause this audio here.

Josiah did many other things during Josiah's reign as king. Josiah faithfully obeyed the Law of Yahweh that Moses wrote down. Someone wrote all the things that Josiah did, from the beginning to the end of Josiah's reign, in the Book or Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

After Josiah restored the **temple**, **King** Neco of Egypt marched towards the city of Carchemish. The temple is the place where the Israelites worship God. A king is someone who rules over a city or territory. **Judah** is the name of a region in Israel where Josiah was king. Use the same word or phrase for temple, king, and Judah as you used in previous passages. For more information on temple, king, and Judah, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Neco sends messengers to Josiah, who say Josiah and Neco do not need to fight. Neco plans to attack a different house. A house refers to a particular family or people group.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will say that Neco plans to attack a different "**house**," or group of people. For more information, refer to **household** in the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

Neco's messengers also tell Josiah that **God** sent them to fight another enemy and told them to hurry. God is the most powerful spiritual being, and God created everything and has power over everything. Use the same word or phrase for God as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Josiah refused to listen to Neco and marched into battle, but some of Neco's archers shot Josiah. An archer is a person who shoots with a bow and arrows.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a bow and arrow. Discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **archer**. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Josiah's servants put Josiah in a **chariot**. The word the storyteller uses can mean servants or military officers. You may choose to use the word servant or officer here. A chariot is a two\-wheeled vehicle that horses pull. People often use chariots during battle. Use the same word or phrase for chariot as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and discuss what word you will use: **servants** or **officers**. If you choose to use the word servant, look up servant in the Master Glossary for more information. Use the same word or phrase for servant as you used in previous passages. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a chariot, if necessary. Pause this audio here.

Josiah's officers take Josiah back to **Jerusalem**. Jerusalem is the name of the most important city to the Jewish people. Use the same word or phrase for **Jerusalem** as you used in previous passages. For more information on Jerusalem, refer to the Master Glossary.

The people in Jerusalem bury Josiah in the royal cemetery or the **tombs** of Josiah's **fathers**. The word "fathers" refers to a person's **ancestors**. A tomb is the name for a place where people bury a dead person. An ancestor is a person from someone's family who lived before that person. Use the same word or phrase for tomb and father or ancestor as you used in previous passages. For more information on tomb, refer to the Master Glossary.

The prophet Jeremiah writes laments to honor Josiah after Josiah's death. A lament is a song people sing to mourn the death of someone or to grieve the loss of something.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for **lament**. Look up lament in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Josiah stayed faithful to Yahweh and obeyed all Yahweh's commands in the "**Law** of **Yahweh**." The Law of Yahweh refers to the Pentateuch, or the first five books in the Old Testament. Yahweh gave this law to Moses, and Moses wrote the law in these books. People sometimes call the Law of Yahweh the "Law of Moses." Use the same word or phrase for "Law of Yahweh" as you used in previous passages. For more information on law and Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Someone writes all the things that Josiah did as king, from the beginning to the end of Josiah's reign, in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. This book is not the same as the books of 1 and 2 Kings in the Old Testament. We no longer have copies of this book. Use the same word or phrase for "Book or Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah\*\*"\*\* as you used in previous passages. For more information on **Israel** and **scroll**, refer to the Master Glossary.

## 2 Chronicles 36:1–16 (id: eng-2ch-p70-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.

Setting the Stage
-----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 36:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the last passage, King Josiah attacked King Neco of Egypt when Neco marched north with his army. Even though Yahweh warned Josiah through Neco to stay away, Josiah attacked the Egyptians anyway. Egyptian archers wounded Josiah badly in battle, and Josiah died.

After the people grieve the loss of their king, the people of Judah make Josiah's son Jehoahaz the new king. Jehoahaz is 23 years old when he begins to rule from Jerusalem. Jehoahaz rules for only three months. Normally, the oldest son becomes king after his father dies. However, the people of Judah choose Jehoahaz, the youngest son, to rule instead.

While Jehoahaz is king, King Neco of Egypt captures Jehoahaz and makes him a prisoner to stop Jehoahaz from ruling in Jerusalem. King Neco demands that the people of Judah pay Neco a fine of 100 talents, or 3,400 kilograms, of silver and 1 talent, or 34 kilograms, of gold. King Neco then forces Josiah's son Eliakim to be the next king of Judah. The king of Egypt has so much power that Neco forces Eliakim to change his name to Jehoiakim. King Neco then brings Jehoahaz to the land of Egypt as a prisoner.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In this passage, leaders of powerful nations controlled who became king in Judah. In your culture, how do outside groups or powerful leaders influence decisions in your community? Pause this audio here.

Jehoiakim, the older brother of Jehoahaz, is 25 years old when he begins to rule from Jerusalem. Jehoiakim rules for 11 years as the king of Judah. Jehoiakim does evil in the eyes of Yahweh or does not live in a way that pleases Yahweh. While Jehoiakim is king, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacks Judah. Nebuchadnezzar is not only king of the city of Babylon but of the whole territory of Babylon.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a map of the kingdom of Judah and the nation of Babylon during the time of Jehoiakim. Pause this audio here.

Nebuchadnezzar defeats Jehoiakim and binds him with bronze chains. It is unclear whether the king of Babylon kills Jehoiakim in Jerusalem or if he takes Jehoiakim as a prisoner to the city of Babylon.

After Nebuchadnezzar defeats Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar takes objects out of the temple of Yahweh and brings them to Babylon. It is unclear whether Nebuchadnezzar places the temple objects in his personal palace or in a temple in Babylon. The storyteller says we can read more about King Jehoiakim and his time as king in the book called The Book or Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah. This book no longer exists. The storyteller emphasizes that Jehoiakim's acts are abominations, or detestable and horrible actions against Yahweh. Yahweh hates these acts. After Jehoiakim dies, his son Jehoiachin becomes the next king of Judah.

Jehoiachin rules from Jerusalem when he is only 18 years old. Jehoiachin rules as king for three months. Like his father, Jehoiachin does not live in a way that pleases Yahweh. In the spring, King Nebuchadnezzar orders his army to surround Jerusalem and bring Jehoiachin to Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon. We know from 2 Kings 24:10–17 that Jehoiachin surrenders and Nebuchadnezzar takes Jehoiachin, Jehoiachin's family, and Jehoiachin's government officials as prisoners to Babylon. While in Jerusalem, the Babylonian army also takes many precious objects from the temple of Yahweh. After this, Nebuchadnezzar chooses Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah, the brother of Jehoiachin's father, to replace Jehoiachin as king of Judah.

Zedekiah becomes king of Judah at age 21 and rules for 11 years in Jerusalem. Zedekiah does not live in a way that pleases Yahweh. The storyteller notes that Zedekiah intentionally ignored what Yahweh said through the prophet Jeremiah. In chapter 21 of the book of Jeremiah, Jeremiah repeatedly urged Zedekiah to submit to Babylon rather than ask for help from Egypt, but Zedekiah did not listen. Zedekiah also rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar after Nebuchadnezzar made him swear by the name of Yahweh that Zedekiah would be loyal to him. It is normal for leaders to take an oath, or swear by the name of a person's god, when leaders make formal promises or agreements with each other. But when Zedekiah breaks his oath and rebels, Zedekiah shows how stiff\-necked, or stubborn, Zedekiah truly is. Zedekiah hardens his heart or stubbornly refuses to obey Yahweh, the God of Israel.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what promises or oaths do people consider unbreakable? What happens if someone breaks one of these promises or oaths? Pause this audio here.

In addition, all of the leaders of the priests and the people of Judah abandon Yahweh for other gods. These people do the same evil practices that other nations are doing, acts that Yahweh hates. These practices make the temple of Yahweh ceremonially unclean or unfit for worship. Yahweh consecrated, or set apart, the temple in Jerusalem for himself, but the leaders choose to make it unclean by bringing in false gods.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what kinds of things do people consider to be sacred or set apart? How would someone make those things or places unclean? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh shows compassion on Yahweh's people and on his temple by sending many messengers to speak to his people. Even though the prophets warn the people to turn back to Yahweh, the people do not respect the prophets and laugh at them instead. Finally, Yahweh becomes so angry with his people that nothing can stop Yahweh from judging Judah.

Defining the Scenes
-------------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 36:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has five scenes.

**In the first scene:** The people of Judah make Josiah's son, Jehoahaz, the next king. Jehoahaz does not follow Yahweh. Jehoahaz rules for three months before King Neco takes Jehoahaz as a prisoner to Egypt. King Neco makes the people of Judah pay Neco a large fine. King Neco makes Jehoiakim, the brother of Jehoahaz, the next king of Judah.

**In the second scene:** Jehoiakim does not follow Yahweh and rules as king for 11 years. While Jehoiakim is king, Nebuchadnezzar's army attacks Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar binds Jehoiakim in metal chains. Nebuchadnezzar takes many of the temple treasures to Nebuchadnezzar's home in Babylon. Jehoiachin, the son of Jehoiakim, becomes the next king of Judah.

**In the third scene:** Jehoiachin rules for three months and does not obey Yahweh. Nebuchadnezzar's army attacks Jerusalem again, takes Jehoiachin prisoner, and carries more temple treasures to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar then appoints Zedekiah as king, who swears by Yahweh's name to be loyal to Nebuchadnezzar.

**In the fourth scene:** Zedekiah is king for 11 years, and Zedekiah does not follow Yahweh. Zedekiah does not listen to Jeremiah. Instead, Zedekiah breaks his vow and rebels against Nebuchadnezzar.

**In the fifth scene:** The leaders and priests of Judah do not listen to Yahweh either. Instead, they make the temple unclean by worshiping false gods. Yahweh sends prophets to talk to them, but the people do not listen. Instead, they laugh at the prophets. Yahweh becomes so angry with his people that no one can stop Yahweh from destroying the people.

The characters in this passage are:

* Jehoahaz
* King Neco of Egypt
* Jehoiakim
* King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon
* The Babylonian army
* Jehoiachin
* Zedekiah
* Jeremiah, the prophet
* Yahweh
* The people of Judah
* And leaders of the priests of Judah

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

After Josiah, only four kings ruled Judah. The storyteller briefly introduces each king and what happened during each king's reign.

The storyteller introduces Jehoahaz in the usual pattern: his name, age, city, and how long he ruled. Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, becomes king at 23 and rules from Jerusalem for three months.

After three months, King Neco of Egypt attacks Judah with his army and captures Jehoahaz so that Jehoahaz can no longer rule as the king of Judah.

King Neco demands that the people of Judah pay Neco 100 talents of silver and 1 talent of gold—about 3,400 kilograms of silver and 34 kilograms of gold.

King Neco appoints Josiah's other son, Eliakim, to be the next king of Judah. King Neco forces Eliakim to change his name to Jehoiakim. King Neco brings Jehoahaz back to Egypt as a prisoner.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of the kingdom of Judah in relation to Egypt. Pause this audio here.

Jehoiakim becomes king when he is 25 years old. Jehoiakim reigns from Jerusalem, and he rules as king for 11 years. Jehoiakim does evil in the sight of Yahweh, or lives in a way that does not please Yahweh.

During Jehoiakim's reign, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacks Judah, defeats Jehoiakim, and binds him with metal chains to take Jehoiakim away. While in Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar also takes valuable items that the people used to serve inside the temple. Nebuchadnezzar takes the items to his palace in Babylon.

Stop here and look, as a group, at a map of the kingdom of Judah and the nation of Babylon during the time of Jehoiakim. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller tells us we can find all of Jehoiakim's acts as king in a book called "The Book or Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah." The storyteller emphasizes that Jehoiakim's acts were abominations, or horrible and detestable actions against Yahweh.

Jehoiakim dies, and Jehoiakim's son, Jehoiachin, becomes the next king of Judah. Jehoiachin is only 18 years old when he becomes king. Jehoiachin rules from Jerusalem, and he is king for three months and 10 days. Jehoiachin does evil in the sight of Yahweh, or lives in a way that does not please Yahweh.

In the first part of the year, when kings usually went to war, Nebuchadnezzar sends his army to besiege, or surround, Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar brings Jehoiachin to Babylon as a prisoner. We know from the 2 Kings story that Jehoiachin surrendered. The Babylonian army raids the temple again and takes many of its valuable treasures. It is important to remember that the temple had a storeroom where kings kept valuable treasures.

King Nebuchadnezzar makes Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah, who is Jehoiakim's brother, the king of Judah. It is important to note that Nebuchadnezzar forced Zedekiah to swear in the name of Yahweh to be loyal to Nebuchadnezzar. This was a normal custom when kings made formal agreements during this time. However, we do not learn this until later.

Zedekiah is 21 years old when he becomes king. Zedekiah rules from Jerusalem, and he is king for 11 years. Zedekiah does evil in the sight of Yahweh, or lives in a way that does not please Yahweh.

Yahweh sends the prophet Jeremiah to speak to Zedekiah, but Zedekiah does not listen to him. Jeremiah speaks the word of Yahweh, or a message from Yahweh, so Zedekiah directly rejects Yahweh. Even though Zedekiah swore to be loyal to Nebuchadnezzar, Zedekiah decides to rebel against Nebuchadnezzar. Zedekiah becomes stiff\-necked, or stubborn, and Zedekiah hardens his heart, or refuses to listen to Yahweh, even though Yahweh is the God of Israel. By using both expressions, the storyteller is making a strong statement that Zedekiah is very stubborn.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How would you describe someone who is "stiff\-necked" or "hard\-hearted"? Do you have words or examples in your language for someone who is persistently stubborn and refuses to listen? Pause this audio here.

All of the leading priests, or religious leaders who serve in the temple, also refuse to obey Yahweh, and they continue to be more and more unfaithful. The leaders and people of Judah do the same evil practices that other nations do. The people defile the temple, or make the temple ceremonially unclean, by worshiping false gods inside the temple.

The temple was a place Yahweh had consecrated for himself. This means Yahweh made the temple set apart for himself so that Yahweh could live among his people. But Yahweh's people defile his house and make it unfit for worship.

The storyteller says Yahweh has compassion for Yahweh's people and for the place where Yahweh lives among his people, the temple. Yahweh sends prophets many times to warn his people to turn back to Yahweh, but the people do not listen. Instead, the people mock and ridicule the prophets.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story of a time when people mocked or ridiculed an important message. Pay attention to what words you use to describe this kind of reaction. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh becomes so angry with his people that Yahweh decides to destroy them. Yahweh's chosen people were beyond healing, which means no one could change Yahweh's mind.

Filling the Gaps
----------------

Listen to an audio version of 2 Chronicles 36:1–16 in the easiest\-to\-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Jehoahaz becomes the next **king** and rules from **Jerusalem**. A king is someone who rules over a city or territory, like a region or a country. Jerusalem was the capital city of Judah. Use the same words or phrases for king and Jerusalem as you used in previous passages. For more information on king or Jerusalem, refer to the Master Glossary.

Jehoahaz was the king of **Judah**. Judah refers to the southern kingdom of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for Judah as you used in previous passages. For more information on **Judah**, refer to the Master Glossary.

King Neco demands that the people of Judah pay him 100 **talents** of silver and one talent of gold. A talent is a measurement that equals 34 kilograms or 75 pounds. One hundred talents of silver would be around 3,400 kilograms of silver. Use the same word or phrase for talent as you used in previous passages. For more information on talent, refer to the Master Glossary.

The storyteller emphasizes that Jehoiakim's actions were **abominations**, or horrible acts that Yahweh hates. Use the same word or phrase for abominations or horrible acts that Yahweh hates as you used in previous passages.

Jehoiakim became king and did **evil in the eyes of Yahweh**. In other words, Jehoiakim continually disobeyed Yahweh and did not live in a way that was pleasing to Yahweh. Evil is the opposite of good. Be sure to use the same word or phrase for "evil in the eyes of Yahweh" as you used in previous passages. For more information on **evil**, refer to the Master Glossary.

Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, attacks the land of Judah and takes valuable items from the **temple** of **Yahweh**. The temple was the place where the Israelites worshiped Yahweh. In the temple, specially appointed people called priests offered gifts and sacrifices to God on behalf of the people. Yahweh is God's personal name and showed God's special relationship with his people. Use the same words for temple and Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on temple or Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

The storyteller says the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim are in the "**Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah**." This was a historical account of the kings of Israel and Judah; however, the book no longer exists. Be sure to translate "The Book or **Scroll** of the Kings of Israel and Judah" in the same way you did in previous passages. For more information about a scroll, refer to the Master Glossary.

Zedekiah did not humble himself before the **prophet** Jeremiah, which means Zedekiah refused to listen to the **word** of Yahweh. The word of Yahweh is anything Yahweh speaks to people. In this case, Yahweh used prophets, or people who give Yahweh's message to people. Use the same words or phrases for "word of Yahweh" and prophet as you used in previous passages. For more information on word or prophet, refer to the Master Glossary.

Nebuchadnezzar forces Zedekiah to make an **oath** of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar in the name of Yahweh. When someone swears an oath, they say, "I will absolutely keep my promise. If I do not, God may punish me." Zedekiah did not keep his promise to Nebuchadnezzar to be loyal, so Zedekiah broke his oath. In that culture, it was a disgraceful and dangerous thing to break an oath. Use the same word or phrase for oath as you used in previous passages. For more information on oath, refer to the Master Glossary.

The storyteller describes Zedekiah as **stiff\-necked** and says Zedekiah hardened his **heart**. Both expressions are different ways to say that Zedekiah was stubborn and refused to listen. In the Bible, the heart is special language for the place where a person's thoughts, feelings, and decisions happen. Use the same words or phrases for "stiff\-necked" and heart as you used in previous passages. For more information on heart, refer to the Master Glossary.

Zedekiah would not turn to Yahweh, the **God** of **Israel**. God refers to the God who created everything. God is the most powerful spiritual being. This is the God who made a covenant, a special promise, to Abraham and his descendants, the Israelites. Here, Israel refers to the nation of God's chosen people. Use the same words or phrases for God and Israel as you used in previous passages. For more information on God or Israel, refer to the Master Glossary.

Judah's unfaithfulness was so bad that even the leading **priests** were worshiping false gods. Priests are people who served in the temple and offered gifts and sacrifices to God on behalf of the people. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh specially **consecrated** the temple as Yahweh's dwelling place, but the people made it unclean. When God consecrates someone or something, God sets them apart for special service to himself. The person or thing now belongs to God, and it is holy or clean. But the people disobey Yahweh and worship false gods, which defiles the temple or makes it unclean. Use the same word or phrase for consecrate and **defile** as you used in previous passages. For more information on consecrate or defile, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh sends prophets to speak to his people, but the people mock the prophets until Yahweh's **wrath** rises against his people. Wrath is the attitude that God has when God sees sin and evil. God is holy and just. Wrath is stronger than anger, and wrath involves punishing people for their sin. Use the same word or phrase for wrath as you used in previous passages. For more information on wrath, refer to the Master Glossary.

## 2 Chronicles 36:17–23 (id: eng-2ch-p71-v1)

Hear and Heart
--------------

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:
